abstract: Analytic solutions to the information-theoretic evolution equa(cid:173) tion of the connection strength of a three-layer feedforward neural net for visual information processing are presented. The results are (1) the receptive fields of the feature-analysing cells corre(cid:173) spond to the eigenvector of the maximum eigenvalue of the Fred(cid:173) holm integral equation of the first kind derived from the evolution equation of the connection strength; (2) a symmetry-breaking mechanism (parity-violation) has been identified to be respon(cid:173) sible for the changes of the morphology of the receptive field; (3) the conditions for the formation of different morphologies are explicitly identified.

The results are (1) the receptive fields of the feature-analysing cells corre(cid:173) spond to the eigenvector of the maximum eigenvalue of the Fred(cid:173) holm integral equation of the first kind derived from the evolution equation of the connection strength; (2) a symmetry-breaking mechanism (parity-violation) has been identified to be respon(cid:173) sible for the changes of the morphology of the receptive field; (3) the conditions for the formation of different morphologies are explicitly identified.

paragraphs: The paper studies how feature-sensitive receptive fields form in a three-layer feedforward network for visual processing. A receptive field describes the pattern of input to which a cell responds. The authors derive analytic solutions to an information-theoretic equation governing how connection strengths evolve, making the resulting receptive-field structure mathematically explicit.

Their first result connects receptive fields to the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue of a derived Fredholm integral equation. In plain language, the equation identifies a dominant mathematical pattern, and that pattern determines the feature-analyzing cell's receptive field. This links the structure that emerges in the network to the governing learning equation.

The analysis also identifies symmetry breaking, described as parity violation, as the mechanism behind changes in receptive-field shape. The authors explicitly specify conditions under which different shapes form. These results move from describing possible receptive fields to explaining their formation: both the dominant pattern and the changes between forms are tied to properties of the mathematical model.
summary.tldr: Analytic solutions connect visual receptive-field formation to a dominant eigenvector and identify symmetry breaking as a cause of changes in shape.

title: Analytic Solutions to the Formation of Feature-Analysing Cells of a Three-Layer Feedforward Visual Information Processing Neural Net

abstract: This paper proposes ajuzzy neural expert system (FNES) with the following two functions: (1) Generalization of the information derived from the training data and embodiment of knowledge in the form of the fuzzy neural network; (2) Extraction of fuzzy If-Then rules with linguistic relative importance of each proposition in an antecedent (I f -part) from a trained neural network. This paper also gives a method to extract automatically fuzzy If-Then rules from the trained neural network. To prove the effectiveness and validity of the proposed fuzzy neural expert system. a fuzzy neural expert system for medical diagnosis has been developed.

This paper also gives a method to extract automatically fuzzy If-Then rules from the trained neural network. paragraphs: The paper proposes a fuzzy neural expert system that combines learning from examples with automatic extraction of readable rules. Its first function is to generalize information from training data and encode that knowledge in a fuzzy neural network. Its second function is to express the trained network's knowledge as fuzzy If-Then statements.

The extracted rules include linguistic descriptions of the relative importance of propositions in their conditions. An If-Then rule links a set of conditions to a conclusion; indicating how much each condition matters adds information beyond simply listing those conditions. The contribution therefore concerns both the rule itself and the relative contributions of its constituent statements.

The authors describe a method for performing this extraction automatically and develop a medical-diagnosis expert system as an application. The approach matters because it connects a learned numerical model to a form of knowledge that can be inspected as rules. The abstract presents the diagnosis system as a demonstration of the proposal, without reporting a numerical measure of diagnostic performance.
summary.tldr: A fuzzy neural expert system automatically turns learned knowledge into If-Then rules that describe the importance of their conditions.

title: A Neural Expert System with Automated Extraction of Fuzzy If-Then Rules and Its Application to Medical Diagnosis

paragraphs: This paper describes a working electronic system for color constancy: keeping perceived object colors relatively stable when illumination changes. Its computational basis is Land's Retinex theory. In the supplied account, that theory applies the same center-surround operation independently to three color channels, relating color processing to the spatial surroundings of an image location.

The researchers implement the system using three custom chips built with subthreshold analog CMOS technology. Resistive grids on the chips perform the smoothing operation that the algorithm requires. This physical implementation carries out that operation at video rates, making spatial color correction something the hardware can perform on a moving stream of images.

The system was built and successfully tested, producing colors that resemble those of human vision in several respects. The electronic implementation also provides a way to investigate the algorithm's strengths and weaknesses. The contribution therefore joins a perceptual theory with functioning hardware, allowing the proposed computation to be examined through the behavior of an actual color-correction system.
summary.tldr: Three custom analog chips implement Retinex color correction, using resistive grids to perform spatial smoothing at video rates.

title: A VLSI Neural Network for Color Constancy

abstract: In this paper we present a neural network architecture that discovers a recursive decomposition of its input space. Based on a generalization of the modular architecture of Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan, and Hinton (1991), the architecture uses competition among networks to recursively split the input space into nested regions and to learn separate associative mappings within each region. The learning algorithm is shown to perform gradient ascent in a log likelihood function that captures the architecture's hierarchical structure.
originalAbstract: In this paper we present a neural network architecture that discovers a recursive decomposition of its input space. Based on a generalization of the modular architecture of Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan, and Hinton (1991), the architecture uses competition among networks to recursively split the input space into nested regions and to learn separate associative mappings within each region. The learning algorithm is shown to perform gradient ascent in a log likelihood function that captures the architecture's hierarchical structure.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a neural-network architecture that learns to divide its input space recursively. Different networks compete, and that competition produces nested regions of inputs. Each region has its own learned associative mapping, allowing different parts of the overall problem to be handled by different specialist networks.

The recursive structure is central to the approach. A division of the input space can itself be subdivided, producing a hierarchy of increasingly specific regions. This gives the architecture a way to organize specialization at multiple levels. The decomposition is discovered during learning, so the structure of the division is part of what the system learns.

The authors show that the learning algorithm performs gradient ascent on a log-likelihood function that reflects the hierarchy. In practical terms, the updates follow a common probabilistic objective consistent with the architecture's organization. This connects the competition and regional mappings within one mathematical account of learning, rather than leaving the hierarchy as an informal arrangement of separate networks.
summary.tldr: Competing expert networks learn nested input regions and specialized mappings through a hierarchical log-likelihood objective.

title: Hierarchies of adaptive experts

abstract: G/SPLINES is an algorithm for building functional models of data. It uses genetic search to discover combinations of basis functions which are then used to build a least-squares regression model. Because it produces a population of models which evolve over time rather than a single model, it allows analysis not possible with other regression-based approaches.
originalAbstract: G/SPLINES is an algorithm for building functional models of data. It uses genetic search to discover combinations of basis functions which are then used to build a least-squares regression model. Because it produces a population of models which evolve over time rather than a single model, it allows analysis not possible with other regression-based approaches.

paragraphs: G/SPLINES builds mathematical models of data by searching for useful combinations of basis functions. Basis functions are the component functions from which a larger model is assembled. Choosing a combination determines the forms of variation that the fitted model can express, making that selection an important part of the modeling problem.

The algorithm uses genetic search to discover combinations and then constructs a least-squares regression model from them. These two parts address different aspects of fitting: the search explores the model's functional building blocks, while regression fits the resulting model to the observations. The proposed procedure therefore includes the choice of representation within model construction.

A distinctive feature is that G/SPLINES maintains an evolving population of models instead of producing only one model during the search. The authors argue that this population enables additional forms of analysis. The emphasis is on retaining multiple evolving descriptions of the data, making the collection of candidate models part of the analytical output.
summary.tldr: G/SPLINES combines genetic search over basis functions with least-squares fitting to produce an evolving population of regression models.

title: Data Analysis using G/SPLINES

abstract: We present a general formulation for a network of stochastic di(cid:173) rectional units. This formulation is an extension of the Boltzmann machine in which the units are not binary, but take on values in a cyclic range, between 0 and 271' radians. The state of each unit in a Directional-Unit Boltzmann Machine (DUBM) is described by a complex variable, where the phase component specifies a direction; the weights are also complex variables. We associate a quadratic energy function, and corresponding probability, with each DUBM configuration. The conditional distribution of a unit's stochastic state is a circular version of the Gaussian probability distribution, known as the von Mises distribution. In a mean-field approxima(cid:173) tion to a stochastic DUBM, the phase component of a unit's state represents its mean direction, and the magnitude component spec(cid:173) ifies the degree of certainty associated with this direction. This combination of a value and a certainty provides additional repre(cid:173) sentational power in a unit. We describe a learning algorithm and simulations that demonstrate a mean-field DUBM'S ability to learn interesting mappings. Many kinds of information can naturally be represented in terms of angular, or directional, variables. A circular range forms a suitable representation for explicitly directional information, such as wind direction, as well as for information where the underlying range is periodic, such as days of the week or months of the year. In computer vision, tangent fields and optic flow fields are represented as fields of oriented line segments, each of which can be described by a magnitude and direction. Directions can also be used to represent a set of symbolic labels, e.g., object label A at 0, and object label B at 71'/2 radians. We discuss below some advantages of representing symbolic labels with directional units.

paragraphs: The paper extends Boltzmann machines to represent directions rather than binary states. Each unit takes a value around a circle, making the representation suitable for angles and periodic quantities. Examples discussed include wind direction, calendar cycles, and visual fields described by oriented segments.

Both unit states and connection weights are complex variables. A state's phase specifies direction, and a quadratic energy function determines probabilities over network configurations. The conditional distribution for a unit is the von Mises distribution, a circular counterpart of a Gaussian. This gives the network a probabilistic formulation suited to values that wrap around.

In a mean-field approximation, phase describes a unit's mean direction while magnitude expresses certainty about it. A unit therefore carries both an estimate and information about how definite that estimate is. The paper describes a learning algorithm and simulations showing that this approximation can learn mappings. It also discusses directional representations of symbolic labels, extending the proposed use beyond quantities that are inherently angular.
summary.tldr: Directional-unit Boltzmann machines use circular states and complex weights to represent directions together with uncertainty.

title: Directional-Unit Boltzmann Machines

abstract: Motivated by mathematical modeling, analog implementation and distributed simulation of neural networks, we present a definition of asynchronous dynamics of general CT dynamical systems defined by ordinary differential equations, based on notions of local times and communication times. We provide some preliminary results on globally asymptotical convergence of asynchronous dynamics for contractive and monotone CT dynamical systems. When ap(cid:173) plying the results to neural networks, we obtain some conditions that ensure additive-type neural networks to be asynchronizable.
originalAbstract: Motivated by mathematical modeling, analog implementation and distributed simulation of neural networks, we present a definition of asynchronous dynamics of general CT dynamical systems defined by ordinary differential equations, based on notions of local times and communication times. We provide some preliminary results on globally asymptotical convergence of asynchronous dynamics for contractive and monotone CT dynamical systems. When ap(cid:173) plying the results to neural networks, we obtain some conditions that ensure additive-type neural networks to be asynchronizable.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to describe continuous-time neural systems when their components do not operate on a single synchronized schedule. The motivation spans mathematical modeling, analog hardware, and distributed simulation. In each setting, understanding asynchronous behavior requires a precise account of when individual components evolve and when information passes between them.

The authors introduce such a definition for dynamical systems expressed through ordinary differential equations. Their formulation uses local times and communication times, separating a component's own progress from the timing of exchanges with other components. This gives a mathematical basis for studying asynchrony within systems ordinarily described using continuous time.

The paper then provides preliminary convergence results for contractive and monotone systems. These results address conditions under which asynchronous dynamics still approach their limiting behavior from across the system's state space. Applying the analysis to neural networks yields conditions under which additive-type networks can be made asynchronous. The contribution is therefore a framework and conditional convergence guarantees, rather than a claim that every continuous-time network tolerates arbitrary asynchrony.
summary.tldr: A mathematical framework identifies conditions under which continuous-time neural networks retain convergence when operating asynchronously.

title: Asynchronous Dynamics of Continuous Time Neural Networks

abstract: In recent years, the interest of investors has shifted to computer(cid:173) ized asset allocation (portfolio management) to exploit the growing dynamics of the capital markets. In this paper, asset allocation is formalized as a Markovian Decision Problem which can be opti(cid:173) mized by applying dynamic programming or reinforcement learning based algorithms. Using an artificial exchange rate, the asset allo(cid:173) cation strategy optimized with reinforcement learning (Q-Learning) is shown to be equivalent to a policy computed by dynamic pro(cid:173) gramming. The approach is then tested on the task to invest liquid capital in the German stock market. Here, neural networks are used as value function approximators. The resulting asset alloca(cid:173) tion strategy is superior to a heuristic benchmark policy. This is a further example which demonstrates the applicability of neural network based reinforcement learning to a problem setting with a high dimensional state space.

paragraphs: The paper formulates asset allocation as a Markov decision problem, treating investment choices as a sequence of decisions. This makes the problem accessible to dynamic programming and reinforcement learning. The aim is to optimize an allocation strategy within that sequential framework, linking current choices to the value of subsequent decisions.

The authors first use an artificial exchange rate to compare the approaches. In this setting, the policy learned through Q-learning is shown to be equivalent to one computed using dynamic programming. This provides a concrete connection between a learned strategy and a policy obtained through the dynamic programming formulation.

The approach is then tested on investing liquid capital in the German stock market. Neural networks approximate the value function, enabling the method to work with a high-dimensional state space. The resulting strategy outperforms a heuristic benchmark policy in the reported test. Together, the two applications support the feasibility of the formulation and the use of neural value approximation for a more complex allocation problem.
summary.tldr: A sequential asset-allocation method matches dynamic programming in an artificial setting and beats a heuristic benchmark in a stock-market test.

title: Optimal Asset Allocation using Adaptive Dynamic Programming

abstract: We solve the dynamics of on-line Hebbian learning in perceptrons exactly, for the regime where the size of the training set scales linearly with the number of inputs. We consider both noiseless and noisy teachers. Our calculation cannot be extended to non-Hebbian rules, but the solution provides a nice benchmark to test more general and advanced theories for solving the dynamics of learning with restricted training sets.
originalAbstract: We solve the dynamics of on-line Hebbian learning in perceptrons exactly, for the regime where the size of the training set scales linearly with the number of inputs. We consider both noiseless and noisy teachers. Our calculation cannot be extended to non-Hebbian rules, but the solution provides a nice benchmark to test more general and advanced theories for solving the dynamics of learning with restricted training sets.

paragraphs: The paper derives an exact account of how a perceptron changes during online Hebbian learning with a restricted training set. Online learning updates the model as examples are presented, making the evolution of learning itself the object of study. The analysis considers a regime where the training-set size grows linearly with the number of inputs.

The solution covers both noiseless and noisy teachers, allowing the dynamics to be examined with and without noise in the teaching signal. Its value lies in providing an exact mathematical reference for this specified setting. A theory of restricted-data learning can therefore be checked against a case whose evolution has already been solved.

The authors explicitly state that their calculation does not extend to non-Hebbian learning rules. This defines its role as a benchmark for broader theories rather than a solution for every update rule. More general methods can be assessed by whether they reproduce this known case, making a narrowly solvable model useful for developing wider accounts of learning dynamics.
summary.tldr: An exact solution for online Hebbian perceptron learning provides a benchmark for theories of learning from restricted training sets.

title: On-Line Learning with Restricted Training Sets: Exact Solution as Benchmark for General Theories

abstract: In this paper we show that the kernel peA algorithm of Sch6lkopf et al (1998) can be interpreted as a form of metric multidimensional scaling (MDS) when the kernel function k(x, y) is isotropic, i.e. it depends only on Ilx - yll. This leads to a metric MDS algorithm where the desired configuration of points is found via the solution of an eigenproblem rather than through the iterative optimization of the stress objective function. The question of kernel choice is also discussed.
originalAbstract: In this paper we show that the kernel peA algorithm of Sch6lkopf et al (1998) can be interpreted as a form of metric multidimensional scaling (MDS) when the kernel function k(x, y) is isotropic, i.e. it depends only on Ilx - yll. This leads to a metric MDS algorithm where the desired configuration of points is found via the solution of an eigenproblem rather than through the iterative optimization of the stress objective function. The question of kernel choice is also discussed.

paragraphs: The paper establishes a connection between kernel principal component analysis and metric multidimensional scaling. Both provide ways to construct a representation of data, but the connection shown here has a specific condition: the kernel must be isotropic. In this setting, its value depends only on the distance between two input points.

Under that condition, the authors show that kernel PCA can be interpreted as a form of metric multidimensional scaling. This connects a kernel-based analysis to the task of arranging points according to their distance relationships. The condition matters because the stated interpretation is tied to distance-dependent kernels, rather than being asserted for every possible kernel function.

The connection yields a metric multidimensional scaling algorithm that obtains its point configuration by solving an eigenproblem. It replaces iterative optimization of a stress objective with that spectral calculation. The paper also discusses kernel choice, linking the choice of similarity function to the resulting representation. Its contribution is both a conceptual equivalence and an associated computational route.
summary.tldr: With an isotropic kernel, kernel PCA becomes a form of metric multidimensional scaling solved through an eigenproblem.

title: On a Connection between Kernel PCA and Metric Multidimensional Scaling

abstract: We developed a robust control policy design method in high-dimensional state space by using differential dynamic programming with a minimax criterion. As an example, we applied our method to a simulated ﬁve link biped robot. The results show lower joint torques from the optimal con- trol policy compared to a hand-tuned PD servo controller. Results also show that the simulated biped robot can successfully walk with unknown disturbances that cause controllers generated by standard differential dy- namic programming and the hand-tuned PD servo to fail. Learning to compensate for modeling error and previously unknown disturbances in conjunction with robust control design is also demonstrated.
originalAbstract: We developed a robust control policy design method in high-dimensional state space by using differential dynamic programming with a minimax criterion. As an example, we applied our method to a simulated ﬁve link biped robot. The results show lower joint torques from the optimal con- trol policy compared to a hand-tuned PD servo controller. Results also show that the simulated biped robot can successfully walk with unknown disturbances that cause controllers generated by standard differential dy- namic programming and the hand-tuned PD servo to fail. Learning to compensate for modeling error and previously unknown disturbances in conjunction with robust control design is also demonstrated.

paragraphs: The paper develops a robust controller-design method for systems with high-dimensional state spaces. It combines differential dynamic programming with a minimax criterion, bringing robustness to disturbances into policy design. The approach is demonstrated on a simulated five-link biped robot, where the policy must generate joint control actions that sustain walking.

The reported optimal policy uses lower joint torques than a hand-tuned proportional–derivative servo controller. The simulated robot also continues walking under unknown disturbances that cause both standard differential dynamic programming controllers and the hand-tuned servo to fail. These comparisons address two practical aspects of the resulting behavior: the required joint torques and the ability to withstand disturbances.

The authors further demonstrate learning to compensate for modeling errors and previously unknown disturbances in conjunction with robust control design. This combines a policy designed for robustness with adjustment based on discrepancies encountered by the system. The findings show benefits in the simulated walking example, supporting the proposed design method without extending the demonstrated result to every disturbance or to a physical robot.
summary.tldr: Minimax differential dynamic programming produces a simulated biped controller that withstands tested unknown disturbances and uses lower torques than a hand-tuned servo.

title: Minimax Differential Dynamic Programming: An Application to Robust Biped Walking

abstract: Semantic taxonomies such as WordNet provide a rich source of knowl- edge for natural language processing applications, but are expensive to build, maintain, and extend. Motivated by the problem of automatically constructing and extending such taxonomies, in this paper we present a new algorithm for automatically learning hypernym (is-a) relations from text. Our method generalizes earlier work that had relied on using small numbers of hand-crafted regular expression patterns to identify hyper- nym pairs. Using "dependency path" features extracted from parse trees, we introduce a general-purpose formalization and generalization of these patterns. Given a training set of text containing known hypernym pairs, our algorithm automatically extracts useful dependency paths and applies them to new corpora to identify novel pairs. On our evaluation task (de- termining whether two nouns in a news article participate in a hypernym relationship), our automatically extracted database of hypernyms attains both higher precision and higher recall than WordNet.

Our method generalizes earlier work that had relied on using small numbers of hand-crafted regular expression patterns to identify hyper- nym pairs. On our evaluation task (de- termining whether two nouns in a news article participate in a hypernym relationship), our automatically extracted database of hypernyms attains both higher precision and higher recall than WordNet.

paragraphs: Semantic taxonomies organize knowledge through relationships such as one category being a kind of another. Building and maintaining resources such as WordNet requires substantial effort. This paper develops an algorithm that learns these hypernym, or is-a, relationships automatically from text.

Earlier approaches used a small collection of manually written text patterns. The proposed method generalizes that idea using dependency paths extracted from sentence parse trees. Given training text containing known hypernym pairs, it identifies useful grammatical connections between the words. It then applies the learned paths to new corpora to discover additional pairs.

The evaluation asks whether two nouns in a news article stand in a hypernym relationship. On that task, the automatically extracted database achieves both higher precision and higher recall than WordNet: its identified relationships are more accurate, and it captures more of the relevant relationships. This supports the usefulness of learned syntactic patterns for extending lexical knowledge, with the reported advantage tied to the specific evaluation task.
summary.tldr: Learning grammatical dependency patterns enables automatic hypernym discovery, with higher precision and recall than WordNet on the reported news-article task.

title: Learning Syntactic Patterns for Automatic Hypernym Discovery

abstract: We consider the problem of deriving class-size independent generaliza- tion bounds for some regularized discriminative multi-category classi- fication methods. In particular, we obtain an expected generalization bound for a standard formulation of multi-category support vector ma- chines. Based on the theoretical result, we argue that the formula- tion over-penalizes misclassification error, which in theory may lead to poor generalization performance. A remedy, based on a generalization of multi-category logistic regression (conditional maximum entropy), is then proposed, and its theoretical properties are examined.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of deriving class-size independent generaliza- tion bounds for some regularized discriminative multi-category classi- fication methods. In particular, we obtain an expected generalization bound for a standard formulation of multi-category support vector ma- chines. Based on the theoretical result, we argue that the formula- tion over-penalizes misclassification error, which in theory may lead to poor generalization performance. A remedy, based on a generalization of multi-category logistic regression (conditional maximum entropy), is then proposed, and its theoretical properties are examined.

paragraphs: The paper studies theoretical guarantees for regularized classifiers that choose among multiple categories. Its goal is to obtain generalization bounds that do not depend on the number of classes. Such bounds help separate the effects of a learning formulation from a dependence on how many categories the task contains.

The authors derive an expected generalization bound for a standard multicategory support vector machine formulation. They use this analysis to argue that its treatment of misclassification imposes too much penalty. Their conclusion is qualified: this over-penalization may lead to poor generalization in theory, rather than establishing that the formulation always performs poorly.

The paper then proposes a remedy built from a generalization of multicategory logistic regression, also described through conditional maximum entropy. It examines the theoretical properties of this alternative. The overall contribution connects a generalization analysis to the design of a learning objective, using the bound to identify a possible weakness and motivate a different treatment of classification errors.
summary.tldr: Class-count-independent bounds suggest a potential over-penalization problem in multicategory SVMs and motivate a logistic-regression-based alternative.

title: Class-size Independent Generalization Analsysis of Some Discriminative Multi-Category Classification

abstract: An important aspect of clustering algorithms is whether the partitions constructed on finite samples converge to a useful clustering of the whole data space as the sample size increases. This paper investigates this question for normalized and unnormalized versions of the popular spec- tral clustering algorithm. Surprisingly, the convergence of unnormalized spectral clustering is more difficult to handle than the normalized case. Even though recently some first results on the convergence of normal- ized spectral clustering have been obtained, for the unnormalized case we have to develop a completely new approach combining tools from numerical integration, spectral and perturbation theory, and probability. It turns out that while in the normalized case, spectral clustering usually converges to a nice partition of the data space, in the unnormalized case the same only holds under strong additional assumptions which are not always satisfied. We conclude that our analysis gives strong evidence for the superiority of normalized spectral clustering. It also provides a basis for future exploration of other Laplacian-based methods.

We conclude that our analysis gives strong evidence for the superiority of normalized spectral clustering. It also provides a basis for future exploration of other Laplacian-based methods.

paragraphs: A clustering algorithm partitions the observations it receives, but those groups may or may not approach a useful partition of the underlying data space as more observations arrive. This paper studies that convergence question for normalized and unnormalized spectral clustering. The focus is the meaning of the large-sample limit, rather than just a partition's appearance on one dataset.

The unnormalized case requires a new analysis combining numerical integration, spectral and perturbation theory, and probability. The authors find that normalized spectral clustering usually converges to a useful partition. Obtaining the same behavior for the unnormalized version requires strong additional assumptions, and those assumptions are not always satisfied.

The analysis therefore gives strong evidence favoring normalized spectral clustering, while stopping short of declaring it universally successful. Its practical importance is that two related algorithms can differ substantially in how their finite-sample results extend to the whole space. The theoretical tools also provide a foundation for examining other methods built around graph Laplacians and their limiting behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper finds that useful convergence requires stronger assumptions for unnormalized spectral clustering than for its normalized counterpart.

title: Limits of Spectral Clustering

abstract: We develop and analyze game-theoretic algorithms for predicting coordinate binding of multiple DNA binding regulators. The allocation of proteins to local neighborhoods and to sites is carried out with resource constraints while explicating competing and coordinate binding relations among proteins with affinity to the site or region. The focus of this paper is on mathematical foundations of the approach. We also briefly demonstrate the approach in the context of the -phage switch.
originalAbstract: We develop and analyze game-theoretic algorithms for predicting coordinate binding of multiple DNA binding regulators. The allocation of proteins to local neighborhoods and to sites is carried out with resource constraints while explicating competing and coordinate binding relations among proteins with affinity to the site or region. The focus of this paper is on mathematical foundations of the approach. We also briefly demonstrate the approach in the context of the -phage switch.

paragraphs: This paper develops game-theoretic algorithms for predicting coordinated binding by multiple DNA-binding regulators. The problem involves allocating proteins both to local DNA neighborhoods and to individual binding sites. Those allocations are subject to resource constraints, so the framework considers how available proteins can be distributed across relevant locations.

The approach explicitly represents competing and coordinated binding relationships among proteins with affinity for a site or region. This matters because the allocation problem includes relationships among regulators as well as their individual affinities. The game-theoretic formulation brings these relationships and the resource constraints into the same mathematical treatment of binding.

The paper concentrates on developing and analyzing the mathematical foundations of this approach. It also gives a brief demonstration in a phage-switch setting. Its main contribution is therefore a formal algorithmic framework for coupled protein-binding decisions. The demonstration illustrates an application of that framework, while the core work concerns how constrained allocation and interactions among multiple regulators can be represented and analyzed.
summary.tldr: Game-theoretic algorithms model protein allocation to DNA while accounting for resource constraints and competing or coordinated binding.

title: Game Theoretic Algorithms for Protein-DNA binding

abstract: It has been shown that adapting a dictionary of basis functions to the statistics of natural images so as to maximize sparsity in the coefficients results in a set of dictionary elements whose spatial properties resemble those of V1 (primary visual cortex) receptive fields. However, the resulting sparse coefficients still exhibit pronounced statistical dependencies, thus violating the independence assumption of the sparse coding model. Here, we propose a model that attempts to capture the dependencies among the basis function coefficients by including a pairwise coupling term in the prior over the coefficient activity states. When adapted to the statistics of natural images, the coupling terms learn a combination of facilitatory and inhibitory interactions among neighboring basis functions. These learned interactions may offer an explanation for the function of horizontal connections in V1, and we discuss the implications of our findings for physiological experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse coding learns image components so that each image can be represented with relatively few active coefficients. When trained on natural images, the learned components can resemble receptive fields in primary visual cortex. However, the resulting coefficients still show substantial statistical dependencies, conflicting with the model's assumption that they are independent.

The paper extends the prior over coefficient activity states with a pairwise coupling term. This gives the model a way to represent relationships between the activity of different image components. Learning from natural-image statistics then adjusts both the representation of activity and the interactions connecting neighboring basis functions.

The learned couplings include facilitatory and inhibitory interactions: relationships that favor or discourage joint activity. The authors suggest that these interactions may help explain the function of horizontal connections in primary visual cortex, and discuss implications for physiological experiments. The biological interpretation remains a possible explanation. The direct modeling result is that accounting for residual dependencies produces learned interactions with both supportive and suppressive effects.
summary.tldr: Adding learned pairwise interactions to sparse coding captures coefficient dependencies and suggests a possible role for horizontal connections in visual cortex.

title: Learning Horizontal Connections in a Sparse Coding Model of Natural Images

abstract: We show that the empirical minimizer of a stochastic strongly convex objective, where the stochastic component is linear, converges to the population minimizer with rate $O(1/n)$. The result applies, in particular, to the SVM objective. Thus, we get a rate of $O(1/n)$ on the convergence of the SVM objective to its infinite data limit. We demonstrate how this is essential for obtaining tight oracle inequalities for SVMs. The results extend also to strong convexity with respect to other $\ellnorm_p$ norms, and so also to objectives regularized using other norms.

We demonstrate how this is essential for obtaining tight oracle inequalities for SVMs. The results extend also to strong convexity with respect to other $\ellnorm_p$ norms, and so also to objectives regularized using other norms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a solution learned from a finite sample approaches the solution defined by the full population. Its main result concerns a stochastic objective that is strongly convex and whose stochastic component is linear. Under these conditions, the empirical minimizer approaches the population minimizer at a rate of O(1/n), where n is the sample size.

The authors show that the result applies to the support vector machine objective. This gives an O(1/n) rate for convergence of that objective toward its infinite-data limit. The claim concerns the regularized objective and its population counterpart, so its meaning is specifically about the learning criterion being optimized.

The paper also explains why this convergence rate is essential for tight oracle inequalities for support vector machines. Such inequalities provide theoretical comparisons with an ideal reference choice. Finally, the analysis extends to strong convexity defined using other lp norms, covering objectives regularized with other norms. The contribution therefore connects a conditional convergence theorem to both SVM analysis and a broader family of regularized objectives.
summary.tldr: Under strong convexity and a linear stochastic component, empirical optimization achieves an O(1/n) convergence rate that applies to SVM objectives.

title: Fast Rates for Regularized Objectives

abstract: The International Monitoring System (IMS) is a global network of sensors whose purpose is to identify potential violations of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT), primarily through detection and localization of seismic events. We report on the first stage of a project to improve on the current automated software system with a Bayesian inference system that computes the most likely global event history given the record of local sensor data. The new system, VISA (Vertically Integrated Seismological Analysis), is based on empirically calibrated, generative models of event occurrence, signal propagation, and signal detection. VISA exhibits significantly improved precision and recall compared to the current operational system and is able to detect events that are missed even by the human analysts who post-process the IMS output.

VISA exhibits significantly improved precision and recall compared to the current operational system and is able to detect events that are missed even by the human analysts who post-process the IMS output.

paragraphs: The International Monitoring System uses sensors around the world to detect and locate seismic events that could indicate violations of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. This paper reports the first stage of a project to improve automated monitoring. Its central task is to infer a global history of events from the local observations made by individual sensors.

The proposed system, VISA, uses Bayesian inference to identify the most likely event history given the sensor records. It combines empirically calibrated generative models of event occurrence, signal propagation, and signal detection. These components connect possible events to the signals that would travel through the environment and ultimately be recorded.

VISA achieves significantly better precision and recall than the operational system used for comparison. It also detects events missed by human analysts who review the existing system's output. The findings support treating seismic monitoring as an integrated inference problem, with event explanations evaluated through a shared model of how observations arise across the sensor network.
summary.tldr: VISA uses Bayesian models of seismic events and sensor observations to improve detection precision and recall over the compared operational system.

title: Global seismic monitoring as probabilistic inference

abstract: We propose a novel Adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to compute the partition function. In particular, we show how to accelerate a flat histogram sampling technique by significantly reducing the number of ``null moves'' in the chain, while maintaining asymptotic convergence properties. Our experiments show that our method converges quickly to highly accurate solutions on a range of benchmark instances, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods such as IJGP, TRW, and Gibbs sampling both in run-time and accuracy. We also show how obtaining a so-called density of states distribution allows for efficient weight learning in Markov Logic theories.

paragraphs: This paper develops an adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm for computing a partition function. The computational focus is a flat histogram sampling technique. The authors identify an opportunity to accelerate this technique by reducing how often the sampling chain makes a null move, a step that does not advance it to another state.

The contribution combines this reduction in unproductive steps with preservation of asymptotic convergence properties. That pairing matters because a faster sampling procedure must still retain the long-run behavior needed for the computation. The claimed acceleration therefore concerns how the chain operates while keeping its eventual convergence properties intact.

On a range of benchmark instances, the method reaches highly accurate solutions quickly and outperforms IJGP, TRW, and Gibbs sampling in both runtime and accuracy. These are reported experimental comparisons. The paper also connects the computation to learning: obtaining a density of states distribution enables efficient weight learning in Markov Logic theories, extending the usefulness of the sampling procedure beyond partition function estimation.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm reduces null moves to accelerate partition function computation while preserving asymptotic convergence.

title: Accelerated Adaptive Markov Chain for Partition Function Computation

abstract: Policy gradient is a useful model-free reinforcement learning approach, but it tends to suffer from instability of gradient estimates. In this paper, we analyze and improve the stability of policy gradient methods. We first prove that the variance of gradient estimates in the PGPE(policy gradients with parameter-based exploration) method is smaller than that of the classical REINFORCE method under a mild assumption. We then derive the optimal baseline for PGPE, which contributes to further reducing the variance. We also theoretically show that PGPE with the optimal baseline is more preferable than REINFORCE with the optimal baseline in terms of the variance of gradient estimates. Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of the improved PGPE method through experiments.

We first prove that the variance of gradient estimates in the PGPE(policy gradients with parameter-based exploration) method is smaller than that of the classical REINFORCE method under a mild assumption. We then derive the optimal baseline for PGPE, which contributes to further reducing the variance. We also theoretically show that PGPE with the optimal baseline is more preferable than REINFORCE with the optimal baseline in terms of the variance of gradient estimates. Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of the improved PGPE method through experiments.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods learn how to act by estimating which changes to a policy would increase reward. They can operate without a model of the environment, but their gradient estimates can vary substantially. This paper investigates that variability and develops an improvement intended to make the estimates more stable.

The analysis focuses on policy gradients with parameter-based exploration, or PGPE, and compares it with the classical REINFORCE method. Under a mild assumption, the authors prove that PGPE has lower gradient-estimation variance. They then derive an optimal baseline for PGPE, a reference used in the estimator to reduce its variability further.

The comparison also covers versions of both methods equipped with their optimal baselines. The authors theoretically favor PGPE on the variance criterion and report experiments demonstrating the usefulness of the improved method. The result concerns the stability of the learning signal: less variable estimates provide a clearer indication of how to adjust the policy. The abstract's theoretical advantage is specifically about variance, with the initial comparison subject to its stated assumption.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes variance advantages for PGPE and derives an optimal baseline that further stabilizes its policy-gradient estimates.

title: Analysis and Improvement of Policy Gradient Estimation

abstract: A weighted graph is used as an underlying structure of many algorithms like semi-supervised learning and spectral clustering. The edge weights are usually deter-mined by a single similarity measure, but it often hard if not impossible to capture all relevant aspects of similarity when using a single similarity measure. In par-ticular, in the case of visual object matching it is beneficial to integrate different similarity measures that focus on different visual representations. In this paper, a novel approach to integrate multiple similarity measures is pro-posed. First pairs of similarity measures are combined with a diffusion process on their tensor product graph (TPG). Hence the diffused similarity of each pair of ob-jects becomes a function of joint diffusion of the two original similarities, which in turn depends on the neighborhood structure of the TPG. We call this process Fusion with Diffusion (FD). However, a higher order graph like the TPG usually means significant increase in time complexity. This is not the case in the proposed approach. A key feature of our approach is that the time complexity of the dif-fusion on the TPG is the same as the diffusion process on each of the original graphs, Moreover, it is not necessary to explicitly construct the TPG in our frame-work. Finally all diffused pairs of similarity measures are combined as a weighted sum. We demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach on the task of visual tracking, where different aspects of the appearance similarity between the target object in frame t and target object candidates in frame t+1 are integrated. The obtained method is tested on several challenge video sequences and the experimental results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art tracking methods.

paragraphs: Visual tracking needs to match an object in one frame with candidates in the next. Different representations capture different aspects of appearance, so a single similarity measure can miss useful evidence. This paper proposes Fusion with Diffusion, a way to combine multiple similarity measures while using the neighborhood relationships encoded by their graphs.

The method first combines pairs of similarity measures through diffusion on a tensor product graph. Each resulting similarity depends on the joint diffusion of the original measures and the neighborhood structure of that combined graph. The pairwise results are then merged through a weighted sum, producing an overall measure that integrates several views of appearance.

Although the tensor product graph is a higher-order structure, the proposed computation does not require explicitly building it. Its diffusion has the same time complexity as diffusion on each original graph. This makes the joint construction computationally practical. On several challenging video sequences, the resulting tracker outperforms the state-of-the-art methods evaluated, supporting the usefulness of neighborhood-aware similarity fusion for tracking.
summary.tldr: Fusion with Diffusion combines appearance similarities through an efficiently computed joint graph and improves tracking on challenging video sequences.

title: Fusion with Diffusion for Robust Visual Tracking

abstract: Active learning can substantially improve the yield of neurophysiology experiments by adaptively selecting stimuli to probe a neuron's receptive field (RF) in real time. Bayesian active learning methods maintain a posterior distribution over the RF, and select stimuli to maximally reduce posterior entropy on each time step. However, existing methods tend to rely on simple Gaussian priors, and do not exploit uncertainty at the level of hyperparameters when determining an optimal stimulus. This uncertainty can play a substantial role in RF characterization, particularly when RFs are smooth, sparse, or local in space and time. In this paper, we describe a novel framework for active learning under hierarchical, conditionally Gaussian priors. Our algorithm uses sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling (''particle filtering'' with MCMC) over hyperparameters to construct a mixture-of-Gaussians representation of the RF posterior, and selects optimal stimuli using an approximate infomax criterion. The core elements of this algorithm are parallelizable, making it computationally efficient for real-time experiments. We apply our algorithm to simulated and real neural data, and show that it can provide highly accurate receptive field estimates from very limited data, even with a small number of hyperparameter samples.

paragraphs: Characterizing a neuron's receptive field means estimating which stimuli influence its response. Active learning makes this process adaptive: each new stimulus is chosen to reduce uncertainty about the receptive field. This paper addresses uncertainty in the hyperparameters that govern the prior distribution over possible receptive fields. Accounting for that uncertainty can matter especially when receptive fields are smooth, sparse, or localized in space and time.

The authors introduce a hierarchical model in which the prior is Gaussian conditional on the hyperparameters. Their algorithm uses sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to track different possible hyperparameter settings. These samples produce a mixture of Gaussian distributions representing uncertainty about the receptive field. An approximate information-maximization rule then chooses stimuli intended to reduce that uncertainty, incorporating uncertainty about the hyperparameters into stimulus selection.

The algorithm's core computations can run in parallel, supporting efficient use in real-time experiments. Applications to simulated and real neural data show that the method can estimate receptive fields very accurately from limited observations, even using few hyperparameter samples. These findings support the practical value of representing uncertainty at multiple levels when deciding which stimulus to present next.
summary.tldr: By accounting for uncertainty in prior hyperparameters, this Bayesian active learning method can select informative stimuli and accurately estimate neural receptive fields from limited data.

title: Bayesian active learning with localized priors for fast receptive field characterization

abstract: Formal exploration approaches in model-based reinforcement learning estimate the accuracy of the currently learned model without consideration of the empirical prediction error. For example, PAC-MDP approaches such as Rmax base their model certainty on the amount of collected data, while Bayesian approaches assume a prior over the transition dynamics. We propose extensions to such approaches which drive exploration solely based on empirical estimates of the learner's accuracy and learning progress. We provide a ``sanity check'' theoretical analysis, discussing the behavior of our extensions in the standard stationary finite state-action case. We then provide experimental studies demonstrating the robustness of these exploration measures in cases of non-stationary environments or where original approaches are misled by wrong domain assumptions.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning must decide where further experience will help improve its learned model. The paper observes that formal exploration methods may judge certainty through data counts or prior assumptions about transition dynamics, without considering empirical prediction error. It investigates exploration driven by what the learner's predictions actually reveal.

The authors propose extensions that base exploration solely on empirical estimates of accuracy and learning progress. Accuracy concerns how well the model predicts, while learning progress concerns changes in the learner's performance. Together, these measurements provide an experience-based basis for exploration rather than relying only on the certainty measures used by the original approaches.

The theoretical analysis is described as a sanity check in stationary environments with finite state and action spaces. Experiments then examine non-stationary environments and situations where incorrect domain assumptions mislead the original methods. The reported robustness in these settings supports empirical accuracy and learning progress as useful exploration signals, while the theoretical discussion remains tied to its stated stationary finite setting.
summary.tldr: Empirical prediction accuracy and learning progress guide exploration, with reported robustness to changing environments and incorrect domain assumptions.

title: Exploration in Model-based Reinforcement Learning by Empirically Estimating Learning Progress

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods based on direct policy search (DPS) have been actively discussed to achieve an efficient approach to complicated Markov decision processes (MDPs). Although they have brought much progress in practical applications of RL, there still remains an unsolved problem in DPS related to model selection for the policy. In this paper, we propose a novel DPS method, {\it weighted likelihood policy search (WLPS)}, where a policy is efficiently learned through the weighted likelihood estimation. WLPS naturally connects DPS to the statistical inference problem and thus various sophisticated techniques in statistics can be applied to DPS problems directly. Hence, by following the idea of the {\it information criterion}, we develop a new measurement for model comparison in DPS based on the weighted log-likelihood.

paragraphs: Direct policy search learns an agent's decision rule directly and has been useful for complicated reinforcement-learning problems. A remaining challenge is choosing the policy model itself. Improving parameters within a chosen model and deciding which model to use are related tasks, but a policy-learning procedure does not automatically provide a model-comparison criterion.

The paper introduces weighted likelihood policy search, which learns a policy through weighted likelihood estimation. This formulation connects direct policy search with statistical inference. The connection matters because it gives statistical techniques a direct role in policy learning, creating a framework in which estimation and comparison of policy models can be considered together.

Building on the idea of an information criterion, the authors develop a measure for comparing policy models using weighted log-likelihood. The contribution thus includes both an efficient policy-estimation method and a model-selection measure expressed within the same statistical formulation. It addresses how a learner can reason about its choice of policy representation as part of direct policy search.
summary.tldr: Weighted likelihood policy search connects policy learning to statistical inference and introduces a corresponding criterion for comparing policy models.

title: Weighted Likelihood Policy Search with Model Selection

abstract: The performance of standard algorithms for Independent Component Analysis quickly deteriorates under the addition of Gaussian noise. This is partially due to a common first step that typically consists of whitening, i.e., applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and rescaling the components to have identity covariance, which is not invariant under Gaussian noise. In our paper we develop the first practical algorithm for Independent Component Analysis that is provably invariant under Gaussian noise. The two main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. We develop and implement a more efficient version of a Gaussian noise invariant decorrelation (quasi-orthogonalization) algorithm using Hessians of the cumulant functions. 2. We propose a very simple and efficient fixed-point GI-ICA (Gradient Iteration ICA) algorithm, which is compatible with quasi-orthogonalization, as well as with the usual PCA-based whitening in the noiseless case. The algorithm is based on a special form of gradient iteration (different from gradient descent). We provide an analysis of our algorithm demonstrating fast convergence following from the basic properties of cumulants. We also present a number of experimental comparisons with the existing methods, showing superior results on noisy data and very competitive performance in the noiseless case.

The paper identifies ordinary whitening as part of the problem: applying PCA and rescaling to identity covariance does not preserve invariance to that noise.

The authors develop a more efficient noise-invariant decorrelation procedure using Hessians of cumulant functions. Experiments report superior results on noisy observations and very competitive results without noise. The contribution therefore addresses both the preprocessing step and the component-finding iteration, showing how a theoretically appropriate treatment of Gaussian noise can be incorporated into an efficient procedure with favorable empirical performance.
summary.tldr: Noise-invariant decorrelation and a fast fixed-point iteration provide practical independent component analysis with provable Gaussian-noise invariance.

title: Fast Algorithms for Gaussian Noise Invariant Independent Component Analysis

abstract: Recent work on mid-level visual representations aims to capture information at the level of complexity higher than typical visual words", but lower than full-blown semantic objects. Several approaches have been proposed to discover mid-level visual elements, that are both 1) representative, i.e. frequently occurring within a visual dataset, and 2) visually discriminative. However, the current approaches are rather ad hoc and difficult to analyze and evaluate. In this work, we pose visual element discovery as discriminative mode seeking, drawing connections to the the well-known and well-studied mean-shift algorithm. Given a weakly-labeled image collection, our method discovers visually-coherent patch clusters that are maximally discriminative with respect to the labels. One advantage of our formulation is that it requires only a single pass through the data. We also propose the Purity-Coverage plot as a principled way of experimentally analyzing and evaluating different visual discovery approaches, and compare our method against prior work on the Paris Street View dataset. We also evaluate our method on the task of scene classification, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on the MIT Scene-67 dataset."

paragraphs: Mid-level visual elements capture image structure more complex than basic visual words but simpler than complete semantic objects. Useful elements should recur in a collection and help distinguish its labels. This paper gives their discovery a more principled formulation, addressing approaches that were difficult to analyze and evaluate.

The method treats discovery as discriminative mode seeking and connects it to the mean-shift algorithm. From a weakly labeled image collection, it identifies clusters of visually coherent patches that are maximally discriminative with respect to the labels. The formulation needs only one pass through the data, making the discovery procedure economical in its access to the collection.

They compare with prior work on the Paris Street View dataset and evaluate the discovered representation for scene classification. The reported scene-classification performance is state of the art on MIT Scene-67. The paper thus contributes a discovery objective, an evaluation tool, and evidence that the resulting elements support recognition.
summary.tldr: Discriminative mode seeking discovers coherent, label-informative image patches in one data pass and supports strong scene classification.

title: Mid-level Visual Element Discovery as Discriminative Mode Seeking

abstract:
In Reinforcement Learning (RL), state-of-the-art algorithms require a large number of samples per state-action pair to estimate the transition kernel $p$. In many problems, a good approximation of $p$ is not needed. For instance, if from one state-action pair $(s,a)$, one can only transit to states with the same value, learning $p(\cdot|s,a)$ accurately is irrelevant (only its support matters). title: How hard is my MDP?" The distribution-norm to the rescue"

abstract: Decision trees and randomized forests are widely used in computer vision and machine learning. Standard algorithms for decision tree induction optimize the split functions one node at a time according to some splitting criteria. This greedy procedure often leads to suboptimal trees. In this paper, we present an algorithm for optimizing the split functions at all levels of the tree jointly with the leaf parameters, based on a global objective. We show that the problem of finding optimal linear-combination (oblique) splits for decision trees is related to structured prediction with latent variables, and we formulate a convex-concave upper bound on the tree's empirical loss. Computing the gradient of the proposed surrogate objective with respect to each training exemplar is O(d^2), where d is the tree depth, and thus training deep trees is feasible. The use of stochastic gradient descent for optimization enables effective training with large datasets. Experiments on several classification benchmarks demonstrate that the resulting non-greedy decision trees outperform greedy decision tree baselines.

paragraphs: Standard decision-tree training chooses splits one node at a time. Each choice is judged locally, even though the usefulness of a split also depends on the rest of the tree. This paper addresses the resulting possibility of suboptimal trees by optimizing split functions throughout the tree together with the parameters at its leaves.

The authors connect learning oblique splits, which use linear combinations of input features, to structured prediction with latent variables. They derive a convex-concave upper bound on the tree's empirical loss and optimize this surrogate global objective. Joint optimization lets training account for how decisions at different levels contribute to the same overall prediction task.

The gradient calculation for each training example costs O(d²), where d is tree depth, making training deep trees feasible. Stochastic gradient descent supports training on large datasets. Across several classification benchmarks, the resulting trees outperform the greedy decision-tree baselines evaluated. These findings support the practical value of coordinating splits across levels, without asserting that the optimization always finds the globally best tree.
summary.tldr: Jointly optimizing tree splits and leaf parameters produces decision trees that outperform greedy baselines on the evaluated classification benchmarks.

title: Efficient Non-greedy Optimization of Decision Trees

abstract: We propose a stochastic optimization method for the minimization of the sum of three convex functions, one of which has Lipschitz continuous gradient as well as restricted strong convexity. Our approach is most suitable in the setting where it is computationally advantageous to process smooth term in the decomposition with its stochastic gradient estimate and the other two functions separately with their proximal operators, such as doubly regularized empirical risk minimization problems. We prove the convergence characterization of the proposed algorithm in expectation under the standard assumptions for the stochastic gradient estimate of the smooth term. Our method operates in the primal space and can be considered as a stochastic extension of the three-operator splitting method. Finally, numerical evidence supports the effectiveness of our method in real-world problems.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems combine a data-fitting term with two separate regularizers. Treating the entire objective as one unit may overlook computational advantages available for its individual pieces. This paper proposes a stochastic method for minimizing a sum of three convex functions, handling one through stochastic gradients and the other two through their own proximal operators.

The smooth function is assumed to have a Lipschitz-continuous gradient and restricted strong convexity. The method is especially suitable when estimating that term’s gradient and processing the remaining terms separately is computationally advantageous. Doubly regularized empirical risk minimization is one motivating setting for this decomposition.

The algorithm works in the primal space and extends three-operator splitting to stochastic optimization. The authors establish convergence in expectation under standard assumptions on the stochastic gradient estimate. Numerical evidence on real-world problems supports its effectiveness. The contribution is a way to retain the useful three-part structure of an objective while allowing noisy, potentially cheaper gradient information for its smooth component.
summary.tldr: A stochastic three-operator method optimizes convex objectives using a gradient estimate for one term and separate proximal updates for two others.

title: Stochastic Three-Composite Convex Minimization

abstract: Planned experiments are the gold standard in reliably comparing the causal effect of switching from a baseline policy to a new policy. % One critical shortcoming of classical experimental methods, however, is that they typically do not take into account the dynamic nature of response to policy changes. For instance, in an experiment where we seek to understand the effects of a new ad pricing policy on auction revenue, agents may adapt their bidding in response to the experimental pricing changes. Thus, causal effects of the new pricing policy after such adaptation period, the {\em long-term causal effects}, are not captured by the classical methodology even though they clearly are more indicative of the value of the new policy. % Here, we formalize a framework to define and estimate long-term causal effects of policy changes in multiagent economies. Central to our approach is behavioral game theory, which we leverage to formulate the ignorability assumptions that are necessary for causal inference. Under such assumptions we estimate long-term causal effects through a latent space approach, where a behavioral model of how agents act conditional on their latent behaviors is combined with a temporal model of how behaviors evolve over time.

paragraphs: A policy change can alter how people behave over time, so its immediate experimental effect may differ from its eventual effect. The paper illustrates this with advertising auctions: a new pricing policy can change revenue directly, while bidders may subsequently adjust their bids. The outcome after adaptation can be more informative about the policy's long-term value.

The authors formalize a framework for defining and estimating these long-term causal effects in economies with multiple interacting agents. Behavioral game theory supplies the basis for ignorability assumptions needed for causal inference. The resulting estimates are conditional on those assumptions, making the behavioral account part of the justification for drawing causal conclusions.

Their estimation approach uses latent behaviors that are not directly observed. One model connects those behaviors to agents' actions, while a temporal model describes how the behaviors evolve. Combining the two provides a way to reason about outcomes after adaptation. The contribution is a framework linking causal policy evaluation to changing behavior, rather than treating experimental responses as fixed throughout time.
summary.tldr: A behavioral game-theoretic framework estimates policy effects after agents adapt, subject to its causal ignorability assumptions.

title: Long-term Causal Effects via Behavioral Game Theory

abstract: A family of learning algorithms generated from additive models have attracted much attention recently for their flexibility and interpretability in high dimensional data analysis. Among them, learning models with grouped variables have shown competitive performance for prediction and variable selection. However, the previous works mainly focus on the least squares regression problem, not the classification task. Thus, it is desired to design the new additive classification model with variable selection capability for many real-world applications which focus on high-dimensional data classification. To address this challenging problem, in this paper, we investigate the classification with group sparse additive models in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. A novel classification method, called as \emph{group sparse additive machine} (GroupSAM), is proposed to explore and utilize the structure information among the input variables. Generalization error bound is derived and proved by integrating the sample error analysis with empirical covering numbers and the hypothesis error estimate with the stepping stone technique. Our new bound shows that GroupSAM can achieve a satisfactory learning rate with polynomial decay. Experimental results on synthetic data and seven benchmark datasets consistently show the effectiveness of our new approach.

GroupSAM addresses that gap through group-sparse additive classification in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. It is designed to use structural relationships among input variables, making grouping part of the classification model. The combination of additive modeling and group sparsity brings together flexible prediction and selective use of inputs within the task the authors target.

The paper derives a generalization bound by combining sample-error analysis based on empirical covering numbers with a hypothesis-error estimate using the stepping stone technique. The resulting learning rate decreases polynomially. Experiments on synthetic data and seven benchmark datasets consistently support the method’s effectiveness, pairing a theoretical account of learning behavior with practical evidence for classification using grouped variables.
summary.tldr: GroupSAM brings group-sparse additive modeling to classification, with a polynomial learning-rate bound and supportive experiments.

title: Group Sparse Additive Machine

abstract: We introduce deep neural networks for end-to-end differentiable theorem proving that operate on dense vector representations of symbols. These neural networks are recursively constructed by following the backward chaining algorithm as used in Prolog. Specifically, we replace symbolic unification with a differentiable computation on vector representations of symbols using a radial basis function kernel, thereby combining symbolic reasoning with learning subsymbolic vector representations. The resulting neural network can be trained to infer facts from a given incomplete knowledge base using gradient descent. By doing so, it learns to (i) place representations of similar symbols in close proximity in a vector space, (ii) make use of such similarities to prove facts, (iii) induce logical rules, and (iv) it can use provided and induced logical rules for complex multi-hop reasoning. On four benchmark knowledge bases we demonstrate that this architecture outperforms ComplEx, a state-of-the-art neural link prediction model, while at the same time inducing interpretable function-free first-order logic rules.

This gives the network a structure organized around proving facts from other facts and rules, while allowing parts of the reasoning process to be learned from data.

The key change replaces symbolic unification with a differentiable comparison between symbol vectors using a radial basis function kernel. Gradient descent can then train the network to infer facts from an incomplete knowledge base. During training, it learns to position similar symbols near one another and use those similarities in its proofs. It can also induce logical rules and combine supplied and learned rules in multi-hop reasoning.

Across four benchmark knowledge bases, the architecture outperforms ComplEx, the neural link prediction model used for comparison. It simultaneously induces interpretable, function-free first-order logic rules. These results demonstrate a way to couple learned similarities with explicit chains of reasoning, producing both predictions and logical rules within the same trainable architecture.
summary.tldr: Differentiable backward chaining learns symbol representations and interpretable logical rules for inferring facts from incomplete knowledge bases.

title: End-to-end Differentiable Proving

abstract: We propose a method for learning landmark detectors for visual objects (such as the eyes and the nose in a face) without any manual supervision. We cast this as the problem of generating images that combine the appearance of the object as seen in a first example image with the geometry of the object as seen in a second example image, where the two examples differ by a viewpoint change and/or an object deformation. In order to factorize appearance and geometry, we introduce a tight bottleneck in the geometry-extraction process that selects and distils geometry-related features. Compared to standard image generation problems, which often use generative adversarial networks, our generation task is conditioned on both appearance and geometry and thus is significantly less ambiguous, to the point that adopting a simple perceptual loss formulation is sufficient. We demonstrate that our approach can learn object landmarks from synthetic image deformations or videos, all without manual supervision, while outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised landmark detectors. We further show that our method is applicable to a large variety of datasets - faces, people, 3D objects, and digits - without any modifications.
