paragraphs: The paper learns visual landmarks, such as facial feature locations, without manually labeled examples. It turns landmark learning into an image-generation task: combine the appearance of an object from one image with its geometry from another. The paired examples differ through a viewpoint change, object deformation, or both.

A tight bottleneck in the geometry-extraction process selects and compresses geometry-related information. This encourages the model to separate object layout from appearance while learning features useful for generating the requested image. Because both appearance and geometry condition the output, the task is substantially less ambiguous than standard image generation. The authors find that a simple perceptual loss is sufficient.

The approach learns landmarks from synthetic image deformations or videos and outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised landmark detectors in the reported evaluation. It also applies without modification to datasets containing faces, people, three-dimensional objects, and digits. The findings show how a carefully structured generation task can provide the learning signal for landmark detection across several kinds of visual data without manual supervision.
summary.tldr: Conditioning image generation on separate appearance and compressed geometry signals teaches landmark detection without manual labels.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Object Landmarks through Conditional Image Generation

abstract: Detecting segments of interest from an input sequence is a challenging problem which often requires not only good knowledge of individual target segments, but also contextual understanding of the entire input sequence and the relationships between the target segments. To address this problem, we propose the Sequence-to-Segment Network (S$^2$N), a novel end-to-end sequential encoder-decoder architecture. S$^2$N first encodes the input into a sequence of hidden states that progressively capture both local and holistic information. It then employs a novel decoding architecture, called Segment Detection Unit (SDU), that integrates the decoder state and encoder hidden states to detect segments sequentially. During training, we formulate the assignment of predicted segments to ground truth as bipartite matching and use the Earth Mover's Distance to calculate the localization errors. We experiment with S$^2$N on temporal action proposal generation and video summarization and show that S$^2$N achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks.

paragraphs: Detecting meaningful segments in a sequence requires understanding both the segments themselves and their wider context. Relationships among target segments can also matter. The Sequence-to-Segment Network addresses these needs with an end-to-end encoder-decoder architecture that converts an input sequence into a sequence of detected segments.

The encoder builds hidden states that progressively capture local information and an understanding of the whole input. A specialized decoder component, the Segment Detection Unit, combines these encoder states with its own state to detect segments one after another. This design lets segment detection draw on the sequence representation and the evolving decoding process together.

During training, predicted and reference segments are assigned through bipartite matching, and localization errors are measured using Earth Mover's Distance. These choices connect training to the task of matching sets of segments and placing them accurately. Experiments on temporal action proposal generation and video summarization report state-of-the-art performance on both tasks, supporting the architecture across two segment-selection applications.
summary.tldr: Sequence-to-Segment Networks combine sequence-wide context with sequential decoding to detect segments effectively in action proposals and video summarization.

title: Sequence-to-Segment Networks for Segment Detection

abstract: A fundamental problem in program verification concerns inferring loop invariants. The problem is undecidable and even practical instances are challenging. Inspired by how human experts construct loop invariants, we propose a reasoning framework Code2Inv that constructs the solution by multi-step decision making and querying an external program graph memory block. By training with reinforcement learning, Code2Inv captures rich program features and avoids the need for ground truth solutions as supervision. Compared to previous learning tasks in domains with graph-structured data, it addresses unique challenges, such as a binary objective function and an extremely sparse reward that is given by an automated theorem prover only after the complete loop invariant is proposed. We evaluate Code2Inv on a suite of 133 benchmark problems and compare it to three state-of-the-art systems. It solves 106 problems compared to 73 by a stochastic search-based system, 77 by a heuristic search-based system, and 100 by a decision tree learning-based system. Moreover, the strategy learned can be generalized to new programs: compared to solving new instances from scratch, the pre-trained agent is more sample efficient in finding solutions.

paragraphs: Loop invariants describe properties that remain true as a program loop executes and help establish program correctness. Inferring them is undecidable in general, and practical cases can still be difficult. Code2Inv treats invariant construction as a sequence of decisions informed by a graph-based memory of the program.

The framework learns through reinforcement learning, avoiding the need for known correct invariants as training labels. An automated theorem prover supplies a binary reward only after a complete candidate is proposed. This makes feedback extremely sparse: the learner must discover useful construction strategies despite receiving no such reward for individual intermediate choices.

On 133 benchmark problems, Code2Inv solves 106, compared with 73 for a stochastic search system, 77 for a heuristic search system, and 100 for a decision tree learning system. The learned strategy also transfers to new programs, where a pretrained agent finds solutions more sample efficiently than solving from scratch. These results demonstrate useful learned guidance on the benchmark while leaving the general undecidability of invariant inference intact.
summary.tldr: Code2Inv learns to construct loop invariants using program-graph memory and sparse feedback from a theorem prover.

title: Learning Loop Invariants for Program Verification

abstract: We present computationally efficient algorithms to test various combinatorial structures of large-scale graphical models. In order to test the hypotheses on their topological structures, we propose two adjacency matrix sketching frameworks: neighborhood sketching and subgraph sketching. The neighborhood sketching algorithm is proposed to test the connectivity of graphical models. This algorithm randomly subsamples vertices and conducts neighborhood regression and screening. The global sketching algorithm is proposed to test the topological properties requiring exponential computation complexity, especially testing the chromatic number and the maximum clique. This algorithm infers the corresponding property based on the sampled subgraph. Our algorithms are shown to substantially accelerate the computation of existing methods. We validate our theory and method through both synthetic simulations and a real application in neuroscience.

paragraphs: Testing the structure of a large graphical model can be computationally demanding, especially for properties involving complex combinations of vertices. This paper develops algorithms that work with sketches of the adjacency matrix. These reduced representations support inference about graph structure while avoiding some of the expense of existing methods.

The neighborhood sketching algorithm targets connectivity. It randomly samples vertices, then uses neighborhood regression and screening. A second approach, subgraph or global sketching, targets properties whose computation can be exponential, particularly the chromatic number and maximum clique. It infers the relevant property from a sampled subgraph.

The two frameworks therefore tailor sampling to different structural questions: neighborhood information for connectivity and sampled subgraphs for harder combinatorial properties. The authors report substantial computational acceleration over existing approaches. They support the theory and method with synthetic simulations and a neuroscience application. The contribution is a set of efficient testing procedures that use partial graph representations to make large-scale structural inference more tractable.
summary.tldr: Neighborhood and subgraph sketches accelerate tests of connectivity and computationally demanding properties in large graphical models.

title: Sketching Method for Large Scale Combinatorial Inference

abstract: Graph-based semi-supervised learning is a very powerful tool in classification tasks, while in most existing literature the labelled nodes are assumed to be randomly sampled. When the labelling status depends on the unobserved node response, ignoring the missingness can lead to significant estimation bias and handicap the classifiers. This situation is called non-ignorable non-response. To solve the problem, we propose a Graph-based joint model with Non-ignorable Non-response (GNN), followed by a joint inverse weighting estimation procedure incorporated with sampling imputation approach. Our method is proved to outperform some state-of-art models in both regression and classification problems, by simulations and real analysis on the Cora dataset.

When the labelling status depends on the unobserved node response, ignoring the missingness can lead to significant estimation bias and handicap the classifiers. This situation is called non-ignorable non-response. To solve the problem, we propose a Graph-based joint model with Non-ignorable Non-response (GNN), followed by a joint inverse weighting estimation procedure incorporated with sampling imputation approach. Our method is proved to outperform some state-of-art models in both regression and classification problems, by simulations and real analysis on the Cora dataset.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses relationships among nodes to learn from a mixture of labeled and unlabeled examples. Much of its existing literature assumes that labeled nodes are sampled randomly. This paper examines a more difficult situation: whether a node receives a label depends on the response that is unobserved when the label is missing.

That dependence is called non-ignorable non-response. It matters because the labeled examples can give a distorted view of the responses across the graph. The authors explain that ignoring this selection process can introduce substantial estimation bias and weaken classification. They propose a joint graph-based model, named GNN, that explicitly incorporates the non-response mechanism.

The estimation procedure combines joint inverse weighting with a sampling-based imputation approach. These components address the selection problem within the proposed model instead of assuming it away. Simulations and an analysis of the Cora dataset show improvements over some state-of-the-art models in regression and classification. The reported evidence supports accounting for response-dependent missingness in these evaluated settings, without establishing superiority over every competing graph-learning method.
summary.tldr: A joint graph model accounts for response-dependent missing labels and improves regression and classification over selected methods in the reported evaluations.

title: Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Learning with Non-ignorable Non-response

abstract: How can neural networks such as ResNet \emph{efficiently} learn CIFAR-10 with test accuracy more than $96 \%$, while other methods, especially kernel methods, fall relatively behind? Can we more provide theoretical justifications for this gap? Recently, there is an influential line of work relating neural networks to kernels in the over-parameterized regime, proving they can learn certain concept class that is also learnable by kernels with similar test error. Yet, can neural networks provably learn some concept class \emph{better} than kernels? We answer this positively in the distribution-free setting. We prove neural networks can efficiently learn a notable class of functions, including those defined by three-layer residual networks with smooth activations, without any distributional assumption. At the same time, we prove there are simple functions in this class such that with the same number of training examples, the test error obtained by neural networks can be \emph{much smaller} than \emph{any} kernel method, including neural tangent kernels (NTK). The main intuition is that \emph{multi-layer} neural networks can implicitly perform hierarchal learning using different layers, which reduces the sample complexity comparing to ``one-shot'' learning algorithms such as kernel methods. In the end, we also prove a computation complexity advantage of ResNet with respect to other learning methods including linear regression over arbitrary feature mappings.

In the end, we also prove a computation complexity advantage of ResNet with respect to other learning methods including linear regression over arbitrary feature mappings.

paragraphs: Connections between overparameterized neural networks and kernel methods explain some neural-network learning behavior, but leave open whether networks can provably do better. This paper establishes such a separation for a particular class of functions. Its results are distribution-free, meaning the learning guarantee does not require assumptions about the input distribution.

The learnable class includes functions represented by three-layer residual networks with smooth activations. Within that class, the authors identify simple functions for which neural networks achieve much lower test error than any kernel method using the same number of training examples. The comparison includes neural tangent kernels, making the result directly relevant to kernel-based accounts of neural learning.

The proposed explanation is hierarchical learning across multiple layers, which can reduce the examples needed compared with the one-shot learning behavior of kernel methods. The paper also proves a computational complexity advantage over other learning methods, including linear regression with arbitrary feature mappings. These are separations for the studied function class, rather than a claim that residual networks outperform kernels on every learning problem.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that residual networks can efficiently learn a function class containing examples where they generalize substantially better than any kernel method.

title: What Can ResNet Learn Efficiently, Going Beyond Kernels?

abstract: We propose a scalable framework for inference in a continuous sigmoidal Cox process that assumes the corresponding intensity function is given by a Gaussian process (GP) prior transformed with a scaled logistic sigmoid function. We present a tractable representation of the likelihood through augmentation with a superposition of Poisson processes. This view enables a structured variational approximation capturing dependencies across variables in the model. Our framework avoids discretization of the domain, does not require accurate numerical integration over the input space and is not limited to GPs with squared exponential kernels. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world data showing that its benefits are particularly pronounced on multivariate input settings where it overcomes the limitations of mean-field methods and sampling schemes. We provide the state of-the-art in terms of speed, accuracy and uncertainty quantification trade-offs.

The task is to perform inference in this model efficiently while retaining useful information about dependencies and uncertainty.

The authors make the likelihood tractable by augmenting the model with a superposition of Poisson processes. This representation supports a structured variational approximation that captures dependencies among model variables. The method avoids dividing the input domain into a discrete grid and does not require accurate numerical integration across that domain.

The framework also accommodates Gaussian-process kernels beyond the squared-exponential family. Evaluations on synthetic and real data show particularly strong benefits when inputs have multiple dimensions, where the approach overcomes limitations of the compared mean-field methods and sampling schemes. The reported outcome is a leading trade-off among speed, accuracy, and uncertainty quantification, connecting the structured approximation to practical inference benefits in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A structured variational method enables scalable continuous Cox-process inference while preserving dependencies and avoiding domain discretization.

title: Structured Variational Inference in Continuous Cox Process Models

abstract: Recently, Charikar and Siminelakis (2017) presented a framework for kernel density estimation in provably sublinear query time, for kernels that possess a certain hashing-based property. However, their data structure requires a significantly increased super-linear storage space, as well as super-linear preprocessing time. These limitations inhibit the practical applicability of their approach on large datasets. In this work, we present an improvement to their framework that retains the same query time, while requiring only linear space and linear preprocessing time. We instantiate our framework with the Laplacian and Exponential kernels, two popular kernels which possess the aforementioned property. Our experiments on various datasets verify that our approach attains accuracy and query time similar to Charikar and Siminelakis (2017), with significantly improved space and preprocessing time.

An existing hashing-based framework can answer queries in provably sublinear time for kernels with a particular property. Its drawback is the work required before querying: both storage and preprocessing grow superlinearly with dataset size, limiting its practicality on large datasets.

This paper improves that framework while retaining the same query-time guarantee. The new construction requires only linear storage and linear preprocessing time. The scope remains tied to the hashing-based property required by the framework. The authors instantiate their approach for the Laplacian and Exponential kernels, both of which satisfy that property.

Experiments on several datasets show accuracy and query time similar to the earlier method, alongside substantial improvements in storage and preprocessing. The contribution makes the setup costs more compatible with the fast-query objective. It shows that, for the supported kernels, preserving sublinear queries does not require retaining the earlier framework's superlinear resource demands.
summary.tldr: An improved hashing-based density estimator preserves sublinear query time while reducing storage and preprocessing to linear complexity.

title: Space and Time Efficient Kernel Density Estimation in High Dimensions

abstract: The method of random projection has been a popular tool for data compression, similarity search, and machine learning. In many practical scenarios, applying quantization on randomly projected data could be very helpful to further reduce storage cost and facilitate more efficient retrievals, while only suffering from little loss in accuracy. In real-world applications, however, data collected from different sources may be quantized under different schemes, which calls for a need to study the asymmetric quantization problem. In this paper, we investigate the cosine similarity estimators derived in such setting under the Lloyd-Max (LM) quantization scheme. We thoroughly analyze the biases and variances of a series of estimators including the basic simple estimators, their normalized versions, and their debiased versions. Furthermore, by studying the monotonicity, we show that the expectation of proposed estimators increases with the true cosine similarity, on a broader family of stair-shaped quantizers. Experiments on nearest neighbor search justify the theory and illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed estimators.

paragraphs: Random projection compresses data, and quantization can further reduce storage by mapping projected values to a limited set of levels. A complication arises when different data sources use different quantization schemes. This paper studies how to estimate cosine similarity in that asymmetric setting, focusing on Lloyd-Max quantization.

The authors analyze several estimators, including simple versions, normalized versions, and versions adjusted to remove bias. Their bias and variance analysis describes both systematic estimation error and variability. This is useful because compressed representations must still support meaningful similarity comparisons even when the two representations were not quantized in the same way.

For a broader class of stair-shaped quantizers, the paper also proves that the proposed estimators' expected values increase as true cosine similarity increases. This is an ordering property in expectation, rather than a guarantee about every individual estimate. Nearest-neighbor experiments support the theoretical analysis and show the estimators' effectiveness, connecting the mathematical results to retrieval from quantized data.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes cosine-similarity estimators for differently quantized random projections and demonstrates their usefulness for nearest-neighbor search.

title: Random Projections with Asymmetric Quantization

abstract: Machine learning classifiers are often trained to recognize a set of pre-defined classes. However, in many applications, it is often desirable to have the flexibility of learning additional concepts, with limited data and without re-training on the full training set. This paper addresses this problem, incremental few-shot learning, where a regular classification network has already been trained to recognize a set of base classes, and several extra novel classes are being considered, each with only a few labeled examples. After learning the novel classes, the model is then evaluated on the overall classification performance on both base and novel classes. To this end, we propose a meta-learning model, the Attention Attractor Network, which regularizes the learning of novel classes. In each episode, we train a set of new weights to recognize novel classes until they converge, and we show that the technique of recurrent back-propagation can back-propagate through the optimization process and facilitate the learning of these parameters. We demonstrate that the learned attractor network can help recognize novel classes while remembering old classes without the need to review the original training set, outperforming various baselines.

paragraphs: Incremental few-shot learning asks a trained classifier to recognize additional classes from only a handful of labeled examples. Success requires recognizing the new classes while continuing to recognize the original ones. This paper studies that combined objective without requiring the model to revisit the complete original training set.

The proposed Attention Attractor Network uses meta-learning to regularize the fitting of new-class weights. During each training episode, those weights are optimized until convergence. Recurrent back-propagation then allows learning through that optimization process, helping train the mechanism that guides adaptation. The approach therefore learns how to constrain new-class learning, rather than relying solely on the few available examples to determine the new weights.

The authors demonstrate that the learned attractor can support recognition of novel classes while retaining recognition of base classes without reviewing the original data. It outperforms various baselines in their evaluations. The findings address the full incremental task: adapting to new categories and maintaining old knowledge are assessed together, making preservation of earlier recognition ability part of the reported success.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned attention attractor guides few-shot class additions while helping preserve recognition of previously learned classes.

title: Incremental Few-Shot Learning with Attention Attractor Networks

abstract: In high-stakes machine learning applications, it is crucial to not only perform well {\em on average}, but also when restricted to {\em difficult} examples. To address this, we consider the problem of training models in a risk-averse manner. We propose an adaptive sampling algorithm for stochastically optimizing the {\em Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR)} of a loss distribution, which measures its performance on the $\alpha$ fraction of most difficult examples. We use a distributionally robust formulation of the CVaR to phrase the problem as a zero-sum game between two players, and solve it efficiently using regret minimization. Our approach relies on sampling from structured Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs), which enables scaling it to large data sets. Finally, we empirically demonstrate its effectiveness on large-scale convex and non-convex learning tasks.

paragraphs: A model can perform well on average while still making large errors on difficult examples. This paper studies training that explicitly emphasizes this difficult portion of the data. Its target is Conditional Value-at-Risk, or CVaR, which measures loss within the fraction of examples with the largest losses. The parameter alpha determines the size of that fraction.

The authors introduce an adaptive sampling algorithm for optimizing this objective using stochastic updates. They express CVaR through a distributionally robust formulation, turning training into a zero-sum game between two players. Regret minimization provides the method for solving that game. This connects the choice of training examples to the risk-sensitive objective rather than treating sampling as an independent implementation decision.

The sampling procedure uses structured Determinantal Point Processes, which the authors identify as enabling the approach to scale to large datasets. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on large-scale learning problems with both convex and nonconvex objectives. The findings support adaptive sampling as a practical way to optimize difficult-example performance, while the stated target remains CVaR rather than a guarantee on every individual example.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling method makes large-scale training for loss on the hardest fraction of examples computationally practical.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Stochastic Risk-Averse Learning

abstract: This paper tackles the modelling of large, complex and multivariate time series panels in a probabilistic setting. To this extent, we present a novel approach reconciling classical state space models with deep learning methods. By augmenting state space models with normalizing flows, we mitigate imprecisions stemming from idealized assumptions in state space models. The resulting model is highly flexible while still retaining many of the attractive properties of state space models, e.g., uncertainty and observation errors are properly accounted for, inference is tractable, sampling is efficient, good generalization performance is observed, even in low data regimes. We demonstrate competitiveness against state-of-the-art deep learning methods on the tasks of forecasting real world data and handling varying levels of missing data.

paragraphs: This paper models collections of complex time series containing many variables. It combines classical state-space models with deep learning in a probabilistic framework. The motivation is to keep the useful treatment of uncertainty found in state-space methods while reducing inaccuracies caused by their idealized modeling assumptions.

The proposed model augments a state-space model with normalizing flows. This increases flexibility while retaining several practical properties: uncertainty and observation errors are accounted for, inference remains tractable, and sampling remains efficient. Those properties matter together because a richer model still needs to support useful probabilistic calculations when analyzing a large collection of time-dependent observations.

The authors observe good generalization, including in low-data settings, and compare the approach with leading deep learning methods on real-world forecasting tasks. They also evaluate its handling of different amounts of missing data and report competitive performance. The findings support combining flexible learned transformations with classical temporal structure, giving a model that can represent more complex observations while preserving the computational and uncertainty-handling advantages emphasized in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Normalizing flows make state-space time-series models more flexible while retaining tractable inference, uncertainty handling, and competitive forecasting performance.

title: Normalizing Kalman Filters for Multivariate Time Series Analysis

abstract: We study an extension of the classic stochastic multi-armed bandit problem which involves multiple plays and Markovian rewards in the rested bandits setting. In order to tackle this problem we consider an adaptive allocation rule which at each stage combines the information from the sample means of all the arms, with the Kullback-Leibler upper confidence bound of a single arm which is selected in round-robin way. For rewards generated from a one-parameter exponential family of Markov chains, we provide a finite-time upper bound for the regret incurred from this adaptive allocation rule, which reveals the logarithmic dependence of the regret on the time horizon, and which is asymptotically optimal. For our analysis we devise several concentration results for Markov chains, including a maximal inequality for Markov chains, that may be of interest in their own right. As a byproduct of our analysis we also establish asymptotically optimal, finite-time guarantees for the case of multiple plays, and i.i.d. rewards drawn from a one-parameter exponential family of probability densities. Additionally, we provide simulation results that illustrate that calculating Kullback-Leibler upper confidence bounds in a round-robin way, is significantly more efficient than calculating them for every arm at each round, and that the expected regrets of those two approaches behave similarly.

It works in the rested-bandit setting and seeks an allocation rule that balances reward collection with learning. The proposed rule combines sample means from every arm with a Kullback-Leibler upper confidence bound computed for just one arm, selected in round-robin order.

For rewards generated by a one-parameter exponential family of Markov chains, the authors prove a finite-time regret bound with logarithmic dependence on the time horizon. The guarantee is asymptotically optimal. Their analysis develops concentration results for Markov chains, including a maximal inequality, and also yields finite-time, asymptotically optimal guarantees for multiple plays with independent rewards from a one-parameter exponential family.

The expected regrets behave similarly in those simulations. Together, the theory and experiments support reducing confidence-bound computation while maintaining strong allocation performance in the specified settings.
summary.tldr: Round-robin confidence-bound updates give asymptotically optimal regret guarantees for specified multi-play bandits while reducing computation in simulations.

title: Finite-Time Analysis of Round-Robin Kullback-Leibler Upper Confidence Bounds for Optimal Adaptive Allocation with Multiple Plays and Markovian Rewards

abstract: Deep neural networks are shown to be susceptible to both adversarial attacks and backdoor attacks. Although many defenses against an individual type of the above attacks have been proposed, the interactions between the vulnerabilities of a network to both types of attacks have not been carefully investigated yet. In this paper, we conduct experiments to study whether adversarial robustness and backdoor robustness can affect each other and find a trade-off—by increasing the robustness of a network to adversarial examples, the network becomes more vulnerable to backdoor attacks. We then investigate the cause and show how such a trade-off can be exploited for either good or bad purposes. Our findings suggest that future research on defense should take both adversarial and backdoor attacks into account when designing algorithms or robustness measures to avoid pitfalls and a false sense of security.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how two kinds of neural-network robustness interact: resistance to adversarial examples and resistance to backdoor attacks. Defenses often address one attack type individually. The authors ask whether improving protection against one can change a model’s vulnerability to the other, making their interaction part of the security assessment.

In their experiments, increasing adversarial robustness makes networks more vulnerable to backdoor attacks. This is an observed trade-off in the studied settings, showing that improvement on one robustness dimension can accompany deterioration on another. The authors also investigate the cause of the interaction and show that it can be exploited for beneficial or harmful purposes.

The main implication concerns how defenses and robustness measures are designed. Evaluating adversarial resistance alone can leave a consequential vulnerability unaccounted for, even when the measured defense improves. The authors therefore suggest considering adversarial and backdoor attacks together. Their findings motivate a joint assessment of these threats rather than treating a gain against one attack family as evidence of broader protection.
summary.tldr: Experiments reveal that improving adversarial robustness can increase backdoor vulnerability, motivating joint evaluation of both threats.

title: On the Trade-off between Adversarial and Backdoor Robustness

abstract: Neuroimaging studies produce gigabytes of spatio-temporal data for a small number of participants and stimuli. Recent work increasingly suggests that the common practice of averaging across participants and stimuli leaves out systematic and meaningful information. We propose Neural Topographic Factor Analysis (NTFA), a probabilistic factor analysis model that infers embeddings for participants and stimuli. These embeddings allow us to reason about differences between participants and stimuli as signal rather than noise. We evaluate NTFA on data from an in-house pilot experiment, as well as two publicly available datasets. We demonstrate that inferring representations for participants and stimuli improves predictive generalization to unseen data when compared to previous topographic methods. We also demonstrate that the inferred latent factor representations are useful for downstream tasks such as multivoxel pattern analysis and functional connectivity.

Averaging across those participants and stimuli can discard systematic differences that carry meaningful information. Neural Topographic Factor Analysis addresses this by explicitly representing those differences within a probabilistic factor analysis model.

NTFA learns embeddings for participants and stimuli, giving each a representation within the model. This allows variation associated with who participated and what they encountered to be treated as signal. The approach therefore aims to retain structured differences that a shared average can obscure, while organizing the observations through latent factors.

The authors evaluate NTFA on an in-house pilot study and two public datasets. Learning participant and stimulus representations improves prediction on unseen data compared with previous topographic methods. The inferred factors also support downstream analyses, including multivoxel pattern analysis and functional connectivity. These results suggest that explicitly modeling participant and stimulus variation can improve both predictive generalization and the usefulness of the resulting representations for further neuroimaging analysis.
summary.tldr: NTFA models participant and stimulus differences in fMRI data, improving predictive generalization and supporting downstream analyses.

title: Neural Topographic Factor Analysis for fMRI Data

abstract: Many problems in statistics and machine learning require the reconstruction of a rank-one signal matrix from noisy data. Enforcing additional prior information on the rank-one component is often key to guaranteeing good recovery performance. One such prior on the low-rank component is sparsity, giving rise to the sparse principal component analysis problem. Unfortunately, there is strong evidence that this problem suffers from a computational-to-statistical gap, which may be fundamental. In this work, we study an alternative prior where the low-rank component is in the range of a trained generative network. We provide a non-asymptotic analysis with optimal sample complexity, up to logarithmic factors, for rank-one matrix recovery under an expansive-Gaussian network prior. Specifically, we establish a favorable global optimization landscape for a nonlinear least squares objective, provided the number of samples is on the order of the dimensionality of the input to the generative model. This result suggests that generative priors have no computational-to-statistical gap for structured rank-one matrix recovery in the finite data, nonasymptotic regime. We present this analysis in the case of both the Wishart and Wigner spiked matrix models.

Sparsity is one common assumption, but sparse principal component analysis has strong evidence of a gap between what data permit statistically and what computation can achieve efficiently. This paper studies a different assumption: the signal component lies in a generative network’s output range.

For an expansive Gaussian network prior, the authors analyze recovery with a finite amount of data. The specific network prior matters to the result: the paper provides guarantees under that structure, and presents the broader absence of a gap as a conclusion suggested by the analysis.
summary.tldr: Under an expansive Gaussian generative prior, rank-one matrix recovery has near-optimal sample complexity and a favorable optimization landscape.

title: Nonasymptotic Guarantees for Spiked Matrix Recovery with Generative Priors

abstract: Current graph neural networks (GNNs) lack generalizability with respect to scales (graph sizes, graph diameters, edge weights, etc..) when solving many graph analysis problems. Taking the perspective of synthesizing graph theory programs, we propose several extensions to address the issue. First, inspired by the dependency of iteration number of common graph theory algorithms on graph size, we learn to terminate the message passing process in GNNs adaptively according to the computation progress. Second, inspired by the fact that many graph theory algorithms are homogeneous with respect to graph weights, we introduce homogeneous transformation layers that are universal homogeneous function approximators, to convert ordinary GNNs to be homogeneous. Experimentally, we show that our GNN can be trained from small-scale graphs but generalize well to large-scale graphs for a number of basic graph theory problems. It also shows generalizability for applications of multi-body physical simulation and image-based navigation problems.

paragraphs: A graph neural network trained on one scale of graph may struggle when graph size, diameter, or edge weights change. This paper approaches that problem by borrowing structural ideas from graph algorithms. The authors aim to make learned computation behave more like an algorithm whose operation adapts to the graph being processed.

The first extension learns when to stop message passing according to computational progress, rather than relying on a fixed number of iterations. The second introduces homogeneous transformation layers, motivated by the consistent way many graph algorithms respond to rescaling weights. These layers can universally approximate homogeneous functions and are used to make otherwise ordinary graph neural networks homogeneous.

Experiments show that the resulting networks can learn from small graphs and generalize well to larger ones on several basic graph-theory problems. The authors also report generalization in multi-body physical simulation and image-based navigation. The results support adaptive computation and weight homogeneity as useful architectural choices for scale transfer, with evidence spanning both graph problems and additional applications.
summary.tldr: Adaptive message-passing termination and homogeneous layers help graph neural networks trained on small graphs generalize to larger-scale problems.

title: Towards Scale-Invariant Graph-related Problem Solving by Iterative Homogeneous GNNs

abstract: Since its introduction a decade ago, relative entropy policy search (REPS) has demonstrated successful policy learning on a number of simulated and real-world robotic domains, not to mention providing algorithmic components used by many recently proposed reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. While REPS is commonly known in the community, there exist no guarantees on its performance when using stochastic and gradient-based solvers. In this paper we aim to fill this gap by providing guarantees and convergence rates for the sub-optimality of a policy learned using first-order optimization methods applied to the REPS objective. We first consider the setting in which we are given access to exact gradients and demonstrate how near-optimality of the objective translates to near-optimality of the policy. We then consider the practical setting of stochastic gradients, and introduce a technique that uses generative access to the underlying Markov decision process to compute parameter updates that maintain favorable convergence to the optimal regularized policy.
originalAbstract: Since its introduction a decade ago, relative entropy policy search (REPS) has demonstrated successful policy learning on a number of simulated and real-world robotic domains, not to mention providing algorithmic components used by many recently proposed reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. While REPS is commonly known in the community, there exist no guarantees on its performance when using stochastic and gradient-based solvers. In this paper we aim to fill this gap by providing guarantees and convergence rates for the sub-optimality of a policy learned using first-order optimization methods applied to the REPS objective. We first consider the setting in which we are given access to exact gradients and demonstrate how near-optimality of the objective translates to near-optimality of the policy. We then consider the practical setting of stochastic gradients, and introduce a technique that uses generative access to the underlying Markov decision process to compute parameter updates that maintain favorable convergence to the optimal regularized policy.

paragraphs: Relative entropy policy search, or REPS, has been used successfully for policy learning in simulated and real robotic domains. The paper addresses a gap between this practical use and theoretical understanding: what performance can be guaranteed when first-order, gradient-based methods optimize the REPS objective, particularly when gradients are stochastic?

The authors first analyze access to exact gradients. They show how getting close to the optimum of the optimization objective translates into getting close to an optimal policy. This link matters because progress on a mathematical training objective is useful only if it supports a corresponding statement about the learned decision-making policy.

They then study stochastic gradients and introduce an update technique that uses generative access to the underlying Markov decision process. Under that access setting, the updates maintain favorable convergence toward the optimal regularized policy. The contribution provides convergence rates and policy-suboptimality guarantees for these solvers, with the stochastic result explicitly relying on generative access and targeting the regularized optimum.
summary.tldr: The paper connects gradient-based optimization of REPS to policy-quality guarantees, including stochastic updates with generative access to the environment.

title: Near Optimal Policy Optimization via REPS

abstract: Bayesian Neural Networks and deep ensembles represent two modern paradigms of uncertainty quantification in deep learning. Yet these approaches struggle to scale mainly due to memory inefficiency, requiring parameter storage several times that of their deterministic counterparts. To address this, we augment each weight matrix with a small inducing weight matrix, projecting the uncertainty quantification into a lower dimensional space. We further extend Matheron’s conditional Gaussian sampling rule to enable fast weight sampling, which enables our inference method to maintain reasonable run-time as compared with ensembles. Importantly, our approach achieves competitive performance to the state-of-the-art in prediction and uncertainty estimation tasks with fully connected neural networks and ResNets, while reducing the parameter size to $\leq 24.3\%$ of that of a single neural network.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks and deep ensembles can quantify predictive uncertainty, but storing their parameters often requires substantially more memory than a deterministic network. This paper addresses that storage burden by representing uncertainty in a lower-dimensional space associated with each network weight matrix.

The method augments each weight matrix with a small inducing weight matrix. These inducing weights provide the compact space in which uncertainty is represented. The authors also extend Matheron’s conditional Gaussian sampling rule to sample network weights quickly. That sampling component matters because reducing storage alone would not make the approach practical if drawing weights remained too expensive.

Experiments with fully connected networks and ResNets show competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods on prediction and uncertainty estimation tasks. The authors report reducing parameter size to at most 24.3% of that of a single neural network while maintaining reasonable runtime relative to ensembles. The findings support a compact uncertainty representation as a way to reduce memory demands without giving up competitive predictive and uncertainty-estimation performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Small inducing weight matrices compress neural-network uncertainty, enabling fast sampling and competitive prediction with sharply reduced parameter storage.

title: Sparse Uncertainty Representation in Deep Learning with Inducing Weights

abstract: One of the central features of modern machine learning models, including deep neural networks, is their generalization ability on structured data in the over-parametrized regime. In this work, we consider an analytically solvable setup to investigate how properties of data impact learning in classification problems, and compare the results obtained for quadratic loss and logistic loss. Using methods from statistical physics, we obtain a precise asymptotic expression for the train and test errors of random feature models trained on a simple model of structured data. The input covariance is built from independent blocks allowing us to tune the saliency of low-dimensional structures and their alignment with respect to the target function.Our results show in particular that in the over-parametrized regime, the impact of data structure on both train and test error curves is greater for logistic loss than for mean-squared loss: the easier the task, the wider the gap in performance between the two losses at the advantage of the logistic. Numerical experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 confirm our insights.

paragraphs: The effect of a classification loss can depend on how useful information is organized in the data. This paper studies that interaction in an analytically solvable model, comparing quadratic and logistic losses. Its focus is the over-parameterized regime, where models have enough capacity to fit training data while still potentially generalizing well.

Using statistical physics methods, the authors derive precise asymptotic expressions for training and test errors of random feature models. Their data model has an input covariance assembled from independent blocks. This lets them vary both the prominence of low-dimensional structure and how that structure aligns with the target function being learned.

Within this setup, data structure has a greater effect on error curves for logistic loss than for mean-squared loss in the over-parameterized regime. As the task becomes easier, the performance advantage of logistic loss grows. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 support these insights. The result connects loss selection to data geometry through a controlled theoretical model, with additional empirical evidence from image classification.
summary.tldr: A solvable random-feature model shows that useful data structure can favor logistic over quadratic loss, supported by image-classification experiments.

title: On the interplay between data structure and loss function in classification problems

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the problem of smoothed online learning, in which the online learner suffers both a hitting cost and a switching cost, and target two performance metrics: competitive ratio and dynamic regret with switching cost. To bound the competitive ratio, we assume the hitting cost is known to the learner in each round, and investigate the simple idea of balancing the two costs by an optimization problem. Surprisingly, we find that minimizing the hitting cost alone is $\max(1, \frac{2}{\alpha})$-competitive for $\alpha$-polyhedral functions and $1 + \frac{4}{\lambda}$-competitive for $\lambda$-quadratic growth functions, both of which improve state-of-the-art results significantly. Moreover, when the hitting cost is both convex and $\lambda$-quadratic growth, we reduce the competitive ratio to $1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ by minimizing the weighted sum of the hitting cost and the switching cost. To bound the dynamic regret with switching cost, we follow the standard setting of online convex optimization, in which the hitting cost is convex but hidden from the learner before making predictions. We modify Ader, an existing algorithm designed for dynamic regret, slightly to take into account the switching cost when measuring the performance. The proposed algorithm, named as Smoothed Ader, attains an optimal $O(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ bound for dynamic regret with switching cost, where $P_T$ is the path-length of the comparator sequence. Furthermore, if the hitting cost is accessible in the beginning of each round, we obtain a similar guarantee without the bounded gradient condition, and establish an $\Omega(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ lower bound to confirm the optimality.

paragraphs: Smoothed online learning charges a learner both for its current decision and for changing that decision over time. The paper studies how to balance these hitting and switching costs under two performance measures. A crucial distinction is whether the learner sees the current hitting cost before acting.

When that cost is available, the authors analyze competitive ratios under specified growth conditions. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone improves existing guarantees for polyhedral functions and functions with quadratic growth. When convexity and quadratic growth both hold, minimizing a weighted combination of hitting and switching costs gives a stronger guarantee.

When the convex hitting cost is hidden until after prediction, the paper modifies Ader to account for switching costs. Smoothed Ader achieves an optimal dynamic-regret bound scaling as the square root of T times one plus comparator path length. This path length measures how much the comparison sequence moves. If costs are revealed beforehand, a similar guarantee holds without bounded gradients, with a matching lower bound confirming optimality.
summary.tldr: Simple cost-balancing strategies and Smoothed Ader improve guarantees for online learning with switching costs under distinct information and growth assumptions.

title: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning

abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive (AR) models for the whole image generation empowered by transformers have achieved comparable or even better performance compared to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Unfortunately, directly applying such AR models to edit/change local image regions, may suffer from the problems of missing global information, slow inference speed, and information leakage of local guidance. To address these limitations, we propose a novel model -- image Local Autoregressive Transformer (iLAT), to better facilitate the locally guided image synthesis. Our iLAT learns the novel local discrete representations, by the newly proposed local autoregressive (LA) transformer of the attention mask and convolution mechanism. Thus iLAT can efficiently synthesize the local image regions by key guidance information. Our iLAT is evaluated on various locally guided image syntheses, such as pose-guided person image synthesis and face editing. Both quantitative and qualitative results show the efficacy of our model.

Directly adapting whole-image generation can lose global information, run slowly, or allow leakage of local guidance information. This paper develops an architecture specifically for image synthesis guided within local regions.

The image Local Autoregressive Transformer, or iLAT, learns local discrete representations using a proposed local autoregressive transformer. Its design includes an attention mask and convolution mechanism tailored to this setting. These components support efficient generation of local image regions using key guidance information, addressing the difficulties identified when whole-image autoregressive models are applied directly.

The authors evaluate iLAT on locally guided synthesis tasks, including pose-guided person image synthesis and face editing. Both numerical evaluations and visual results support the model’s effectiveness. The contribution centers on matching the representation and autoregressive mechanism to the local synthesis task. This matters because producing a guided region calls for handling the relationship between that region, its guidance, and the rest of the image.
summary.tldr: iLAT uses local discrete representations and a tailored autoregressive transformer to efficiently synthesize guided image regions.

title: The Image Local Autoregressive Transformer

abstract: Generative modeling of multivariate time series has remained challenging partly due to the complex, non-deterministic dynamics across long-distance timesteps. In this paper, we propose deep probabilistic methods that combine state-space models (SSMs) with transformer architectures. In contrast to previously proposed SSMs, our approaches use attention mechanism to model non-Markovian dynamics in the latent space and avoid recurrent neural networks entirely. We also extend our models to include several layers of stochastic variables organized in a hierarchy for further expressiveness. Compared to transformer models, ours are probabilistic, non-autoregressive, and capable of generating diverse long-term forecasts with uncertainty estimates. Extensive experiments show that our models consistently outperform competitive baselines on various tasks and datasets, including time series forecasting and human motion prediction.

paragraphs: Multivariate time series involve several quantities evolving together, often with uncertain relationships across distant time steps. This paper combines state-space models with transformers to represent those dynamics probabilistically. Its aim is to generate plausible long-term futures while also representing uncertainty about how the sequence will develop.

The models use attention to capture non-Markovian dynamics in the latent space, allowing the hidden evolution to depend on a broader history. They avoid recurrent neural networks entirely. The authors also introduce versions with multiple layers of stochastic variables arranged hierarchically, giving the model additional expressive capacity for uncertain sequence structure.

The resulting models are probabilistic and non-autoregressive, and can produce diverse long-term forecasts with uncertainty estimates. Experiments across multiple tasks and datasets, including time series forecasting and human motion prediction, show consistent improvements over competitive baselines. The findings support combining attention's ability to model long-range relationships with the stochastic structure of state-space models. The contribution concerns both predictive performance and the ability to describe multiple possible futures.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic transformers combine attention and stochastic state-space models to generate diverse long-term forecasts with uncertainty estimates.

title: Probabilistic Transformer For Time Series Analysis

abstract: We present a novel approach for tracking multiple people in video. Unlike past approaches which employ 2D representations, we focus on using 3D representations of people, located in three-dimensional space. To this end, we develop a method, Human Mesh and Appearance Recovery (HMAR) which in addition to extracting the 3D geometry of the person as a SMPL mesh, also extracts appearance as a texture map on the triangles of the mesh. This serves as a 3D representation for appearance that is robust to viewpoint and pose changes. Given a video clip, we first detect bounding boxes corresponding to people, and for each one, we extract 3D appearance, pose, and location information using HMAR. These embedding vectors are then sent to a transformer, which performs spatio-temporal aggregation of the representations over the duration of the sequence. The similarity of the resulting representations is used to solve for associations that assigns each person to a tracklet. We evaluate our approach on the Posetrack, MuPoTs and AVA datasets. We find that 3D representations are more effective than 2D representations for tracking in these settings, and we obtain state-of-the-art performance. Code and results are available at: https://brjathu.github.io/T3DP.

paragraphs: Tracking several people through video requires recognizing the same person despite changes in pose and viewpoint. This paper represents people through three-dimensional geometry, appearance, and location. Its Human Mesh and Appearance Recovery method extracts a SMPL body mesh and places appearance information on that mesh as a texture map.

Attaching appearance to the body’s surface provides a representation that is robust to changes in viewing angle and pose. For each detected person, the system extracts embeddings describing appearance, pose, and location. A transformer then combines these representations across space and time over the video sequence, allowing information from multiple observations to contribute to the tracking representation.

The system compares the resulting representations to associate detections with tracklets. Evaluations on Posetrack, MuPoTs, and AVA find the three-dimensional representations more effective than two-dimensional ones in these settings, with state-of-the-art tracking performance. The findings support using body-centered appearance together with geometry and temporal aggregation to maintain identity through visual changes, rather than relying solely on the appearance of an isolated two-dimensional detection.
summary.tldr: Combining textured 3D body representations with temporal aggregation improves multi-person tracking across the evaluated video datasets.

title: Tracking People with 3D Representations

abstract: Understanding how grid cells perform path integration calculations remains a fundamental problem. In this paper, we conduct theoretical analysis of a general representation model of path integration by grid cells, where the 2D self-position is encoded as a higher dimensional vector, and the 2D self-motion is represented by a general transformation of the vector. We identify two conditions on the transformation. One is a group representation condition that is necessary for path integration. The other is an isotropic scaling condition that ensures locally conformal embedding, so that the error in the vector representation translates conformally to the error in the 2D self-position. Then we investigate the simplest transformation, i.e., the linear transformation, uncover its explicit algebraic and geometric structure as matrix Lie group of rotation, and explore the connection between the isotropic scaling condition and a special class of hexagon grid patterns. Finally, with our optimization-based approach, we manage to learn hexagon grid patterns that share similar properties of the grid cells in the rodent brain. The learned model is capable of accurate long distance path integration. Code is available at https://github.com/ruiqigao/grid-cell-path.

paragraphs: Path integration means updating an estimate of position using self-motion. The paper studies a grid-cell representation in which a two-dimensional position becomes a higher-dimensional vector, and movement transforms that vector. The question is what properties these transformations need for coherent position updates and well-behaved representation errors.

The analysis identifies two conditions with different roles. A group-representation condition is necessary for path integration. An isotropic-scaling condition ensures a locally conformal embedding, so local errors in the representation translate conformally into position errors. The authors then examine linear transformations, describing their algebraic and geometric structure through a matrix Lie group of rotations.

The paper also explores a connection between isotropic scaling and a special class of hexagonal grid patterns. An optimization-based approach learns hexagonal patterns with properties similar to rodent grid cells, and the resulting model performs accurate long-distance path integration. These results connect mathematical conditions on movement representations to learned spatial patterns and navigation behavior without establishing that the brain necessarily uses this model.
summary.tldr: The paper connects group-structured motion updates and isotropic scaling to grid-cell representations and learned hexagonal patterns.

title: On Path Integration of Grid Cells: Group Representation and Isotropic Scaling

abstract: Rule-based models, e.g., decision trees, are widely used in scenarios demanding high model interpretability for their transparent inner structures and good model expressivity. However, rule-based models are hard to optimize, especially on large data sets, due to their discrete parameters and structures. Ensemble methods and fuzzy/soft rules are commonly used to improve performance, but they sacrifice the model interpretability. To obtain both good scalability and interpretability, we propose a new classifier, named Rule-based Representation Learner (RRL), that automatically learns interpretable non-fuzzy rules for data representation and classification. To train the non-differentiable RRL effectively, we project it to a continuous space and propose a novel training method, called Gradient Grafting, that can directly optimize the discrete model using gradient descent. An improved design of logical activation functions is also devised to increase the scalability of RRL and enable it to discretize the continuous features end-to-end. Exhaustive experiments on nine small and four large data sets show that RRL outperforms the competitive interpretable approaches and can be easily adjusted to obtain a trade-off between classification accuracy and model complexity for different scenarios. Our code is available at: https://github.com/12wang3/rrl.

paragraphs: Rule-based classifiers offer transparent structures, but their discrete rules and parameters make optimization difficult, especially on large datasets. This paper introduces the Rule-based Representation Learner, or RRL, to learn explicit, non-fuzzy rules for both representing data and classifying it. The aim is to combine interpretability with scalable training.

RRL is non-differentiable, so the authors project it into a continuous space and introduce a training procedure called Gradient Grafting. This procedure enables gradient descent to directly optimize the discrete model. They also redesign logical activation functions to improve scalability and allow continuous input features to be discretized as part of end-to-end training.

The model can also be adjusted to trade classification accuracy against model complexity for different settings. These results support a route to learning expressive discrete rules while retaining the ability to control how complicated the resulting classifier becomes.
summary.tldr: RRL uses Gradient Grafting to learn scalable, interpretable discrete-rule classifiers with adjustable accuracy-complexity trade-offs.

title: Scalable Rule-Based Representation Learning for Interpretable Classification

abstract: We release 70 small and discriminative test sets for machine translation (MT) evaluation called variance-aware test sets (VAT), covering 35 translation directions from WMT16 to WMT20 competitions. VAT is automatically created by a novel variance-aware filtering method that filters the indiscriminative test instances of the current MT benchmark without any human labor. Experimental results show that VAT outperforms the original WMT benchmark in terms of the correlation with human judgment across mainstream language pairs and test sets. Further analysis on the properties of VAT reveals the challenging linguistic features (e.g., translation of low-frequency words and proper nouns) for the competitive MT systems, providing guidance for constructing future MT test sets. The test sets and the code for preparing variance-aware MT test sets are freely available at https://github.com/NLP2CT/Variance-Aware-MT-Test-Sets.

paragraphs: A translation test set is useful when it distinguishes between systems in ways that agree with human judgment. This paper develops variance-aware test sets, or VAT, by removing benchmark examples that offer little discrimination between systems. The filtering method is automatic and does not require human labor to construct the resulting sets.

The release contains 70 small test sets covering 35 translation directions from the WMT16 through WMT20 competitions. In experiments across mainstream language pairs and test sets, evaluation on VAT correlates better with human judgments than evaluation on the original WMT benchmarks. The finding concerns the quality of system assessment rather than an improvement to the translation systems themselves.

The authors also examine what makes the retained examples challenging. Their analysis identifies features such as low-frequency words and proper nouns as difficulties for competitive translation systems. These observations offer guidance for future test-set construction: selecting examples that expose meaningful differences can improve evaluation even when the resulting test sets are small.
summary.tldr: Automatically filtered translation test sets distinguish systems more effectively and correlate better with human judgments in the reported experiments.

title: Variance-Aware Machine Translation Test Sets

abstract: Monocular 3D object detection (Mono3D) in mobile settings (e.g., on a vehicle, a drone, or a robot) is an important yet challenging task. Due to the near-far disparity phenomenon of monocular vision and the ever-changing camera pose, it is hard to acquire high detection accuracy, especially for far objects. Inspired by the insight that the depth of an object can be well determined according to the depth of the ground where it stands, in this paper, we propose a novel Mono3D framework, called MoGDE, which constantly estimates the corresponding ground depth of an image and then utilizes the estimated ground depth information to guide Mono3D. To this end, we utilize a pose detection network to estimate the pose of the camera and then construct a feature map portraying pixel-level ground depth according to the 3D-to-2D perspective geometry. Moreover, to improve Mono3D with the estimated ground depth, we design an RGB-D feature fusion network based on the transformer structure, where the long-range self-attention mechanism is utilized to effectively identify ground-contacting points and pin the corresponding ground depth to the image feature map. We conduct extensive experiments on the real-world KITTI dataset. The results demonstrate that MoGDE can effectively improve the Mono3D accuracy and robustness for both near and far objects. MoGDE yields the best performance compared with the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin and is ranked number one on the KITTI 3D benchmark.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from a single camera is difficult when the camera moves and objects appear at different distances. MoGDE uses the observation that an object's depth can be inferred from the ground where it stands. It repeatedly estimates ground depth and uses that information to guide object detection.

A pose detection network first estimates the camera's pose. Perspective geometry then produces a feature map describing ground depth at the pixel level. A transformer-based fusion network combines this estimated depth with image features. Its long-range attention helps identify ground-contact points and associate their ground depth with the relevant image information.

Experiments on KITTI show improvements in detection accuracy and robustness for both nearby and distant objects. The paper reports a large advantage over state-of-the-art methods and first place on the KITTI 3D benchmark. The approach makes ground contact a useful geometric reference for mobile monocular detection, linking camera pose estimation, depth construction, and visual features within one framework.
summary.tldr: MoGDE improves monocular 3D detection by estimating ground depth from camera pose and attaching it to object image features.

title: MoGDE: Boosting Mobile Monocular 3D Object Detection with Ground Depth Estimation

abstract: Laplace approximation (LA) and its linearized variant (LLA) enable effortless adaptation of pretrained deep neural networks to Bayesian neural networks. The generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is typically introduced to improve their tractability. However, LA and LLA are still confronted with non-trivial inefficiency issues and should rely on Kronecker-factored, diagonal, or even last-layer approximate GGN matrices in practical use. These approximations are likely to harm the fidelity of learning outcomes. To tackle this issue, inspired by the connections between LLA and neural target kernels (NTKs), we develop a Nystrom approximation to NTKs to accelerate LLA. Our method benefits from the capability of popular deep learning libraries for forward mode automatic differentiation, and enjoys reassuring theoretical guarantees. Extensive studies reflect the merits of the proposed method in aspects of both scalability and performance. Our method can even scale up to architectures like vision transformers. We also offer valuable ablation studies to diagnose our method. Code is available at https://github.com/thudzj/ELLA.

paragraphs: Laplace approximation provides a way to adapt a pretrained neural network into a Bayesian neural network. Its linearized version offers a related route, but both remain computationally demanding. Practical implementations therefore simplify the generalized Gauss–Newton matrix, sometimes using only diagonal information or restricting the approximation to the last layer. These shortcuts can reduce the fidelity of the resulting approximation.

The paper develops a different acceleration strategy by exploiting a connection between linearized Laplace approximation and neural kernels. It applies a Nyström approximation to those kernels, making the kernel connection the basis for reducing computation. The method also uses forward mode automatic differentiation available in popular deep learning libraries.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and report empirical benefits in both scalability and performance, including applicability to vision transformers. They also use ablation studies to examine the method. The contribution is a route to making Bayesian adaptation more practical while addressing the fidelity concerns associated with the matrix simplifications described in the paper.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based approximation accelerates linearized Laplace inference, with theoretical guarantees and demonstrated scalability to vision transformers.

title: Accelerated Linearized Laplace Approximation for Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: We present a self-supervised depth estimation approach using a unified volumetric feature fusion for surround-view images. Given a set of surround-view images, our method constructs a volumetric feature map by extracting image feature maps from surround-view images and fuse the feature maps into a shared, unified 3D voxel space. The volumetric feature map then can be used for estimating a depth map at each surround view by projecting it into an image coordinate. A volumetric feature contains 3D information at its local voxel coordinate; thus our method can also synthesize a depth map at arbitrary rotated viewpoints by projecting the volumetric feature map into the target viewpoints. Furthermore, assuming static camera extrinsics in the multi-camera system, we propose to estimate a canonical camera motion from the volumetric feature map. Our method leverages 3D spatio- temporal context to learn metric-scale depth and the canonical camera motion in a self-supervised manner. Our method outperforms the prior arts on DDAD and nuScenes datasets, especially estimating more accurate metric-scale depth and consistent depth between neighboring views.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from surround-view cameras requires combining information from several perspectives. This paper creates a shared three-dimensional representation by extracting image features from each view and fusing them into a common voxel space. The resulting volume brings the cameras' information together before producing a depth map for each view.

To obtain a depth map, the method projects the volumetric features into the desired image coordinates. Because each voxel carries local 3D information, the same representation can also synthesize depth at arbitrarily rotated viewpoints. Assuming the cameras' relative positions and orientations remain fixed, the method additionally estimates a canonical camera motion from the volume.

The approach uses spatial and temporal context to learn metric-scale depth and canonical motion through self-supervision. On DDAD and nuScenes, it outperforms prior methods, particularly in metric-scale depth accuracy and consistency between neighboring views. The shared volume therefore supports both improved individual depth estimates and agreement across cameras, with the fixed-extrinsics assumption underpinning the proposed motion estimation.
summary.tldr: Fusing surround-view image features into a shared 3D volume improves self-supervised metric depth and consistency between neighboring camera views.

title: Self-supervised surround-view depth estimation with volumetric feature fusion

abstract: We propose focal modulation networks (FocalNets in short), where self-attention (SA) is completely replaced by a focal modulation module for modeling token interactions in vision. Focal modulation comprises three components: $(i)$ hierarchical contextualization, implemented using a stack of depth-wise convolutional layers, to encode visual contexts from short to long ranges, $(ii)$ gated aggregation to selectively gather contexts for each query token based on its content, and $(iii)$ element-wise modulation or affine transformation to fuse the aggregated context into the query. Extensive experiments show FocalNets outperform the state-of-the-art SA counterparts (e.g., Swin and Focal Transformers) with similar computational cost on the tasks of image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Specifically, FocalNets with tiny and base size achieve 82.3% and 83.9% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. After pretrained on ImageNet-22K, it attains 86.5% and 87.3% top-1 accuracy when finetuned with resolution 224$^2$ and 384$^2$, respectively. When transferred to downstream tasks, FocalNets exhibit clear superiority. For object detection with Mask R-CNN, FocalNet base trained with 1$\times$ outperforms the Swin counterpart by 2.1 points and already surpasses Swin trained with 3$\times$ schedule (49.0 v.s. 48.5). For semantic segmentation with UPerNet, FocalNet base at single-scale outperforms Swin by 2.4, and beats Swin at multi-scale (50.5 v.s. 49.7). Using large FocalNet and mask2former, we achieve 58.5 mIoU for ADE20K semantic segmentation, and 57.9 PQ for COCO Panoptic Segmentation. These results render focal modulation a favorable alternative to SA for effective and efficient visual modeling. Code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/FocalNet.
