paragraphs: FocalNets replace self-attention entirely with a different mechanism for exchanging information between visual tokens. The proposed focal modulation module first builds contextual information at several ranges, then selects useful context for each token, and finally uses that context to modify the token's representation. The aim is effective visual modeling at computational costs similar to attention-based alternatives.

The module uses a stack of depth-wise convolutions to gather context from nearby and more distant regions. Gates select which contextual information matters for each query token based on its content. An element-wise modulation or affine transformation then combines the selected context with the query. These stages separate constructing context, selecting it, and applying it.

Experiments show improvements over self-attention counterparts, including Swin and Focal Transformers, on classification, detection, and segmentation. Tiny and base FocalNets reach 82.3% and 83.9% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy. In the reported Mask R-CNN comparison, a base FocalNet with a shorter training schedule also surpasses a Swin model trained with a longer schedule. The results support focal modulation as a practical alternative across several vision tasks.
summary.tldr: FocalNets replace self-attention with selective multiscale context modulation and outperform attention-based counterparts across several vision benchmarks.

title: Focal Modulation Networks

abstract: We investigate a practical domain adaptation task, called source-free domain adaptation (SFUDA), where the source pretrained model is adapted to the target domain without access to the source data. Existing techniques mainly leverage self-supervised pseudo-labeling to achieve class-wise global alignment [1] or rely on local structure extraction that encourages the feature consistency among neighborhoods [2]. While impressive progress has been made, both lines of methods have their own drawbacks – the “global” approach is sensitive to noisy labels while the “local” counterpart suffers from the source bias. In this paper, we present Divide and Contrast (DaC), a new paradigm for SFUDA that strives to connect the good ends of both worlds while bypassing their limitations. Based on the prediction confidence of the source model, DaC divides the target data into source-like and target-specific samples, where either group of samples is treated with tailored goals under an adaptive contrastive learning framework. Specifically, the source-like samples are utilized for learning global class clustering thanks to their relatively clean labels. The more noisy target-specific data are harnessed at the instance level for learning the intrinsic local structures. We further align the source-like domain with the target-specific samples using a memory bank-based Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) loss to reduce the distribution mismatch. Extensive experiments on VisDA, Office-Home, and the more challenging DomainNet have verified the superior performance of DaC over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/ZyeZhang/DaC.git.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation updates a pretrained model for a new domain without access to its original training data. Existing approaches either organize target examples into classes using predicted labels or emphasize consistency among nearby examples. The former can suffer from incorrect labels; the latter can retain biases from the source domain.

Divide and Contrast uses the source model's prediction confidence to split target examples into source-like and target-specific groups. The more reliable source-like examples support global class clustering. The noisier target-specific examples support learning local structure at the individual-example level. An adaptive contrastive learning framework gives these groups different learning goals according to their roles.

The method also uses a memory bank and a Maximum Mean Discrepancy loss to reduce the distribution mismatch between the groups. This connects their representations while preserving the distinction between their learning objectives. Experiments on VisDA, Office-Home, and DomainNet report better performance than existing state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the strategy of treating target examples differently according to confidence.
summary.tldr: Divide and Contrast adapts a model without source data by using confident target examples for class structure and noisier examples for local structure.

title: Divide and Contrast: Source-free Domain Adaptation via Adaptive Contrastive Learning

abstract: Kernel $k$-means is arguably one of the most common approaches to clustering. In this paper, we investigate the efficiency of kernel $k$-means combined with randomized sketches in terms of both statistical analysis and computational requirements. More precisely, we propose a unified randomized sketches framework to kernel $k$-means and investigate its excess risk bounds, obtaining the state-of-the-art risk bound with only a fraction of computations. Indeed, we prove that it suffices to choose the sketch dimension $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ to obtain the same accuracy of exact kernel $k$-means with greatly reducing the computational costs, for sub-Gaussian sketches, the randomized orthogonal system (ROS) sketches, and Nystr\"{o}m kernel $k$-means, where $n$ is the number of samples. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result of this kind for unsupervised learning. Finally, the numerical experiments on simulated data and real-world datasets validate our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Kernel k-means is a clustering method whose computational demands motivate compressed approximations. This paper studies randomized sketches, which provide smaller representations for the clustering computation. The authors ask whether these approximations can reduce computational work while preserving the statistical accuracy associated with exact kernel k-means.

They propose a unified framework covering sub-Gaussian sketches, randomized orthogonal system sketches, and Nyström kernel k-means. Their excess-risk analysis establishes a state-of-the-art bound using only a fraction of the computations. In particular, they show that a sketch dimension on the square-root-of-n scale, expressed as an Omega requirement, suffices to obtain the same accuracy as exact kernel k-means, where n is the sample count.

The result makes the tradeoff between compression and statistical quality explicit across several sketching approaches. Matching accuracy here refers to the analyzed statistical performance, rather than requiring identical cluster assignments. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets validate the theoretical analysis. Together, the framework and evidence support randomized compression as a way to make kernel clustering computationally cheaper without sacrificing its stated accuracy.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis shows that randomized sketches can preserve kernel k-means accuracy while substantially reducing computation.

title: Randomized Sketches for Clustering: Fast and Optimal Kernel $k$-Means

abstract: Over the years, state-of-the-art (SoTA) image captioning methods have achieved promising results on some evaluation metrics (e.g., CIDEr). However, recent findings show that the captions generated by these methods tend to be biased toward the "average" caption that only captures the most general mode (a.k.a, language pattern) in the training corpus, i.e., the so-called mode collapse problem. Affected by it, the generated captions are limited in diversity and usually less informative than natural image descriptions made by humans. In this paper, we seek to avoid this problem by proposing a Discrete Mode Learning (DML) paradigm for image captioning. Our innovative idea is to explore the rich modes in the training caption corpus to learn a set of "mode embeddings", and further use them to control the mode of the generated captions for existing image captioning models. Specifically, the proposed DML optimizes a dual architecture that consists of an image-conditioned discrete variational autoencoder (CdVAE) branch and a mode-conditioned image captioning (MIC) branch. The CdVAE branch maps each image caption to one of the mode embeddings stored in a learned codebook, and is trained with a pure non-autoregressive generation objective to make the modes distinct and representative. The MIC branch can be simply modified from an existing image captioning model, where the mode embedding is added to the original word embeddings as the control signal. In the experiments, we apply the proposed DML to two widely used image captioning models, Transformer and AoANet. The results show that the learned mode embedding successfully facilitates these models to generate high-quality image captions with different modes, further leading to better performance for both diversity and quality on the MS COCO dataset.

paragraphs: Image-captioning models can score well while repeatedly producing generic descriptions. The paper treats this as mode collapse: the model favors a dominant language pattern instead of reflecting the variety present in human captions. Discrete Mode Learning, or DML, aims to learn multiple representative patterns and make them available as explicit controls during generation.

The method has two connected branches. An image-conditioned discrete variational autoencoder assigns captions to embeddings stored in a learned codebook. It uses a non-autoregressive generation objective to encourage distinct, representative modes. A mode-conditioned captioning branch then adds the chosen mode embedding to its word embeddings, allowing an existing captioning model to use the learned pattern as a generation signal.

The authors apply DML to Transformer and AoANet captioning models. On MS COCO, the learned embeddings help these models produce high-quality captions in different modes, improving both diversity and quality. The approach matters because it represents variation within the training captions as something the model can deliberately use, rather than relying on a single dominant description pattern.
summary.tldr: Discrete Mode Learning gives captioning models learned language-pattern controls that improve caption diversity and quality on MS COCO.

title: Learning Distinct and Representative Modes for Image Captioning

abstract: Transformation invariances are present in many real-world problems. For example, image classification is usually invariant to rotation and color transformation: a rotated car in a different color is still identified as a car. Data augmentation, which adds the transformed data into the training set and trains a model on the augmented data, is one commonly used technique to build these invariances into the learning process. However, it is unclear how data augmentation performs theoretically and what the optimal algorithm is in presence of transformation invariances. In this paper, we study PAC learnability under transformation invariances in three settings according to different levels of realizability: (i) A hypothesis fits the augmented data; (ii) A hypothesis fits only the original data and the transformed data lying in the support of the data distribution; (iii) Agnostic case. One interesting observation is that distinguishing between the original data and the transformed data is necessary to achieve optimal accuracy in setting (ii) and (iii), which implies that any algorithm not differentiating between the original and transformed data (including data augmentation) is not optimal. Furthermore, this type of algorithms can even ``harm'' the accuracy. In setting (i), although it is unnecessary to distinguish between the two data sets, data augmentation still does not perform optimally. Due to such a difference, we propose two combinatorial measures characterizing the optimal sample complexity in setting (i) and (ii)(iii) and provide the optimal algorithms.

paragraphs: A transformation can change an input without changing its correct label: rotating an image of a car is one example. Data augmentation tries to teach this behavior by adding transformed examples to training. This paper asks when that strategy is theoretically effective and what a statistically optimal learning algorithm should do with transformation invariances.

The analysis separates three situations. In the first, some hypothesis correctly labels all augmented data. In the second, a hypothesis fits the original data and transformed examples within the data distribution’s support. The third is agnostic, allowing imperfect fit. These distinctions matter because transformed examples do not always have the same theoretical status as original observations.

In the second and third settings, achieving optimal accuracy requires distinguishing original from transformed data; methods that ignore the distinction can even hurt accuracy. In the first setting, that distinction is unnecessary, but ordinary augmentation still has suboptimal sample complexity. The authors introduce two combinatorial measures characterizing optimal sample requirements across these settings and provide algorithms achieving those optima.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal learning under transformation invariances and shows why ordinary data augmentation can be theoretically suboptimal.

title: A Theory of PAC Learnability under Transformation Invariances

abstract: We address the problem of incremental semantic segmentation (ISS) recognizing novel object/stuff categories continually without forgetting previous ones that have been learned. The catastrophic forgetting problem is particularly severe in ISS, since pixel-level ground-truth labels are available only for the novel categories at training time. To address the problem, regularization-based methods exploit probability calibration techniques to learn semantic information from unlabeled pixels. While such techniques are effective, there is still a lack of theoretical understanding of them. Replay-based methods propose to memorize a small set of images for previous categories. They achieve state-of-the-art performance at the cost of large memory footprint. We propose in this paper a novel ISS method, dubbed ALIFE, that provides a better compromise between accuracy and efficiency. To this end, we first show an in-depth analysis on the calibration techniques to better understand the effects on ISS. Based on this, we then introduce an adaptive logit regularizer (ALI) that enables our model to better learn new categories, while retaining knowledge for previous ones. We also present a feature replay scheme that memorizes features, instead of images directly, in order to reduce memory requirements significantly. Since a feature extractor is changed continually, memorized features should also be updated at every incremental stage. To handle this, we introduce category-specific rotation matrices updating the features for each category separately. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with extensive experiments on standard ISS benchmarks, and show that our method achieves a better trade-off in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Incremental semantic segmentation asks a model to keep learning new categories of pixels without losing its ability to recognize earlier categories. This is especially difficult when each training stage supplies labels only for the new categories. Previously learned objects can still appear in images, but their pixels no longer provide explicit supervision for their old labels.

ALIFE combines a change to the learning objective with a more compact form of memory. The authors analyze probability calibration techniques used to extract semantic information from unlabeled pixels, then introduce an adaptive regularizer on the model’s prediction scores. It is designed to support learning new categories while preserving earlier knowledge.

The memory component stores features instead of complete images, reducing storage requirements. Because the feature extractor changes during learning, ALIFE updates stored features using a separate rotation matrix for each category. Experiments on standard benchmarks show a better balance between accuracy and efficiency, supporting the combination of adaptive regularization and updated feature replay.
summary.tldr: ALIFE combines adaptive regularization with updated feature memories to improve the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff in incremental semantic segmentation.

title: ALIFE: Adaptive Logit Regularizer and Feature Replay for Incremental Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this problem by trading off model quality to reduce the compute complexity, but often do not achieve wall-clock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware---accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory. We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, showing that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard attention, and is optimal for a range of SRAM sizes. We also extend FlashAttention, yielding an approximate attention algorithm that is faster than any existing approximate attention method. FlashAttention, 3x speedup on GPT-2 (seq. length 1K), and 2.4x speedup on long-range arena (seq. length 1K-4K). FlashAttention, yielding higher quality models (0.7 better perplexity on GPT-2 and 6.4 points of lift on long-document classification) and entirely new capabilities: the first Transformers to achieve better-than-chance performance on the Path-X challenge (seq. length 16K, 61.4% accuracy) and Path-256 (seq. length 64K, 63.1% accuracy).

Its analysis proves fewer high-bandwidth-memory accesses and optimality over a range of SRAM sizes.

The supplied abstract reports a 3x speedup on GPT-2 at sequence length 1K and 2.4x on Long Range Arena at lengths 1K–4K. It also describes an approximate extension. Some result sentences are fragmented, so the precise training configurations require the linked paper.

Reported quality outcomes include 0.7 better GPT-2 perplexity and 6.4 points on long-document classification. Long-sequence demonstrations achieve 61.4% on Path-X at length 16K and 63.1% on Path-256 at length 64K. The central algorithm computes exact attention; these broader quality gains concern the enabled experimental systems rather than changing the mathematical attention operation itself.
summary.tldr: FlashAttention accelerates exact attention by reducing movement between GPU memory levels.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNN) are an effective framework that exploit inter-relationships within graph-structured data for learning. Principal component analysis (PCA) involves the projection of data on the eigenspace of the covariance matrix and draws similarities with the graph convolutional filters in GNNs. Motivated by this observation, we study a GNN architecture, called coVariance neural network (VNN), that operates on sample covariance matrices as graphs. We theoretically establish the stability of VNNs to perturbations in the covariance matrix, thus, implying an advantage over standard PCA-based data analysis approaches that are prone to instability due to principal components associated with close eigenvalues. Our experiments on real-world datasets validate our theoretical results and show that VNN performance is indeed more stable than PCA-based statistical approaches. Moreover, our experiments on multi-resolution datasets also demonstrate that VNNs are amenable to transferability of performance over covariance matrices of different dimensions; a feature that is infeasible for PCA-based approaches.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis represents data using directions derived from its covariance matrix. Those directions can be unstable when their associated eigenvalues are close together. This paper connects covariance-based analysis with graph neural networks, which learn from relationships between elements, and asks whether that connection can yield a more stable approach.

The proposed coVariance neural network, or VNN, treats a sample covariance matrix as a graph on which the network operates. The motivation comes from similarities between PCA's use of covariance eigenspaces and graph convolutional filters. The authors theoretically establish stability to perturbations in the covariance matrix, providing a basis for handling changes that can disrupt standard PCA-based analysis.

Experiments on real datasets support the stability result and show more stable performance than PCA-based statistical approaches. Experiments involving multiple resolutions also demonstrate transfer of performance across covariance matrices with different dimensions, a capability the abstract contrasts with PCA-based approaches. These findings support using covariance relationships as a learnable structure for stable analysis and transfer across resolutions.
summary.tldr: VNNs treat covariance matrices as graphs, with theoretical stability guarantees and experimental evidence of stability and transfer across matrix dimensions.

title: coVariance Neural Networks

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) seeks predictors which perform well on unseen test distributions by leveraging data drawn from multiple related training distributions or domains. To achieve this, DG is commonly formulated as an average- or worst-case problem over the set of possible domains. However, predictors that perform well on average lack robustness while predictors that perform well in the worst case tend to be overly-conservative. To address this, we propose a new probabilistic framework for DG where the goal is to learn predictors that perform well with high probability. Our key idea is that distribution shifts seen during training should inform us of probable shifts at test time, which we realize by explicitly relating training and test domains as draws from the same underlying meta-distribution. To achieve probable DG, we propose a new optimization problem called Quantile Risk Minimization (QRM). By minimizing the $\alpha$-quantile of predictor's risk distribution over domains, QRM seeks predictors that perform well with probability $\alpha$. To solve QRM in practice, we propose the Empirical QRM (EQRM) algorithm and provide: (i) a generalization bound for EQRM; and (ii) the conditions under which EQRM recovers the causal predictor as $\alpha \to 1$. In our experiments, we introduce a more holistic quantile-focused evaluation protocol for DG, and demonstrate that EQRM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on datasets from WILDS and DomainBed.

paragraphs: Domain generalization seeks models that work on unseen data distributions using experience from several training domains. This paper proposes a probabilistic objective between average performance and worst-case protection. Its key modeling assumption is that training and test domains are draws from a shared underlying distribution over domains, allowing observed shifts to inform which future shifts are probable.

Quantile Risk Minimization targets a chosen quantile of the predictor’s risk across domains. Choosing probability level alpha asks for a predictor whose risk is low with probability alpha under that domain distribution. This makes the desired coverage explicit, rather than treating all possible shifts as equally relevant or summarizing them only through their average.

The authors introduce Empirical QRM as a practical algorithm and establish a generalization bound. They also identify conditions under which it recovers the causal predictor as alpha approaches one; that recovery is conditional. A quantile-focused evaluation protocol accompanies experiments on WILDS and DomainBed datasets, where EQRM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The results support evaluating robustness through the distribution of domain-level outcomes, as well as optimizing for it.
summary.tldr: Quantile Risk Minimization targets strong performance with a chosen probability over domains drawn from a shared meta-distribution.

title: Probable Domain Generalization via Quantile Risk Minimization

abstract: Predicting energetically favorable 3-dimensional conformations of organic molecules frommolecular graph plays a fundamental role in computer-aided drug discovery research.However, effectively exploring the high-dimensional conformation space to identify (meta) stable conformers is anything but trivial.In this work, we introduce RMCF, a novel framework to generate a diverse set of low-energy molecular conformations through samplingfrom a regularized molecular conformation field.We develop a data-driven molecular segmentation algorithm to automatically partition each molecule into several structural building blocks to reduce the modeling degrees of freedom.Then, we employ a Markov Random Field to learn the joint probability distribution of fragment configurations and inter-fragment dihedral angles, which enables us to sample from different low-energy regions of a conformation space.Our model constantly outperforms state-of-the-art models for the conformation generation task on the GEOM-Drugs dataset.We attribute the success of RMCF to modeling in a regularized feature space and learning a global fragment configuration distribution for effective sampling.The proposed method could be generalized to deal with larger biomolecular systems.

paragraphs: A molecular graph describes chemical connectivity, but discovering favorable three-dimensional shapes requires searching a large space of possible conformations. This paper introduces RMCF to generate diverse, low-energy conformations by sampling a learned molecular conformation field. Its approach reduces the complexity of describing each molecule before learning how its parts fit together.

A data-driven segmentation algorithm partitions the molecule into structural building blocks, reducing the number of degrees of freedom the model must handle. A Markov Random Field then learns the joint distribution of fragment configurations and the dihedral angles connecting fragments. Modeling these quantities jointly allows sampling to reach different low-energy regions while accounting for relationships across the molecule.

On the GEOM-Drugs conformation-generation task, the authors report consistent improvements over leading models. They attribute the gains to the regularized feature space and the global distribution over fragment configurations. The method therefore combines a reduced representation with coordinated sampling of molecular parts. The authors suggest that it could extend to larger biomolecular systems, presenting that extension as a possibility rather than an established experimental result.
summary.tldr: RMCF generates diverse low-energy molecular shapes by learning a joint distribution over structural fragments and the angles connecting them.

title: Regularized Molecular Conformation Fields

abstract: Most recent self-supervised learning methods learn visual representation by contrasting different augmented views of images. Compared with supervised learning, more aggressive augmentations have been introduced to further improve the diversity of training pairs. However, aggressive augmentations may distort images' structures leading to a severe semantic shift problem that augmented views of the same image may not share the same semantics, thus degrading the transfer performance. To address this problem, we propose a new SSL paradigm, which counteracts the impact of semantic shift by balancing the role of weak and aggressively augmented pairs. Specifically, semantically inconsistent pairs are of minority, and we treat them as noisy pairs. Note that deep neural networks (DNNs) have a crucial memorization effect that DNNs tend to first memorize clean (majority) examples before overfitting to noisy (minority) examples. Therefore, we set a relatively large weight for aggressively augmented data pairs at the early learning stage. With the training going on, the model begins to overfit noisy pairs. Accordingly, we gradually reduce the weights of aggressively augmented pairs. In doing so, our method can better embrace aggressive augmentations and neutralize the semantic shift problem. Experiments show that our model achieves 73.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with ResNet-50 for 200 epochs, which is a 2.5% improvement over BYOL. Moreover, experiments also demonstrate that the learned representations can transfer well for various downstream tasks. Code is released at: https://github.com/tmllab/RSA.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning often treats differently augmented versions of one image as semantically related. Aggressive transformations increase training diversity, but they can alter image structure enough that the paired views no longer share meaning. RSA addresses this semantic shift by changing the balance between weakly and aggressively augmented pairs during training.

The method treats semantically inconsistent pairs as a noisy minority. Its weighting schedule draws on the tendency of neural networks to learn clean majority examples before overfitting noisy ones. Aggressive pairs receive relatively large weights early in training, then gradually smaller weights as training progresses and fitting noisy pairs becomes a concern.

With ResNet-50 trained for 200 epochs, the reported ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy is 73.1%, a 2.5% improvement over BYOL as stated by the authors. Additional experiments show good transfer to downstream tasks. The results support retaining the diversity of aggressive augmentation while adjusting its influence over time to reduce the harm from semantically inconsistent pairs.
summary.tldr: RSA gradually reduces the weight of aggressive augmentation pairs to limit semantic-shift noise while preserving their early training benefits.

title: RSA: Reducing Semantic Shift from Aggressive Augmentations for Self-supervised Learning

abstract: In this paper, we provide an in-depth study of Stochastic Backpropagation (SBP) when training deep neural networks for standard image classification and object detection tasks. During backward propagation, SBP calculates gradients by using only a subset of feature maps to save GPU memory and computational cost. We interpret SBP as an efficient way to implement stochastic gradient decent by performing backpropagation dropout, which leads to significant memory saving and training run-time reduction, with a minimal impact on the overall model accuracy. We offer best practices to apply SBP for training image recognition models, which can be adopted in learning a wide range of deep neural networks. Experiments on image classification and object detection show that SBP can save up to 40% of GPU memory with less than 1% accuracy degradation. Code is available at: https://github.com/amazon-research/stochastic-backpropagation

paragraphs: Training deep image models requires computing gradients through their internal feature maps, which consumes GPU memory and computation. This paper studies Stochastic Backpropagation, or SBP, as a way to reduce those costs. During the backward pass, SBP calculates gradients using only a subset of feature maps, reducing the amount of information involved in gradient computation.

The authors interpret this procedure as a form of dropout applied during backpropagation and as an efficient implementation of stochastic gradient descent. That perspective connects the resource savings to the training process itself: the model learns from selectively computed backward information. The paper also develops practical recommendations for applying SBP when training image-recognition networks.

Experiments cover standard image classification and object detection. The reported results show savings of up to 40% in GPU memory with less than 1% accuracy degradation, alongside reduced training runtime. These are empirical tradeoffs observed in the studied tasks. They suggest that computing every feature map's contribution during backpropagation can sometimes be unnecessary for retaining nearly all of a model's accuracy.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Backpropagation reduces backward-pass computation, with reported GPU memory savings up to 40% and accuracy degradation below 1%.

title: An In-depth Study of Stochastic Backpropagation

abstract: Randomized smoothing is considered to be the state-of-the-art provable defense against adversarial perturbations. However, it heavily exploits the fact that classifiers map input objects to class probabilities and do not focus on the ones that learn a metric space in which classification is performed by computing distances to embeddings of class prototypes. In this work, we extend randomized smoothing to few-shot learning models that map inputs to normalized embeddings. We provide analysis of the Lipschitz continuity of such models and derive a robustness certificate against $\ell_2$-bounded perturbations that may be useful in few-shot learning scenarios. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on different datasets.

However, it heavily exploits the fact that classifiers map input objects to class probabilities and do not focus on the ones that learn a metric space in which classification is performed by computing distances to embeddings of class prototypes. In this work, we extend randomized smoothing to few-shot learning models that map inputs to normalized embeddings. We provide analysis of the Lipschitz continuity of such models and derive a robustness certificate against $\ell_2$-bounded perturbations that may be useful in few-shot learning scenarios. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on different datasets.

paragraphs: Few-shot classifiers can make predictions by comparing an input's embedding with embeddings representing class prototypes. This differs from directly producing class probabilities. Existing randomized smoothing defenses rely heavily on the latter structure, leaving a gap for models whose decisions are based on distances in a learned representation space.

The paper extends randomized smoothing to few-shot models that produce normalized embeddings. Its analysis studies Lipschitz continuity, which describes how strongly a model's output can change as its input changes. The authors use this analysis to derive a robustness certificate for adversarial perturbations bounded in Euclidean, or l2, norm, bringing provable protection into the embedding-based setting.

Experiments on multiple datasets confirm the theoretical results. The significance is that robustness analysis can be adapted to the representation used for prototype comparisons, rather than depending only on class-probability outputs. The certificate concerns the stated normalized-embedding models and bounded perturbations. The authors describe its usefulness for few-shot scenarios as a possibility supported by the theory and experiments, rather than a guarantee covering every few-shot learning method.
summary.tldr: The paper extends randomized smoothing to normalized embeddings and derives l2 robustness certificates relevant to prototype-based few-shot learning.

title: Smoothed Embeddings for Certified Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Recent research has demonstrated the capability of behavior signals captured by smartphones and wearables for longitudinal behavior modeling. However, there is a lack of a comprehensive public dataset that serves as an open testbed for fair comparison among algorithms. Moreover, prior studies mainly evaluate algorithms using data from a single population within a short period, without measuring the cross-dataset generalizability of these algorithms. We present the first multi-year passive sensing datasets, containing over 700 user-years and 497 unique users’ data collected from mobile and wearable sensors, together with a wide range of well-being metrics. Our datasets can support multiple cross-dataset evaluations of behavior modeling algorithms’ generalizability across different users and years. As a starting point, we provide the benchmark results of 18 algorithms on the task of depression detection. Our results indicate that both prior depression detection algorithms and domain generalization techniques show potential but need further research to achieve adequate cross-dataset generalizability. We envision our multi-year datasets can support the ML community in developing generalizable longitudinal behavior modeling algorithms.

paragraphs: Smartphones and wearables capture behavioral signals that can support models of people's well-being over time. However, evaluating a model within one population over a short period leaves an important question unresolved: whether it also works for different people or different years. GLOBEM supplies data intended to make those comparisons possible.

The collection contains more than 700 user-years of passive mobile and wearable sensing data from 497 distinct users, together with a range of well-being measures. Its multi-year structure supports multiple evaluations across datasets. This gives researchers an open testbed for comparing algorithms under changes in users and time, extending evaluation beyond a single population observed briefly.

As an initial benchmark, the authors evaluate 18 algorithms on depression detection. Both previous depression detection approaches and domain generalization techniques show promise, but the results indicate that further research is needed for adequate generalization across datasets. The resource's significance lies in making that transfer problem measurable and providing initial evidence that existing approaches have not yet resolved it.
summary.tldr: GLOBEM provides multi-year sensing data to test behavioral models across users and years, revealing remaining generalization challenges in depression detection.

title: GLOBEM Dataset: Multi-Year Datasets for Longitudinal Human Behavior Modeling Generalization

abstract: In computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), virtual screening (VS) is used for comparing a library of compounds against known active ligands to identify the drug candidates that are most likely to bind to a molecular target. Most VS methods to date have focused on using canonical compound representations (e.g., SMILES strings, Morgan fingerprints) or generating alternative fingerprints of the compounds by training progressively more complex variational autoencoders (VAEs) and graph neural networks (GNNs). Although VAEs and GNNs led to significant improvements in VS performance, these methods suffer from reduced performance when scaling to large virtual compound datasets. The performance of these methods has shown only incremental improvements in the past few years. To address this problem, we developed a novel method using multiparameter persistence (MP) homology that produces topological fingerprints of the compounds as multidimensional vectors. Our primary contribution is framing the VS process as a new topology-based graph ranking problem by partitioning a compound into chemical substructures informed by the periodic properties of its atoms and extracting their persistent homology features at multiple resolution levels. We show that the margin loss fine-tuning of pretrained Triplet networks attains highly competitive results in differentiating between compounds in the embedding space and ranking their likelihood of becoming effective drug candidates. We further establish theoretical guarantees for the stability properties of our proposed MP signatures, and demonstrate that our models, enhanced by the MP signatures, outperform state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets by a wide and highly statistically significant margin (e.g., 93\% gain for Cleves-Jain and 54\% gain for DUD-E Diverse dataset).

paragraphs: Virtual screening compares candidate compounds with known active ligands to prioritize molecules likely to bind a target. ToDD approaches this as a topology-based graph-ranking problem. The motivation is to improve compound representations beyond established fingerprints and learned alternatives whose performance can decline on large virtual compound collections.

These are virtual-screening benchmark findings: the contribution is a stable representation and ranking approach for prioritizing candidates, with empirical evidence that the topological information improves the tested models.
summary.tldr: ToDD uses stable topological compound fingerprints to improve virtual-screening rankings, reporting substantial gains on two named benchmarks.

title: ToDD: Topological Compound Fingerprinting in Computer-Aided Drug Discovery

abstract: When taking photos under an environment with insufficient light, the exposure time and the sensor gain usually require to be carefully chosen to obtain images with satisfying visual quality. For example, the images with high ISO usually have inescapable noise, while the long-exposure ones may be blurry due to camera shake or object motion. Existing solutions generally suggest to seek a balance between noise and blur, and learn denoising or deblurring models under either full- or self-supervision. However, the real-world training pairs are difficult to collect, and the self-supervised methods merely rely on blurry or noisy images are limited in performance. In this work, we tackle this problem by jointly leveraging the short-exposure noisy image and the long-exposure blurry image for better image restoration. Such setting is practically feasible due to that short-exposure and long-exposure images can be either acquired by two individual cameras or synthesized by a long burst of images. Moreover, the short-exposure images are hardly blurry, and the long-exposure ones have negligible noise. Their complementarity makes it feasible to learn restoration model in a self-supervised manner. Specifically, the noisy images can be used as the supervision information for deblurring, while the sharp areas in the blurry images can be utilized as the auxiliary supervision information for self-supervised denoising. By learning in a collaborative manner, the deblurring and denoising tasks in our method can benefit each other. Experiments on synthetic and real-world images show the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed method. Codes are available at https://github.com/cszhilu1998/SelfIR.

paragraphs: Low-light photography often trades noise against blur. Short exposures can produce noisy images, while long exposures can blur motion or camera shake. This paper pairs the two types of image so their complementary strengths can support restoration: short exposures are nearly free of blur, and long exposures have negligible noise.

The method learns deblurring and denoising collaboratively without requiring clean target images. Noisy short-exposure images provide supervision for deblurring. Sharp regions within the long-exposure images supply auxiliary supervision for denoising. Each task therefore receives useful information from an image degraded mainly in a different way, allowing the two restoration processes to benefit one another.

The paired input setting can be obtained with two cameras or synthesized from a long image burst. Experiments on synthetic and real-world images demonstrate effectiveness and practicality. The contribution is a self-supervised training arrangement that uses the different imperfections of the two exposures as complementary evidence, rather than depending on a single kind of degraded image.
summary.tldr: Paired short and long exposures provide complementary supervision so denoising and deblurring can improve each other without clean targets.

title: Self-Supervised Image Restoration with Blurry and Noisy Pairs

abstract: Randomly masking and predicting word tokens has been a successful approach in pre-training language models for a variety of downstream tasks. In this work, we observe that the same idea also applies naturally to sequential decision making, where many well-studied tasks like behavior cloning, offline RL, inverse dynamics, and waypoint conditioning correspond to different sequence maskings over a sequence of states, actions, and returns. We introduce the UniMASK framework, which provides a unified way to specify models which can be trained on many different sequential decision making tasks. We show that a single UniMASK model is often capable of carrying out many tasks with performance similar to or better than single-task models. Additionally, after fine-tuning, our UniMASK models consistently outperform comparable single-task models.

In this work, we observe that the same idea also applies naturally to sequential decision making, where many well-studied tasks like behavior cloning, offline RL, inverse dynamics, and waypoint conditioning correspond to different sequence maskings over a sequence of states, actions, and returns. We introduce the UniMASK framework, which provides a unified way to specify models which can be trained on many different sequential decision making tasks. paragraphs: UniMASK applies the idea of hiding and predicting sequence elements to sequential decision problems. A sequence contains states, actions, and returns, and different choices of what to hide correspond to different inference tasks. This gives a shared formulation for behavior cloning, offline reinforcement learning, inverse dynamics, and waypoint conditioning.

The framework uses these masking choices to specify models that can train on many decision-making tasks. The common prediction format allows one model to handle different requests by changing which sequence information is available and which information must be inferred. The contribution is a unified way to express and train across tasks that are often studied separately.

The authors report that a single UniMASK model can often perform multiple tasks as well as, or better than, models trained for individual tasks. After fine-tuning, their UniMASK models consistently outperform comparable single-task models in the reported comparisons. These findings support shared masked-sequence training as a useful foundation for several decision problems, with further benefits from adapting the trained model to a particular task.
summary.tldr: UniMASK expresses multiple sequential decision tasks as masked prediction, enabling shared models that often match single-task performance and improve further with fine-tuning.

title: Uni[MASK]: Unified Inference in Sequential Decision Problems

abstract: We study the problem of training deep networks while quantizing parameters and activations into low-precision numeric representations, a setting central to reducing energy consumption and inference time of deployed models. We propose a method that learns different precisions, as measured by bits in numeric representations, for different weights in a neural network, yielding a heterogeneous allocation of bits across parameters. Learning precisions occurs alongside learning weight values, using a strategy derived from a novel framework wherein the intractability of optimizing discrete precisions is approximated by training per-parameter noise magnitudes. We broaden this framework to also encompass learning precisions for hidden state activations, simultaneously with weight precisions and values. Our approach exposes the objective of constructing a low-precision inference-efficient model to the entirety of the training process. Experiments show that it finds highly heterogeneous precision assignments for CNNs trained on CIFAR and ImageNet, improving upon previous state-of-the-art quantization methods. Our improvements extend to the challenging scenario of learning reduced-precision GANs.

paragraphs: Low-precision representations can reduce the energy and inference time of deployed neural networks. This paper asks how to allocate precision differently across individual weights and hidden activations while training the model. Its premise is that an efficient allocation need not give every parameter the same number of bits.

summary.tldr: Training parameter-specific noise magnitudes enables joint learning of network values and heterogeneous numerical precisions.

title: Not All Bits have Equal Value: Heterogeneous Precisions via Trainable Noise

abstract: This paper considers a class of reinforcement learning problems, which involve systems with two types of states: stochastic and pseudo-stochastic. In such systems, stochastic states follow a stochastic transition kernel while the transitions of pseudo-stochastic states are deterministic {\em given} the stochastic states/transitions. We refer to such systems as mixed systems, which are widely used in various applications, including Manufacturing systems, communication networks, and queueing networks. We propose a sample-efficient RL method that accelerates learning by generating augmented data samples. The proposed algorithm is data-driven (model-free), but it learns the policy from data samples from both real and augmented samples. This method significantly improves learning by reducing the sample complexity such that the dataset only needs to have sufficient coverage of the stochastic states. We analyze the sample complexity of the proposed method under Fitted Q Iteration (FQI) and demonstrate that the optimality gap decreases as $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}}\right),$ where $n$ represents the number of real samples, and $m$ is the number of augmented samples per real sample. It is important to note that without augmented samples, the optimality gap is $O(1)$ due to the insufficient data coverage of the pseudo-stochastic states. Our experimental results on multiple queueing network applications confirm that the proposed method indeed significantly accelerates both deep Q-learning and deep policy gradient.

paragraphs: The paper considers systems whose states combine genuinely stochastic components with pseudo-stochastic components. The latter evolve deterministically once the stochastic states or transitions are given. This structure appears in manufacturing, communication, and queueing networks, and provides an opportunity to extract more learning value from observed transitions.

The proposed model-free reinforcement learning method trains on both real samples and augmented samples. Exploiting the mixed-system structure reduces the required data coverage: real observations only need sufficient coverage of the stochastic states. Augmentation addresses gaps in coverage of the pseudo-stochastic part of the system.

Without augmentation, the stated insufficient-coverage setting leaves an O(1) gap. Experiments on multiple queueing-network applications show accelerated learning for both deep Q-learning and deep policy-gradient methods. The result connects a specific structural property of the dynamics to improved sample efficiency.
summary.tldr: For systems with conditionally deterministic state components, sample augmentation reduces coverage requirements and accelerates reinforcement learning.

title: Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Mixed Systems through Augmented Samples and Its Applications to Queueing Networks

abstract: We develop and analyze a general technique for learning with an unknown distribution drift. Given a sequence of independent observations from the last $T$ steps of a drifting distribution, our algorithm agnostically learns a family of functions with respect to the current distribution at time $T$. Unlike previous work, our technique does not require prior knowledge about the magnitude of the drift. Instead, the algorithm adapts to the sample data. Without explicitly estimating the drift, the algorithm learns a family of functions with almost the same error as a learning algorithm that knows the magnitude of the drift in advance. Furthermore, since our algorithm adapts to the data, it can guarantee a better learning error than an algorithm that relies on loose bounds on the drift. We demonstrate the application of our technique in two fundamental learning scenarios: binary classification and linear regression.

paragraphs: When a data distribution changes over time, past observations may no longer describe the situation a model must handle now. This paper studies learning from independent observations collected over the last T time steps, with performance measured against the distribution at the current step. The challenge is that the amount of distribution drift is unknown.

The authors develop an algorithm that adapts directly to the observed data without explicitly estimating the drift. Its analysis compares it with a learner that already knows the magnitude of the drift. The adaptive method achieves almost the same error, showing that advance knowledge of this quantity is not required to approach that reference level of performance.

The method can also guarantee lower learning error than an approach based on overly loose drift bounds. This makes adaptation useful beyond simply removing an input requirement: it can avoid the cost of pessimistic assumptions about change. The paper demonstrates the general technique in binary classification and linear regression, retaining independent observations as a stated premise.
summary.tldr: A data-adaptive learning algorithm handles unknown distribution drift with error close to a learner that knows the drift magnitude.

title: An Adaptive Algorithm for Learning with Unknown Distribution Drift

abstract: Language models are increasingly being deployed for general problem solving across a wide range of tasks, but are still confined to token-level, left-to-right decision-making processes during inference. This means they can fall short in tasks that require exploration, strategic lookahead, or where initial decisions play a pivotal role. To surmount these challenges, we introduce a new framework for language model inference, Tree of Thoughts (ToT), which generalizes over the popular Chain of Thought approach to prompting language models, and enables exploration over coherent units of text (thoughts) that serve as intermediate steps toward problem solving. ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices.Our experiments show that ToT significantly enhances language models’ problem-solving abilities on three novel tasks requiring non-trivial planning or search: Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords. For instance, in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4\% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74\%. Code repo with all prompts: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm.

paragraphs: Some problems require exploring alternatives before committing to a solution, especially when early choices determine what is possible later. This paper introduces Tree of Thoughts, an inference framework that lets language models search across intermediate reasoning steps. It extends chain-of-thought prompting by treating coherent pieces of text as units of exploration.

The model can consider several reasoning paths and evaluate its own candidate steps to decide how to proceed. It can also look ahead or backtrack when needed. This creates a process in which intermediate decisions can be compared and revisited, giving the model a way to make choices based on more than its immediate continuation.

Experiments examine Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords, three tasks requiring substantial planning or search. The authors report significant improvements across these tasks. In Game of 24, GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting solves 4% of tasks, while Tree of Thoughts reaches 74%. The result illustrates how changing the inference procedure can substantially improve problem solving in settings where exploring alternative paths matters.
summary.tldr: Tree of Thoughts improves language-model problem solving by searching, evaluating, and revisiting alternative intermediate reasoning paths.

title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

abstract: Parallelization is a popular strategy for improving the performance of methods. Optimization methods are no exception: design of efficient parallel optimization methods and tight analysis of their theoretical properties are important research endeavors. While the minimax complexities are well known for sequential optimization methods, the theory of parallel optimization methods is less explored. In this paper, we propose a new protocol that generalizes the classical oracle framework approach. Using this protocol, we establish minimax complexities for parallel optimization methods that have access to an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with bounded variance. We consider a fixed computation model characterized by each worker requiring a fixed but worker-dependent time to calculate stochastic gradient. We prove lower bounds and develop optimal algorithms that attain them. Our results have surprising consequences for the literature of asynchronous optimization methods.

paragraphs: Parallel optimization distributes computation across workers, but understanding its best possible running time requires accounting for how quickly those workers operate. This paper develops a theoretical framework for that question. It focuses on a fixed computation model in which each worker takes a constant amount of time to calculate a stochastic gradient, with that time allowed to differ between workers.

The authors propose a protocol that generalizes the classical oracle framework used to analyze optimization algorithms. Algorithms receive unbiased stochastic gradient estimates with bounded variance. Within this setting, the paper establishes minimax time complexities: limits on the performance achievable in the worst case by the best available methods.

The contribution includes both lower bounds and algorithms that attain them. This combination identifies achievable time guarantees and shows their optimality under the stated computation and oracle assumptions. The authors also report consequences for the theory of asynchronous optimization. The central value is a rigorous connection between heterogeneous worker speeds and optimal parallel optimization time, rather than a complexity analysis based only on sequential gradient counts.
summary.tldr: A generalized oracle framework establishes optimal parallel optimization times when workers have fixed, potentially different gradient-computation speeds.

title: Optimal Time Complexities of Parallel Stochastic Optimization Methods Under a Fixed Computation Model

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems possess significant potential to drive societal progress. However, their deployment often faces obstacles due to substantial safety concerns. Safe reinforcement learning (SafeRL) emerges as a solution to optimize policies while simultaneously adhering to multiple constraints, thereby addressing the challenge of integrating reinforcement learning in safety-critical scenarios. In this paper, we present an environment suite called Safety-Gymnasium, which encompasses safety-critical tasks in both single and multi-agent scenarios, accepting vector and vision-only input. Additionally, we offer a library of algorithms named Safe Policy Optimization (SafePO), comprising 16 state-of-the-art SafeRL algorithms. This comprehensive library can serve as a validation tool for the research community. By introducing this benchmark, we aim to facilitate the evaluation and comparison of safety performance, thus fostering the development of reinforcement learning for safer, more reliable, and responsible real-world applications. The website of this project can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/safety-gymnasium.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning studies how to improve a policy while respecting constraints on its behavior. Evaluating such methods requires environments where task performance and safety requirements can be considered together. Safety Gymnasium provides a unified suite intended to support this evaluation across several kinds of safety-critical learning scenarios.

The suite includes tasks with a single agent and tasks with multiple agents. It also accepts vector observations and vision-only inputs, allowing evaluation under different forms of information available to the policy. Alongside the environments, the authors introduce Safe Policy Optimization, or SafePO, a library containing 16 state-of-the-art safe reinforcement learning algorithms.

Together, the environment suite and algorithm library provide a shared basis for validating methods and comparing safety performance. Their contribution is research infrastructure spanning multiple settings and approaches. The intended longer-term benefit is progress toward safer and more reliable reinforcement learning applications; the abstract presents that as the benchmark's aim rather than a demonstrated guarantee of safety in deployment.
summary.tldr: Safety Gymnasium combines safety-focused learning environments with a 16-algorithm library for evaluating and comparing safe reinforcement learning methods.

title: Safety Gymnasium: A Unified Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmark

abstract: Designing efficient algorithms to compute a Nash Equilibrium (NE) in multiplayer games is still an open challenge. In this paper, we focus on computing an NE that optimizes a given objective function. For example, when there is a team of players independently playing against an adversary in a game (e.g., several groups in a forest trying to interdict illegal loggers in green security games), these team members may need to find an NE minimizing the adversary’s utility. Finding an optimal NE in multiplayer games can be formulated as a mixed-integer bilinear program by introducing auxiliary variables to represent bilinear terms, leading to a huge number of bilinear terms, making it hard to solve. To overcome this challenge, we first propose a general framework for this formulation based on a set of correlation plans. We then develop a novel algorithm called CRM based on this framework, which uses correlation plans with their relations to strictly reduce the feasible solution space after the convex relaxation of bilinear terms while minimizing the number of correlation plans to significantly reduce the number of bilinear terms. We show that our techniques can significantly reduce the time complexity and CRM can be several orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art baseline.

paragraphs: A multiplayer game can have several Nash equilibria, and the equilibrium selected may matter for an additional objective. This paper studies computing an equilibrium that optimizes such an objective. One motivating case involves independently acting team members who want an equilibrium that minimizes an adversary’s utility.

The problem can be expressed as a mixed-integer bilinear program, but representing interactions introduces many products of variables. Those bilinear terms make the optimization difficult. The authors develop a framework based on correlation plans and an algorithm called CRM that uses relationships among those plans to organize the formulation.

CRM improves the optimization in two connected ways: it reduces the feasible region created by convex relaxation, and it limits the number of correlation plans to reduce bilinear terms. The paper reports significant reductions in time complexity and cases where CRM is several orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art baseline. These findings show that the formulation itself can make objective-driven equilibrium computation substantially more tractable.
summary.tldr: CRM makes optimal Nash equilibrium computation faster by reducing bilinear terms and tightening the relaxed optimization problem.

title: Computing Optimal Nash Equilibria in Multiplayer Games

abstract: The dominant paradigm in 3D human pose estimation that lifts a 2D pose sequence to 3D heavily relies on long-term temporal clues (i.e., using a daunting number of video frames) for improved accuracy, which incurs performance saturation, intractable computation and the non-causal problem. This can be attributed to their inherent inability to perceive spatial context as plain 2D joint coordinates carry no visual cues. To address this issue, we propose a straightforward yet powerful solution: leveraging the $\textit{readily available}$ intermediate visual representations produced by off-the-shelf (pre-trained) 2D pose detectors -- no finetuning on the 3D task is even needed. The key observation is that, while the pose detector learns to localize 2D joints, such representations (e.g., feature maps) implicitly encode the joint-centric spatial context thanks to the regional operations in backbone networks. We design a simple baseline named $\textbf{Context-Aware PoseFormer}$ to showcase its effectiveness. $\textit{Without access to any temporal information}$, the proposed method significantly outperforms its context-agnostic counterpart, PoseFormer, and other state-of-the-art methods using up to $\textit{hundreds of}$ video frames regarding both speed and precision. $\textit{Project page:}$ https://qitaozhao.github.io/ContextAware-PoseFormer

paragraphs: Estimating a person's three-dimensional pose from two-dimensional joint coordinates is difficult because those coordinates omit the surrounding visual information. Many methods compensate by processing long video sequences. This paper argues that the missing spatial context helps explain why that strategy can become computationally expensive, show diminishing accuracy gains, and depend on future frames.

The proposed solution reuses intermediate features from an existing pretrained 2D pose detector. While learning to locate joints, the detector also develops representations of the image regions around them. Those features therefore provide useful context beyond joint coordinates alone. The authors build Context-Aware PoseFormer to use this information, without needing to fine-tune the detector for the 3D task.

In the reported comparisons, the method uses no temporal information yet substantially exceeds PoseFormer and other leading methods that process up to hundreds of frames in both speed and precision. The finding shows that, in these experiments, richer information from one frame can be more useful than extending a sequence of context-poor joint coordinates.
summary.tldr: Reusing visual features from a pretrained 2D pose detector enables accurate, fast 3D pose estimation from a single frame.

title: A Single 2D Pose with Context is Worth Hundreds for 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: We obtain essentially tight upper bounds for a strengthened notion of regret in the stochastic linear bandits framework. The strengthening---referred to as Nash regret---is defined as the difference between the (a priori unknown) optimum and the geometric mean of expected rewards accumulated by the linear bandit algorithm. Since the geometric mean corresponds to the well-studied Nash social welfare (NSW) function, this formulation quantifies the performance of a bandit algorithm as the collective welfare it generates across rounds. NSW is known to satisfy fairness axioms and, hence, an upper bound on Nash regret provides a principled fairness guarantee. We consider the stochastic linear bandits problem over a horizon of $\mathsf{T}$ rounds and with a set of arms ${\cal X}$ in ambient dimension $d$. Furthermore, we focus on settings in which the stochastic reward---associated with each arm in ${\cal X}$---is a non-negative, sub-Poisson random variable. For this setting, we develop an algorithm that achieves a Nash regret of $O\left( \sqrt{\frac{d}{\mathsf{T}}} \log(\mathsf{T} |{\cal X}|)\right)$. In addition, addressing linear bandit instances in which the set of arms ${\cal X}$ is not necessarily finite, we obtain a Nash regret upper bound of $O\left( \frac{d^\frac{5}{4}}{\sqrt{\mathsf{T}}} \log(\mathsf{T})\right)$. Since bounded random variables are sub-Poisson, these results hold for bounded, non-negative rewards. Our linear bandit algorithm is built upon the successive elimination method with novel technical insights, including tailored concentration bounds and the use of sampling via John ellipsoid in conjunction with the Kiefer–Wolfowitz optimal design.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm learns which actions yield high rewards while making decisions over time. This paper evaluates its performance using Nash regret: the difference between the unknown optimum and the geometric mean of expected rewards across rounds. Through its connection to Nash social welfare, this measure provides a principled way to express fairness across rounds.

The analysis assumes stochastic linear rewards that are nonnegative and sub-Poisson, a condition that includes bounded nonnegative rewards. For a finite action set in dimension d over T rounds, the authors obtain a bound scaling as the square root of d/T times log(T times the number of actions). They also give a bound for potentially infinite action sets, scaling as d to the power 5/4 times log(T), divided by the square root of T.

The algorithm builds on successive elimination, supported by tailored concentration bounds and geometric sampling techniques. The authors establish essentially tight upper bounds, showing that this stronger welfare-based objective admits rigorous learning guarantees under the stated reward assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper gives essentially tight linear-bandit guarantees for Nash regret, a geometric-mean reward criterion that expresses fairness across rounds.

title: Nash Regret Guarantees for Linear Bandits

abstract: In sampling-based Bayesian models of brain function, neural activities are assumed to be samples from probability distributions that the brain uses for probabilistic computation. However, a comprehensive understanding of how mechanistic models of neural dynamics can sample from arbitrary distributions is still lacking. We use tools from functional analysis and stochastic differential equations to explore the minimum architectural requirements for $\textit{recurrent}$ neural circuits to sample from complex distributions. We first consider the traditional sampling model consisting of a network of neurons whose outputs directly represent the samples ($\textit{sampler-only}$ network). We argue that synaptic current and firing-rate dynamics in the traditional model have limited capacity to sample from a complex probability distribution. We show that the firing rate dynamics of a recurrent neural circuit with a separate set of output units can sample from an arbitrary probability distribution. We call such circuits $\textit{reservoir-sampler networks}$ (RSNs). We propose an efficient training procedure based on denoising score matching that finds recurrent and output weights such that the RSN implements Langevin sampling. We empirically demonstrate our model's ability to sample from several complex data distributions using the proposed neural dynamics and discuss its applicability to developing the next generation of sampling-based Bayesian brain models.

paragraphs: Sampling-based theories of brain function interpret neural activity as samples from probability distributions used in computation. A key mechanistic question is how neural dynamics could generate samples from complicated distributions. This paper investigates which recurrent network architectures have sufficient expressive capacity for that role.

The authors first examine traditional sampler-only networks, where neuron outputs directly serve as samples. They argue that standard synaptic-current and firing-rate dynamics in this arrangement have limited sampling capacity. They then show that adding a separate set of output units gives recurrent firing-rate circuits the capacity to sample from arbitrary probability distributions. They call this architecture a reservoir-sampler network.

To train these networks, the paper uses denoising score matching to find recurrent and output weights that implement Langevin sampling. Experiments demonstrate sampling from several complex data distributions. Together, the architectural result and training procedure provide a route from an abstract probabilistic account of neural computation to an explicit model of neural dynamics with substantially greater sampling expressiveness.
summary.tldr: Separating recurrent dynamics from output units enables expressive neural samplers trained through denoising score matching.

title: Expressive probabilistic sampling in recurrent neural networks

abstract: Gaussian processes are a powerful framework for quantifying uncertainty and for sequential decision-making but are limited by the requirement of solving linear systems. In general, this has a cubic cost in dataset size and is sensitive to conditioning. We explore stochastic gradient algorithms as a computationally efficient method of approximately solving these linear systems: we develop low-variance optimization objectives for sampling from the posterior and extend these to inducing points. Counterintuitively, stochastic gradient descent often produces accurate predictions, even in cases where it does not converge quickly to the optimum. We explain this through a spectral characterization of the implicit bias from non-convergence. We show that stochastic gradient descent produces predictive distributions close to the true posterior both in regions with sufficient data coverage, and in regions sufficiently far away from the data. Experimentally, stochastic gradient descent achieves state-of-the-art performance on sufficiently large-scale or ill-conditioned regression tasks. Its uncertainty estimates match the performance of significantly more expensive baselines on a large-scale Bayesian~optimization~task.
originalAbstract: Gaussian processes are a powerful framework for quantifying uncertainty and for sequential decision-making but are limited by the requirement of solving linear systems. In general, this has a cubic cost in dataset size and is sensitive to conditioning. We explore stochastic gradient algorithms as a computationally efficient method of approximately solving these linear systems: we develop low-variance optimization objectives for sampling from the posterior and extend these to inducing points. Counterintuitively, stochastic gradient descent often produces accurate predictions, even in cases where it does not converge quickly to the optimum. We explain this through a spectral characterization of the implicit bias from non-convergence. We show that stochastic gradient descent produces predictive distributions close to the true posterior both in regions with sufficient data coverage, and in regions sufficiently far away from the data. Experimentally, stochastic gradient descent achieves state-of-the-art performance on sufficiently large-scale or ill-conditioned regression tasks. Its uncertainty estimates match the performance of significantly more expensive baselines on a large-scale Bayesian~optimization~task.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes provide predictions with uncertainty, but their computations require solving linear systems that generally have cubic cost in dataset size and can be sensitive to poor conditioning. This paper explores stochastic gradient methods for approximately solving those systems, with the aim of making posterior sampling more computationally efficient.

The authors design low-variance optimization objectives for posterior sampling and extend them to inducing-point methods. They investigate why stochastic gradient descent can produce accurate predictions even when optimization converges slowly. A spectral analysis characterizes the implicit bias caused by stopping before convergence and explains how incomplete optimization affects predictions.

The analysis shows that predictive distributions remain close to the true posterior in regions with sufficient data coverage and regions sufficiently far from the data. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on regression tasks that are sufficiently large or ill-conditioned. On a large-scale Bayesian optimization task, the uncertainty estimates match those of substantially more expensive baselines, supporting the practical value of approximate solves in these settings.
summary.tldr: Stochastic gradient descent can efficiently approximate Gaussian-process posterior samples while preserving accurate predictive uncertainty in the studied settings.

title: Sampling from Gaussian Process Posteriors using Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Video highlight detection is a task to automatically select the most engaging moments from a long video. This problem is highly challenging since it aims to learn a general way of finding highlights from a variety of videos in the real world.The task has an innate subjectivity because the definition of a highlight differs across individuals. Therefore, to detect consistent and meaningful highlights, prior benchmark datasets have been labeled by multiple (5-20) raters. Due to the high cost of manual labeling, most existing public benchmarks are in extremely small scale, containing only a few tens or hundreds of videos. This insufficient benchmark scale causes multiple issues such as unstable evaluation or high sensitivity in traintest splits. We present Mr. HiSum, a large-scale dataset for video highlight detection and summarization, containing 31,892 videos and reliable labels aggregated over 50,000+ users per video. We empirically prove reliability of the labels as frame importance by cross-dataset transfer and user study.
