That judgment is subjective, so useful labels need to reflect more than one person's preferences. Earlier benchmarks used multiple raters, but the cost of manual labeling restricted many public datasets to only tens or hundreds of videos.

Mr. HiSum expands the scale of this evaluation setting with 31,892 videos for highlight detection and summarization. Its labels aggregate information from more than 50,000 users per video. The dataset therefore combines a much larger collection of videos with broad user participation in the importance labels associated with each one.

The authors evaluate label reliability through cross-dataset transfer and a user study, providing empirical support for interpreting the labels as frame importance. The dataset addresses the small benchmark sizes associated with unstable evaluation and sensitivity to training-test splits. Its contribution is an evaluation and learning resource for studying highlights across varied videos while drawing on aggregated user judgments to account for the task's subjectivity.
summary.tldr: Mr. HiSum provides 31,892 videos with broadly aggregated user labels and empirical evidence of their reliability for highlight detection and summarization.

title: Mr. HiSum: A Large-scale Dataset for Video Highlight Detection and Summarization

abstract: Our ability to use deep learning approaches to decipher neural activity would likely benefit from greater scale, in terms of both the model size and the datasets. However, the integration of many neural recordings into one unified model is challenging, as each recording contains the activity of different neurons from different individual animals. In this paper, we introduce a training framework and architecture designed to model the population dynamics of neural activity across diverse, large-scale neural recordings. Our method first tokenizes individual spikes within the dataset to build an efficient representation of neural events that captures the fine temporal structure of neural activity. We then employ cross-attention and a PerceiverIO backbone to further construct a latent tokenization of neural population activities. Utilizing this architecture and training framework, we construct a large-scale multi-session model trained on large datasets from seven nonhuman primates, spanning over 158 different sessions of recording from over 27,373 neural units and over 100 hours of recordings. In a number of different tasks, we demonstrate that our pretrained model can be rapidly adapted to new, unseen sessions with unspecified neuron correspondence, enabling few-shot performance with minimal labels. This work presents a powerful new approach for building deep learning tools to analyze neural data and stakes out a clear path to training at scale for neural decoding models.

paragraphs: Combining neural recordings is difficult because different recording sessions capture different neurons, sometimes from different animals. A model cannot simply assume that the same input position refers to the same neuron everywhere. This paper introduces an architecture and training framework for learning shared patterns of neural population activity across these varied recordings.

The method starts by representing individual neural spikes as tokens, preserving fine timing information in an efficient format. Cross-attention and a PerceiverIO backbone then transform these events into latent tokens that represent population activity. This gives the model a way to process diverse recordings through a common internal representation.

The authors train a shared model using recordings from seven nonhuman primates, covering 158 sessions, more than 27,373 neural units, and over 100 hours. Across several tasks, the pretrained model adapts rapidly to unseen sessions with few labels and without specified neuron correspondence. These results support using large collections of recordings to learn reusable neural representations that can reduce the labeled data needed for a new session.
summary.tldr: A shared neural decoding model learns across animals and recording sessions, then adapts to new sessions with few labels.

title: A Unified, Scalable Framework for Neural Population Decoding

abstract: We tackle the task of conditional music generation. We introduce MusicGen, a single Language Model (LM) that operates over several streams of compressed discrete music representation, i.e., tokens. Unlike prior work, MusicGen is comprised of a single-stage transformer LM together with efficient token interleaving patterns, which eliminates the need for cascading several models, e.g., hierarchically or upsampling. Following this approach, we demonstrate how MusicGen can generate high-quality samples, both mono and stereo, while being conditioned on textual description or melodic features, allowing better controls over the generated output. We conduct extensive empirical evaluation, considering both automatic and human studies, showing the proposed approach is superior to the evaluated baselines on a standard text-to-music benchmark. Through ablation studies, we shed light over the importance of each of the components comprising MusicGen. Music samples, code, and models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/audiocraft

paragraphs: MusicGen tackles music generation conditioned on a user's description or melodic information. It represents music using several streams of compressed discrete tokens and models them with a single transformer language model. The paper's central architectural contribution is to organize those streams so that one generation stage can handle the task.

Efficient token interleaving patterns let the model work across the streams without requiring a cascade of hierarchical or upsampling models. Text descriptions and melodic features provide ways to influence the generated output. The authors demonstrate high-quality mono and stereo samples, connecting the simplified model structure with both audio generation and user control.

Evaluation includes automatic measures and human studies on a standard text-to-music benchmark, where MusicGen outperforms the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies examine the importance of its individual components, helping explain which design choices contribute to the approach. The paper also releases music examples, code, and models, providing access to the system underlying the reported results and the demonstrated forms of conditioning.
summary.tldr: MusicGen uses a single transformer over interleaved audio tokens to generate mono or stereo music controlled by text or melodic features.

title: Simple and Controllable Music Generation

abstract: Dataset Distillation is the task of synthesizing small datasets from large ones while still retaining comparable predictive accuracy to the original uncompressed dataset. Despite significant empirical progress in recent years, there is little understanding of the theoretical limitations/guarantees of dataset distillation, specifically, what excess risk is achieved by distillation compared to the original dataset, and how large are distilled datasets? In this work, we take a theoretical view on kernel ridge regression (KRR) based methods of dataset distillation such as Kernel Inducing Points. By transforming ridge regression in random Fourier features (RFF) space, we provide the first proof of the existence of small (size) distilled datasets and their corresponding excess risk for shift-invariant kernels. We prove that a small set of instances exists in the original input space such that its solution in the RFF space coincides with the solution of the original data. We further show that a KRR solution can be generated using this distilled set of instances which gives an approximation towards the KRR solution optimized on the full input data. The size of this set is linear in the dimension of the RFF space of the input set or alternatively near linear in the number of effective degrees of freedom, which is a function of the kernel, number of data points, and the regularization parameter $\lambda$. The error bound of this distilled set is also a function of $\lambda$. We verify our bounds analytically and empirically.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks a small synthetic dataset that retains the predictive value of a much larger one. This paper studies theoretical questions behind that compression: how small the distilled set can be and how much prediction risk it adds. The analysis focuses on kernel ridge regression with shift-invariant kernels.

The authors reformulate ridge regression in a random Fourier feature space. They prove that a small set of instances exists in the original input space whose solution in that feature space matches the full dataset’s solution. Using those instances for kernel ridge regression then gives an approximation to the solution obtained from the complete data.

Those degrees of freedom depend on the kernel, dataset size, and regularization parameter; the error bound also depends on regularization. Analytical and empirical checks support the bounds. The result distinguishes exact agreement in the random-feature formulation from approximation of the full kernel solution, providing explicit theoretical structure for the compression tradeoff.
summary.tldr: For shift-invariant kernels, the paper proves small distilled datasets exist and bounds their size and approximation error.

title: On the Size and Approximation Error of Distilled Datasets

abstract: Computational cognitive models are a fundamental tool in behavioral neuroscience. They embody in software precise hypotheses about the cognitive mechanisms underlying a particular behavior. Constructing these models is typically a difficult iterative process that requires both inspiration from the literature and the creativity of an individual researcher. Here, we adopt an alternative approach to learn parsimonious cognitive models directly from data. We fit behavior data using a recurrent neural network that is penalized for carrying excess information between timesteps, leading to sparse, interpretable representations and dynamics. When fitting synthetic behavioral data from known cognitive models, our method recovers the underlying form of those models. When fit to choice data from rats performing a bandit task, our method recovers simple and interpretable models that make testable predictions about neural mechanisms.

paragraphs: Computational cognitive models express specific hypotheses about the mechanisms underlying behavior. Building them usually involves researchers repeatedly proposing and refining explanations. This paper explores a data-driven alternative: learning compact cognitive models directly from behavioral observations while keeping their internal representations and dynamics interpretable.

The method fits a recurrent neural network to behavior but penalizes it for carrying excessive information from one time step to the next. This pressure encourages sparse representations and simpler dynamics. The information passed through time is therefore part of the model-discovery problem, rather than an unrestricted resource used only to improve fit.

On synthetic behavior generated by known cognitive models, the method recovers the underlying forms of those models. On choice data from rats performing a bandit task, it produces simple, interpretable models that generate testable predictions about neural mechanisms. The synthetic result demonstrates recovery where the generating model is known; the animal-data result shows how the same approach can propose hypotheses for further testing. The predictions are candidates for investigation, rather than established neural explanations.
summary.tldr: Penalizing information carried through a recurrent network yields compact cognitive models that recover known behavioral mechanisms and suggest testable new hypotheses.

title: Cognitive Model Discovery via Disentangled RNNs

abstract: Low-rank matrix recovery is a fundamental problem in machine learning with numerous applications. In practice, the problem can be solved by convex optimization namely nuclear norm minimization, or by non-convex optimization as it is well-known that for low-rank matrix problems like matrix sensing and matrix completion, all local optima of the natural non-convex objectives are also globally optimal under certain ideal assumptions.In this paper, we study new approaches for matrix sensing in a semi-random model where an adversary can add any number of arbitrary sensing matrices. More precisely, the problem is to recover a low-rank matrix $X^\star$ from linear measurements $b_i = \langle A_i, X^\star \rangle$, where an unknown subset of the sensing matrices satisfies the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) and the rest of the $A_i$'s are chosen adversarially.It is known that in the semi-random model, existing non-convex objectives can have bad local optima. To fix this, we present a descent-style algorithm that provably recovers the ground-truth matrix $X^\star$. For the closely-related problem of semi-random matrix completion, prior work [CG18] showed that all bad local optima can be eliminated by reweighting the input data. However, the analogous approach for matrix sensing requires reweighting a set of matrices to satisfy RIP, which is a condition that is NP-hard to check. Instead, we build on the framework proposed in [KLL$^+$23] for semi-random sparse linear regression, where the algorithm in each iteration reweights the input based on the current solution, and then takes a weighted gradient step that is guaranteed to work well locally. Our analysis crucially exploits the connection between sparsity in vector problems and low-rankness in matrix problems, which may have other applications in obtaining robust algorithms for sparse and low-rank problems.

paragraphs: Matrix sensing reconstructs a low-rank matrix from linear measurements. The measurements still correspond to the same underlying matrix, but the added sensing directions can create bad local optima for existing non-convex objectives.

The authors develop a descent-style algorithm with a guarantee of recovering the underlying matrix in this model. A tempting strategy would globally reweight the sensing matrices to enforce the desired geometric property, but checking that property is NP-hard. The proposed algorithm instead adapts its weights to the current solution at each iteration and takes a weighted gradient step that is guaranteed to work well locally.

The analysis builds on a framework for semi-random sparse regression and exploits the relationship between sparse vectors and low-rank matrices. The result provides a recovery method despite the problematic optimization landscape caused by adversarial additions. The authors also identify this sparsity–low-rank connection as a possible route toward other robust algorithms.
summary.tldr: An adaptively reweighted descent algorithm provably recovers low-rank matrices when adversarial sensing matrices accompany an unknown RIP-satisfying subset.

title: Robust Matrix Sensing in the Semi-Random Model

abstract: Learning representations on large-sized graphs is a long-standing challenge due to the inter-dependence nature involved in massive data points. Transformers, as an emerging class of foundation encoders for graph-structured data, have shown promising performance on small graphs due to its global attention capable of capturing all-pair influence beyond neighboring nodes. Even so, existing approaches tend to inherit the spirit of Transformers in language and vision tasks, and embrace complicated models by stacking deep multi-head attentions. In this paper, we critically demonstrate that even using a one-layer attention can bring up surprisingly competitive performance across node property prediction benchmarks where node numbers range from thousand-level to billion-level. This encourages us to rethink the design philosophy for Transformers on large graphs, where the global attention is a computation overhead hindering the scalability. We frame the proposed scheme as Simplified Graph Transformers (SGFormer), which is empowered by a simple attention model that can efficiently propagate information among arbitrary nodes in one layer. SGFormer requires none of positional encodings, feature/graph pre-processing or augmented loss. Empirically, SGFormer successfully scales to the web-scale graph ogbn-papers100M and yields up to 141x inference acceleration over SOTA Transformers on medium-sized graphs. Beyond current results, we believe the proposed methodology alone enlightens a new technical path of independent interest for building Transformers on large graphs.

SGFormer questions whether this ability requires deeply stacked, multi-head attention. The paper reports that even one attention layer can achieve surprisingly competitive node-property prediction across benchmarks spanning thousands to billions of nodes.

They support reconsidering architectural complexity in graph Transformers: a simple global-information mechanism can be competitive while substantially reducing the inference burden in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: SGFormer shows that a single simple attention layer can deliver competitive graph prediction while scaling efficiently to very large graphs.

title: SGFormer: Simplifying and Empowering Transformers for Large-Graph Representations

abstract: Optimizing Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to obtain high-quality models for efficient real-world deployment has posed multi-faceted challenges to machine learning engineers. Existing methods either search for neural architectures in heuristic design spaces or apply low-level adjustments to computation primitives to improve inference efficiency on hardware. We present Automated Graph Optimization (AutoGO), a framework to evolve neural networks in a low-level Computation Graph (CG) of primitive operations to improve both its performance and hardware friendliness. Through a tokenization scheme, AutoGO performs variable-sized segment mutations, making both primitive changes and larger-grained changes to CGs. We introduce our segmentation and mutation algorithms, efficient frequent segment mining technique, as well as a pretrained context-aware predictor to estimate the impact of segment replacements. Extensive experimental results show that AutoGO can automatically evolve several typical large convolutional networks to achieve significant task performance improvement and FLOPs reduction on a range of CV tasks, ranging from Classification, Semantic Segmentation, Human Pose Estimation, to Super Resolution, yet without introducing any newer primitive operations. We also demonstrate the lightweight deployment results of AutoGO-optimized super-resolution and denoising U-Nets on a cycle simulator for a Neural Processing Unit (NPU), achieving PSNR improvement and latency/power reduction simultaneously. Code available at https://github.com/Ascend-Research/AutoGO.

paragraphs: AutoGO improves neural networks by editing their computation graphs: the collections of basic operations that carry out a model’s calculations. This connects model design with deployment efficiency. Instead of searching only among predefined architectures, the framework can change both individual operations and larger pieces of a network through the same graph representation.

The approach converts graph components into tokens and mutates segments of varying sizes. Its supporting techniques identify frequently occurring segments and use a pretrained predictor to estimate how replacing a segment will affect the network in context. Together, these components provide a way to explore changes at multiple scales while considering their likely consequences.

Experiments show improvements in task performance alongside reductions in floating-point operations across classification, segmentation, human pose estimation, and super resolution, without adding new primitive operations. Tests of optimized super-resolution and denoising U-Nets on an NPU cycle simulator also show improved PSNR with lower latency and power. These results support graph-level evolution as a route toward models that combine useful predictions with more efficient execution.
summary.tldr: AutoGO evolves neural networks by replacing computation-graph segments, improving task performance and deployment efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: AutoGO: Automated Computation Graph Optimization for Neural Network Evolution

abstract: Leveraging planning during learning and decision-making is central to the long-term development of intelligent agents. Recent works have successfully combined tree-based search methods and self-play learning mechanisms to this end. However, these methods typically face scaling challenges due to the sequential nature of their search. While practical engineering solutions can partly overcome this, they often result in a negative impact on performance. In this paper, we introduce SPO: Sequential Monte Carlo Policy Optimisation, a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm grounded within the Expectation Maximisation (EM) framework. We show that SPO provides robust policy improvement and efficient scaling properties. The sample-based search makes it directly applicable to both discrete and continuous action spaces without modifications. We demonstrate statistically significant improvements in performance relative to model-free and model-based baselines across both continuous and discrete environments. Furthermore, the parallel nature of SPO’s search enables effective utilisation of hardware accelerators, yielding favourable scaling laws.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo Policy Optimisation, or SPO, combines planning with reinforcement learning. The paper targets a scaling difficulty in approaches that use tree search and self-play: much of their search proceeds sequentially. Engineering workarounds can improve practical execution, but the authors note that these can also reduce performance.

SPO is a model-based reinforcement-learning algorithm developed within the Expectation Maximisation framework. It uses sample-based search, which applies to both discrete and continuous action spaces without changing the algorithm. The authors show robust policy improvement and emphasize that the search can run in parallel, making it suitable for hardware accelerators.

Experiments report statistically significant performance improvements over both model-free and model-based baselines across continuous and discrete environments. The parallel search also exhibits favorable scaling behavior. These results connect the algorithm's planning design to two practical outcomes: stronger performance in the evaluated tasks and effective use of additional computing resources. Its shared treatment of different action spaces broadens the settings in which the same method can be applied.
summary.tldr: SPO uses parallel sample-based planning to improve reinforcement-learning policies across discrete and continuous tasks while scaling effectively on accelerators.

title: SPO: Sequential Monte Carlo Policy Optimisation

abstract: Language models have shown vulnerability against backdoor attacks, threatening the security of services based on them. To mitigate the threat, existing solutions attempted to search for backdoor triggers, which can be time-consuming when handling a large search space. Looking into the attack process, we observe that poisoned data will create a long-tailed effect in the victim model, causing the decision boundary to shift towards the attack targets. Inspired by this observation, we introduce LT-Defense, the first searching-free backdoor defense via exploiting the long-tailed effect. Specifically, LT-Defense employs a small set of clean examples and two metrics to distinguish backdoor-related features in the target model. Upon detecting a backdoor model, LT-Defense additionally provides test-time backdoor freezing and attack target prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LT-Defense in both detection accuracy and efficiency, e.g., in task-agnostic scenarios, LT-Defense achieves 98% accuracy across 1440 models with less than 1% of the time cost of state-of-the-art solutions.

Looking into the attack process, we observe that poisoned data will create a long-tailed effect in the victim model, causing the decision boundary to shift towards the attack targets. Inspired by this observation, we introduce LT-Defense, the first searching-free backdoor defense via exploiting the long-tailed effect. Specifically, LT-Defense employs a small set of clean examples and two metrics to distinguish backdoor-related features in the target model. Upon detecting a backdoor model, LT-Defense additionally provides test-time backdoor freezing and attack target prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LT-Defense in both detection accuracy and efficiency, e.g., in task-agnostic scenarios, LT-Defense achieves 98% accuracy across 1440 models with less than 1% of the time cost of state-of-the-art solutions.

paragraphs: LT-Defense detects backdoors in language models by examining effects left by poisoned training data. Existing defenses search for the triggers that activate malicious behavior, which can become expensive when there are many possibilities. The authors instead observe a long-tailed effect in poisoned models, accompanied by a decision-boundary shift toward the attacker's targets.

The method uses a small collection of clean examples and two metrics to distinguish features associated with a backdoor. This makes the observed model behavior, rather than a search over possible triggers, the basis for detection. After identifying a backdoored model, the framework also provides test-time backdoor freezing and prediction of the attack target.

Experiments support both detection accuracy and efficiency. In task-agnostic scenarios, the authors report 98% accuracy across 1,440 models while using less than 1% of the time required by leading comparison solutions. The result indicates that the poisoning effect can provide a practical detection signal without incurring the cost of trigger search.
summary.tldr: LT-Defense detects language-model backdoors through poisoning-induced effects, avoiding trigger searches and sharply reducing reported detection time.

title: LT-Defense: Searching-free Backdoor Defense via Exploiting the Long-tailed Effect

abstract: Prevalent text-to-video retrieval methods represent multimodal text-video data in a joint embedding space, aiming at bridging the relevant text-video pairs and pulling away irrelevant ones. One main challenge in state-of-the-art retrieval methods lies in the modality gap, which stems from the substantial disparities between text and video and can persist in the joint space. In this work, we leverage the potential of Diffusion models to address the text-video modality gap by progressively aligning text and video embeddings in a unified space. However, we identify two key limitations of existing Diffusion models in retrieval tasks: The L2 loss does not fit the ranking problem inherent in text-video retrieval, and the generation quality heavily depends on the varied initial point drawn from the isotropic Gaussian, causing inaccurate retrieval. To this end, we introduce a new Diffusion-Inspired Truncated Sampler (DITS) that jointly performs progressive alignment and modality gap modeling in the joint embedding space. The key innovation of DITS is to leverage the inherent proximity of text and video embeddings, defining a truncated diffusion flow from the fixed text embedding to the video embedding, enhancing controllability compared to adopting the isotropic Gaussian. Moreover, DITS adopts the contrastive loss to jointly consider the relevant and irrelevant pairs, not only facilitating alignment but also yielding a discriminatively structured embedding. Experiments on five benchmark datasets suggest the state-of-the-art performance of DITS. We empirically find that DITS can also improve the structure of the CLIP embedding space. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiamian- Wang/DITS-text-video-retrieval

paragraphs: Text-video retrieval often places descriptions and videos in a shared representation space, where matching pairs should be close together. However, the differences between language and video can persist within that space. DITS addresses this remaining modality gap through a diffusion-inspired process that progressively aligns their representations.

The method changes both where this process starts and how it is trained. It also replaces an L2 objective with contrastive learning, which considers matching and nonmatching pairs together and better reflects retrieval’s ranking task.

summary.tldr: DITS improves text-video retrieval through a controlled alignment process that starts from text embeddings and learns with contrastive loss.

title: Diffusion-Inspired Truncated Sampler for Text-Video Retrieval

abstract: Diffusion models represent a promising avenue for image generation, having demonstrated competitive performance in pose-guided person image generation. However, existing methods are limited to generating target images from a source image and a target pose, overlooking two critical user scenarios: generating multiple target images with different poses simultaneously and generating target images from multi-view source images.To overcome these limitations, we propose IMAGPose, a unified conditional framework for pose-guided image generation, which incorporates three pivotal modules: a feature-level conditioning (FLC) module, an image-level conditioning (ILC) module, and a cross-view attention (CVA) module. Firstly, the FLC module combines the low-level texture feature from the VAE encoder with the high-level semantic feature from the image encoder, addressing the issue of missing detail information due to the absence of a dedicated person image feature extractor. Then, the ILC module achieves an alignment of images and poses to adapt to flexible and diverse user scenarios by injecting a variable number of source image conditions and introducing a masking strategy.Finally, the CVA module introduces decomposing global and local cross-attention, ensuring local fidelity and global consistency of the person image when multiple source image prompts. The three modules of IMAGPose work together to unify the task of person image generation under various user scenarios.Extensive experiment results demonstrate the consistency and photorealism of our proposed IMAGPose under challenging user scenarios. The code and model will be available at https://github.com/muzishen/IMAGPose.

paragraphs: Pose-guided person generation aims to create images of a person in specified poses. IMAGPose expands this task beyond using one source image to produce one target image. It supports generating several poses together and using source images from multiple viewpoints, bringing these different user scenarios into a single conditional framework.

Three modules handle complementary parts of the problem. Feature-level conditioning combines texture information from a VAE encoder with higher-level semantic information from an image encoder. Image-level conditioning aligns images with poses, using a variable number of source images and a masking strategy. Cross-view attention separates global and local attention to support detailed appearance and overall consistency when multiple source images are provided.

These components jointly address the need to preserve a person’s appearance while accommodating flexible inputs and outputs. The reported experiments demonstrate consistent and photorealistic generation under challenging scenarios. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a broader formulation of pose-guided generation and a coordinated architecture for retaining detail and consistency across that wider range of conditions.
summary.tldr: IMAGPose unifies multi-pose and multi-view person generation through complementary feature, image, and cross-view conditioning modules.

title: IMAGPose: A Unified Conditional Framework for Pose-Guided Person Generation

abstract: Recent work in interpretability shows that large language models (LLMs) can be adapted for new tasks in a learning-free way: it is possible to intervene on LLM representations to elicit desired behaviors for alignment. For instance, adding certain bias vectors to the outputs of certain attention heads is reported to boost the truthfulness of models. In this work, we show that localized fine-tuning serves as an effective alternative to such representation intervention methods. We introduce a framework called Localized Fine-Tuning on LLM Representations (LoFiT), which identifies a subset of attention heads that are most important for learning a specific task, then trains offset vectors to add to the model's hidden representations at those selected heads. LoFiT localizes to a sparse set of heads (3%-10%) and learns the offset vectors from limited training data, comparable to the settings used for representation intervention. For truthfulness and reasoning tasks, we find that LoFiT's intervention vectors are more effective for LLM adaptation than vectors from representation intervention methods such as Inference-time Intervention. We also find that the localization step is important: selecting a task-specific set of attention heads can lead to higher performance than intervening on heads selected for a different task. Finally, across 7 tasks we study, LoFiT achieves comparable performance to other parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA, despite modifying 20x-200x fewer parameters than these methods.

paragraphs: LoFiT adapts language models by learning small changes at selected locations inside their representations. It builds on work showing that adding vectors to attention-head outputs can encourage desired behaviors. The paper asks whether learning these changes at task-relevant locations can provide a more effective adaptation method than existing representation interventions.

The procedure first identifies attention heads important for the target task, then learns offset vectors to add to hidden representations at those heads. It selects a sparse subset, comprising 3%–10% of the heads, and uses limited training data. Localization is part of the method's effectiveness: the authors find that choosing heads for the target task can outperform using heads selected for a different task.

On truthfulness and reasoning tasks, LoFiT's learned vectors outperform representation-intervention vectors such as those from Inference-time Intervention. Across seven studied tasks, performance is comparable to parameter-efficient methods including LoRA while modifying 20–200 times fewer parameters. These findings support both learning the offsets and selecting where to apply them as useful ingredients in compact adaptation.
summary.tldr: LoFiT learns offsets at task-selected attention heads, matching other efficient fine-tuning methods with far fewer modified parameters.

title: LoFiT: Localized Fine-tuning on LLM Representations

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows multiple clients to collaboratively train models without directly sharing their private data. While various data augmentation techniques have been actively studied in the FL environment, most of these methods share input-level or feature-level data information over communication, posing potential privacy leakage. In response to this challenge, we introduce a federated data augmentation algorithm named FedAvP that shares only the augmentation policies, not the data-related information. For data security and efficient policy search, we interpret the policy loss as a meta update loss in standard FL algorithms and utilize the first-order gradient information to further enhance privacy and reduce communication costs. Moreover, we propose a meta-learning method to search for adaptive personalized policies tailored to heterogeneous clients. Our approach outperforms existing best performing augmentation policy search methods and federated data augmentation methods, in the benchmarks for heterogeneous FL.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate on training while keeping their private datasets local. Data augmentation can help this training, but some augmentation methods communicate information about inputs or learned features, creating potential privacy exposure. FedAvP changes what is shared: clients exchange augmentation policies, which specify how to transform data, rather than the data-related information used by those earlier approaches.

The method connects augmentation-policy search to the federated training process by interpreting policy loss as a meta-update loss. It uses first-order gradient information to improve privacy and reduce communication costs. This makes policy learning part of the collaborative optimization procedure instead of requiring clients to exchange the underlying examples or features for augmentation.

FedAvP also uses meta-learning to find personalized policies for clients with different data distributions. Personalization matters because one augmentation strategy may not suit every client's local data. On heterogeneous federated-learning benchmarks, the method outperforms the compared leading policy-search and federated-augmentation approaches, supporting the combination of policy sharing and local adaptation.
summary.tldr: FedAvP shares augmentation policies and personalizes them across federated clients, improving benchmark performance while reducing communication and potential privacy exposure.

title: FedAvP: Augment Local Data via Shared Policy in Federated Learning

abstract: The Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) field has seen significant advancements, yet its progression has been hindered by challenges in comprehending fine-grained visual content due to limited resolution. Recent efforts have aimed to enhance the high-resolution understanding capabilities of LVLMs, yet they remain capped at approximately 1500 $\times$ 1500 pixels and constrained to a relatively narrow resolution range. This paper represents InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD, a groundbreaking exploration into elevating LVLM resolution capabilities up to 4K HD (3840 × 1600) and beyond. Concurrently, considering the ultra-high resolution may not be necessary in all scenarios, it supports a wide range of diverse resolutions from 336 pixels to 4K standard, significantly broadening its scope of applicability. Specifically, this research advances the patch division paradigm by introducing a novel extension: dynamic resolution with automatic patch configuration. It maintains the training image aspect ratios while automatically varying patch counts and configuring layouts based on a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) (336 $\times$ 336), leading to dynamic training resolution from 336 pixels to 4K standard. Our research demonstrates that scaling training resolution up to 4K HD leads to consistent performance enhancements without hitting the ceiling of potential improvements. InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD shows superb capability that matches or even surpasses GPT-4V and Gemini Pro in 10 of the 16 benchmarks.

paragraphs: InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD targets fine-grained visual understanding by expanding the image resolutions a vision-language model can handle. The paper identifies limited resolution as a barrier to understanding visual detail. It also recognizes that very high resolution is unnecessary for every image, motivating support for a broad range rather than a single large input size.

The method automatically configures image patches according to resolution while preserving the training image’s aspect ratio. It builds on a pretrained vision transformer that operates on 336-by-336 inputs, varying the number and arrangement of patches. This enables dynamic training resolutions ranging from 336 pixels to the paper’s 4K HD setting of 3840 by 1600.

The authors observe consistent performance improvements as training resolution increases to 4K HD, without seeing those gains reach a ceiling within that range. The model matches or surpasses GPT-4V and Gemini Pro on 10 of 16 benchmarks. These findings support flexible high-resolution processing as a useful way to improve visual understanding across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Automatic patch configuration enables flexible image resolutions up to 4K HD, with reported gains in vision-language performance.

title: InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD: A Pioneering Large Vision-Language Model Handling Resolutions from 336 Pixels to 4K HD

abstract: We study the problem of estimating the body movements of a camera wearer from egocentric videos. Current methods for ego-body pose estimation rely on temporally dense sensor data, such as IMU measurements from spatially sparse body parts like the head and hands. However, we propose that even temporally sparse observations, such as hand poses captured intermittently from egocentric videos during natural or periodic hand movements, can effectively constrain overall body motion. Naively applying diffusion models to generate full-body pose from head pose and sparse hand pose leads to suboptimal results. To overcome this, we develop a two-stage approach that decomposes the problem into temporal completion and spatial completion. First, our method employs masked autoencoders to impute hand trajectories by leveraging the spatiotemporal correlations between the head pose sequence and intermittent hand poses, providing uncertainty estimates. Subsequently, we employ conditional diffusion models to generate plausible full-body motions based on these temporally dense trajectories of the head and hands, guided by the uncertainty estimates from the imputation. The effectiveness of our methods was rigorously tested and validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on various HMD setup with AMASS and Ego-Exo4D datasets. Project page: https://sgchi.github.io/dsposer

paragraphs: Estimating a camera wearer's body motion is difficult when observations cover only a few body parts and are also intermittent. This paper investigates whether occasional hand poses visible in egocentric video, together with head motion, can meaningfully constrain full-body movement. The authors find that directly applying a diffusion model to these sparse inputs gives suboptimal results.

Their solution divides the problem into two stages. First, a masked autoencoder fills gaps in hand trajectories using relationships across time and between head and hand poses. It also estimates uncertainty in those filled-in observations. Second, a conditional diffusion model uses the now temporally dense head and hand trajectories to generate plausible full-body motion.

Uncertainty from the first stage guides the second, so the completed hand trajectories are accompanied by information about their reliability. Experiments using AMASS and Ego-Exo4D across different head-mounted display setups validate the approach. The findings support handling missing observations over time before reconstructing the unobserved parts of the body.
summary.tldr: A two-stage method completes intermittent hand trajectories and uses their uncertainty to guide full-body motion generation.

title: Estimating Ego-Body Pose from Doubly Sparse Egocentric Video Data

abstract: Presenting users with diverse responses from foundation models is crucial for enhancing user experience and accommodating varying preferences. However, generating multiple high-quality and diverse responses without sacrificing accuracy remains a challenge, especially when using greedy sampling. In this work, we propose a novel framework, Synthesize-Partition-Adapt (SPA), that leverages the abundant synthetic data available in many domains to elicit diverse responses from foundation models.By leveraging signal provided by data attribution methods such as influence functions, SPA partitions data into subsets, each targeting unique aspects of the data, and trains multiple model adaptations optimized for these subsets.Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in diversifying foundation model responses while maintaining high quality, showcased through the HumanEval and MBPP tasks in the code generation domain and several tasks in the natural language understanding domain, highlighting its potential to enrich user experience across various applications.

paragraphs: A foundation model may need to offer several useful responses to accommodate different user preferences. Producing those alternatives while preserving accuracy is difficult, particularly with greedy sampling. Synthesize-Partition-Adapt, or SPA, addresses this problem by using synthetic data to train multiple adaptations that emphasize different aspects of the available examples.

The framework uses signals from data attribution methods, including influence functions, to divide synthetic data into subsets. Each subset targets distinct aspects of the data, and a separate model adaptation is optimized for it. Diversity is therefore encouraged through the organization of training data and the resulting adaptations, giving the models different learned emphases.

Experiments on HumanEval and MBPP for code generation, together with several natural-language-understanding tasks, show more diverse responses while maintaining high quality. The results support SPA as a way to elicit useful variation from foundation models using abundant synthetic examples. Its potential value lies in offering a broader selection of responses without requiring the reported gains in diversity to come at the expense of response quality.
summary.tldr: SPA partitions synthetic data using attribution signals and trains specialized adaptations that produce more diverse, high-quality responses.

title: Synthesize, Partition, then Adapt: Eliciting Diverse Samples from Foundation Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit hallucinations in long-form question-answering tasks across various domains and wide applications. Current hallucination detection and mitigation datasets are limited in domain and size, which struggle to scale due to prohibitive labor costs and insufficient reliability of existing hallucination annotators. To facilitate the scalable oversight of LLM hallucinations, this paper introduces an iterative self-training framework that simultaneously and progressively scales up the annotation dataset and improves the accuracy of the annotator. Based on the Expectation Maximization algorithm, in each iteration, the framework first applies an automatic hallucination annotation pipeline for a scaled dataset and then trains a more accurate annotator on the dataset. This new annotator is adopted in the annotation pipeline for the next iteration. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the finally obtained hallucination annotator with only 7B parameters surpasses GPT-4 and obtains new state-of-the-art hallucination detection results on HaluEval and HalluQA by zero-shot inference. Such an annotator can not only evaluate the hallucination levels of various LLMs on the large-scale dataset but also help to mitigate the hallucination of LLMs generations, with the Natural Language Inference metric increasing from 25% to 37% on HaluEval.

paragraphs: Detecting hallucinations in long answers requires annotated examples, but collecting those examples is expensive and automatic annotators can be unreliable. ANAH-v2 addresses these linked problems with an iterative training process that expands the annotation dataset while improving the model responsible for labeling it. The aim is to make hallucination oversight scale beyond small, narrowly focused datasets.

The framework follows an expectation-maximization approach. Each round uses an automatic pipeline to annotate an expanded dataset, then trains an improved annotator on that data. The updated annotator becomes part of the pipeline for the next round. Dataset growth and annotator improvement are therefore connected within the same repeated procedure.

The resulting model has 7 billion parameters and, in the reported evaluations, surpasses GPT-4 and achieves leading zero-shot hallucination detection results on HaluEval and HalluQA. The authors also use it to assess other language models and help reduce hallucinations in generated answers. On HaluEval, that mitigation raises the reported Natural Language Inference metric from 25% to 37%.
summary.tldr: ANAH-v2 iteratively expands hallucination annotations and improves its annotator, producing a 7-billion-parameter model with strong reported detection and mitigation results.

title: ANAH-v2: Scaling Analytical Hallucination Annotation of Large Language Models

abstract: The use of guidance in diffusion models was originally motivated by the premise that the guidance-modified score is that of the data distribution tilted by a conditional likelihood raised to some power. In this work we clarify this misconception by rigorously proving that guidance fails to sample from the intended tilted distribution. Our main result is to give a fine-grained characterization of the dynamics of guidance in two cases, (1) mixtures of compactly supported distributions and (2) mixtures of Gaussians, which reflect salient properties of guidance that manifest on real-world data. In both cases, we prove that as the guidance parameter increases, the guided model samples more heavily from the boundary of the support of the conditional distribution. We also prove that for any nonzero level of score estimation error, sufficiently large guidance will result in sampling away from the support, theoretically justifying the empirical finding that large guidance results in distorted generations. In addition to verifying these results empirically in synthetic settings, we also show how our theoretical insights can offer useful prescriptions for practical deployment.

paragraphs: Guidance steers diffusion generation toward a condition, but a common explanation of its effect is mathematically misleading. This paper rigorously shows that guidance does not sample from the intended distribution obtained by reweighting the data distribution with a powered conditional likelihood. It then examines what guidance actually does in two tractable settings.

The analysis considers mixtures of compactly supported distributions and mixtures of Gaussians. In both cases, the authors prove that increasing guidance shifts sampling more heavily toward the boundary of the conditional distribution's support. They also show that, for any nonzero score-estimation error, sufficiently strong guidance causes sampling away from the support.

That second result provides a theoretical explanation for the observed distortion of generations at high guidance levels: stronger steering can amplify the consequences of imperfect score estimates. Synthetic experiments verify the theoretical findings, and the authors discuss practical prescriptions informed by them. The paper's contribution is a detailed account of guidance dynamics in simplified settings that captures behaviors also observed with real-world data.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how strong diffusion guidance shifts samples toward distribution boundaries and, with score error, beyond the support.

title: What does guidance do? A fine-grained analysis in a simple setting

abstract: In this work we consider the problem of discretization of neural operators in a general setting. Using category theory, we give a no-go theorem that shows that diffeomorphisms between Hilbert spaces may not admit any continuous approximations by diffeomorphisms on finite spaces, even if the discretization is non-linear. This shows how infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and finite-dimensional vector spaces fundamentally differ. A key take-away is that to obtain discretization invariance, considerable effort is needed to ensure that finite-dimensional approximations of neural operator converge not only as sequences of functions, but that their representations converge in a suitable sense as well. With this perspective, we give several positive results. We first show that strongly monotone diffeomorphism operators always admit finite-dimensional strongly monotone diffeomorphisms. Next we show that bilipschitz neural operators may always be written via the repeated alternating composition of strongly monotone neural operators and invertible linear maps. We also show that such operators may be inverted locally via iteration provided that such inverse exists. Finally, we conclude by showing how our framework may be used `out of the box' to prove quantitative approximation results for discretization of neural operators.
originalAbstract: In this work we consider the problem of discretization of neural operators in a general setting. Using category theory, we give a no-go theorem that shows that diffeomorphisms between Hilbert spaces may not admit any continuous approximations by diffeomorphisms on finite spaces, even if the discretization is non-linear. This shows how infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and finite-dimensional vector spaces fundamentally differ. A key take-away is that to obtain discretization invariance, considerable effort is needed to ensure that finite-dimensional approximations of neural operator converge not only as sequences of functions, but that their representations converge in a suitable sense as well. With this perspective, we give several positive results. We first show that strongly monotone diffeomorphism operators always admit finite-dimensional strongly monotone diffeomorphisms. Next we show that bilipschitz neural operators may always be written via the repeated alternating composition of strongly monotone neural operators and invertible linear maps. We also show that such operators may be inverted locally via iteration provided that such inverse exists. Finally, we conclude by showing how our framework may be used `out of the box' to prove quantitative approximation results for discretization of neural operators.

paragraphs: Neural operators can act on infinite-dimensional spaces, but their implementation requires finite-dimensional representations. This paper asks whether such representations can always approximate an operator continuously while preserving invertibility. Using category theory, it proves a negative result: some diffeomorphisms between Hilbert spaces do not admit the required continuous finite-dimensional approximations, even when nonlinear discretization is allowed.

The consequence concerns what discretization invariance demands. Convergence of the approximating functions alone is insufficient; their representations must also converge appropriately. This exposes a structural difference between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and finite-dimensional vector spaces, rather than simply a difficulty caused by choosing an inadequate numerical resolution.

The authors also establish positive results under additional structure. Strongly monotone diffeomorphism operators admit finite-dimensional strongly monotone counterparts. Bilipschitz neural operators can be decomposed into alternating strongly monotone operators and invertible linear maps, and local iterative inversion is possible provided the inverse exists. The framework also yields quantitative discretization bounds. Together, these results identify both an obstruction to unrestricted discretization and useful structures for obtaining constructive guarantees.
summary.tldr: Continuous finite-dimensional discretization is not always possible for neural operators, but additional operator structure enables positive approximation results.

title: Can neural operators always be continuously discretized?

abstract: Bilevel optimization has gained prominence in various applications. In this study, we introduce a framework for solving bilevel optimization problems, where the variables in both the lower and upper levels are constrained on Riemannian manifolds. We present several hypergradient estimation strategies on manifolds and analyze their estimation errors. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive convergence and complexity analyses for the proposed hypergradient descent algorithm on manifolds. We also extend our framework to encompass stochastic bilevel optimization and incorporate the use of general retraction. The efficacy of the proposed framework is demonstrated through several applications.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems: the decision made at the upper level depends on the solution found at the lower level. This paper develops a framework for cases where both sets of variables must lie on Riemannian manifolds. These geometric constraints shape how the optimization process can move and how derivatives are defined.

A central contribution concerns hypergradients, which describe how changing an upper-level variable affects the objective through the lower-level problem. The authors introduce several ways to estimate these quantities on manifolds and analyze their estimation errors. They also study convergence and computational complexity for a hypergradient descent algorithm that operates within this geometric setting.

The framework also covers stochastic bilevel optimization and general retractions, which provide a way to perform updates on a manifold. Applications demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution brings gradient estimation, algorithm design, and theoretical analysis together, providing a framework for nested optimization problems whose variables must respect geometric constraints at both levels.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes methods for bilevel optimization when both levels have variables constrained to Riemannian manifolds.

title: A Framework for Bilevel Optimization on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: This paper explores the realm of infinite horizon average reward Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to delve into the regret and constraint violation analysis of average reward CMDPs with a general policy parametrization. To address this challenge, we propose a primal dual-based policy gradient algorithm that adeptly manages the constraints while ensuring a low regret guarantee toward achieving a global optimal policy. In particular, our proposed algorithm achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ objective regret and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ constraint violation bounds.

In particular, our proposed algorithm achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ objective regret and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ constraint violation bounds.

paragraphs: Infinite-horizon constrained Markov decision processes balance long-run reward with restrictions on behavior. This paper studies average reward with a general parameterized policy, asking how performance shortfall and constraint violations accumulate during learning rather than only analyzing a final policy.

The authors propose a primal-dual policy-gradient algorithm. The formulation manages the reward objective and constraints together, with the stated aim of approaching a globally optimal policy while keeping cumulative regret and violations controlled.

The reported bounds are approximately O(T^(4/5)) for both objective regret and constraint violation, up to logarithmic factors. Since these grow sublinearly, their per-step averages diminish under the analysis. The abstract does not state the full assumptions, policy-approximation conditions, or empirical results. The contribution is a theoretical extension to this average-reward setting, not a claim that constraints are never violated at any individual learning step.
summary.tldr: Primal-dual policy gradients receive regret and constraint-violation bounds for average-reward constrained control.

title: Learning General Parameterized Policies for Infinite Horizon Average Reward Constrained MDPs via Primal-Dual Policy Gradient Algorithm

abstract: The information processing in the brain and embodied agents form a sensory-action loop to interact with the world. An important step in the loop is motion planning which selects motor actions based on the current world state and task need. In goal-directed navigation, the brain chooses and generates motor actions to bring the current state into the goal state. It is unclear about the neural circuit mechanism of motor action selection, nor its underlying theory. The present study formulates the motion planning as a Lie group operator search problem, and uses the 1D rotation group as an example to provide insight into general operator search in neural circuits. We found the abstract group operator search can be implemented by a two-layer feedforward circuit utilizing circuit motifs of connection phase shift, nonlinear activation function, and pooling, similar to Drosophila's goal-directed navigation neural circuits. And the computational complexity of the feedforward circuit can be even lower than common signal processing algorithms in certain conditions. We also provide geometric interpretations of circuit computation in the group representation space. The feedforward motion planning circuit is further combined with sensory and motor circuit modules into a full circuit of the sensory-action loop implementing goal-directed navigation. Our work for the first time links the abstract operator search with biological neural circuits.

paragraphs: Goal-directed navigation requires choosing actions that transform the current state into a desired state. This paper formulates that choice as a search for an operator in a Lie group, a mathematical structure for transformations. It uses the one-dimensional rotation group as a concrete example for investigating how such a search could be carried out by neural circuits.

The authors further combine the planning circuit with sensory and motor modules to form a complete navigation loop. The work establishes a connection between abstract transformation search and biologically inspired circuit computation, with the rotation example serving as its concrete demonstration.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how a two-layer neural circuit can implement Lie-group operator search for navigation, using one-dimensional rotation as its example.

title: The motion planning neural circuit in goal-directed navigation as Lie group operator search

abstract: Backdoor attacks on deep learning represent a recent threat that has gained significant attention in the research community. Backdoor defenses are mainly based on backdoor inversion, which has been shown to be generic, model-agnostic, and applicable to practical threat scenarios. State-of-the-art backdoor inversion recovers a mask in the feature space to locate prominent backdoor features, where benign and backdoor features can be disentangled. However, it suffers from high computational overhead, and we also find that it overly relies on prominent backdoor features that are highly distinguishable from benign features. To tackle these shortcomings, this paper improves backdoor feature inversion for backdoor detection by incorporating extra neuron activation information. In particular, we adversarially increase the loss of backdoored models with respect to weights to activate the backdoor effect, based on which we can easily differentiate backdoored and clean models. Experimental results demonstrate our defense, BAN, is 1.37$\times$ (on CIFAR-10) and 5.11$\times$ (on ImageNet200) more efficient with an average 9.99\% higher detect success rate than the state-of-the-art defense BTI DBF. Our code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/xiaoyunxxy/ban.

paragraphs: Backdoor detection methods can search a model’s internal features for evidence of hidden malicious behavior. The paper examines an existing inversion approach that finds a feature-space mask separating backdoor features from benign ones. BAN adds information from neuron activations to this detection process. The method adversarially changes weights to increase the model’s loss, aiming to activate the backdoor effect. These findings support activation information as a useful addition to feature inversion. They establish gains for the evaluated defense setting without implying that every possible backdoor becomes detectable.
summary.tldr: BAN activates hidden backdoor behavior through adversarial weight perturbations, improving detection success and efficiency in the reported comparisons.

title: BAN: Detecting Backdoors Activated by Adversarial Neuron Noise

abstract: Diffusion planning has been recognized as an effective decision-making paradigm in various domains. The capability of generating high-quality long-horizon trajectories makes it a promising research direction. However, existing diffusion planning methods suffer from low decision-making frequencies due to the expensive iterative sampling cost. To alleviate this, we introduce DiffuserLite, a super fast and lightweight diffusion planning framework, which employs a planning refinement process (PRP) to generate coarse-to-fine-grained trajectories, significantly reducing the modeling of redundant information and leading to notable increases in decision-making frequency. Our experimental results demonstrate that DiffuserLite achieves a decision-making frequency of $122.2$Hz ($112.7$x faster than predominant frameworks) and reaches state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, Robomimic, and FinRL benchmarks. In addition, DiffuserLite can also serve as a flexible plugin to increase the decision-making frequency of other diffusion planning algorithms, providing a structural design reference for future works. More details and visualizations are available at https://diffuserlite.github.io/.

paragraphs: Diffusion planning generates trajectories that describe how a decision-making process could unfold over a long horizon. Although these trajectories can be high quality, producing them through repeated sampling is expensive. That cost limits how frequently a system can make a new decision, creating a practical obstacle for fast planning.

DiffuserLite introduces a planning refinement process that develops trajectories from coarse descriptions into finer detail. The framework reduces the modeling of redundant information through this progression. Its central design choice connects the amount of trajectory detail being generated to the computational work required, aiming to preserve useful planning capability while increasing decision frequency.

The reported experiments achieve 122.2 decisions per second, or 112.7 times the frequency of predominant frameworks, alongside state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, Robomimic, and FinRL. The authors also describe DiffuserLite as a plugin for accelerating other diffusion planners. The results support coarse-to-fine refinement as a useful structural approach to making diffusion-based decision making faster.
summary.tldr: DiffuserLite refines trajectories from coarse to fine detail, reporting much faster diffusion planning and state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

title: DiffuserLite: Towards Real-time Diffusion Planning

abstract: Most incremental learners excessively prioritize object classes while neglecting various kinds of states (e.g. color and material) attached to the objects. As a result, they are limited in the ability to model state-object compositionality accurately. To remedy this limitation, we propose a novel task called Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL), which enables the model to recognize a variety of state-object compositions in an incremental learning fashion. Since the lack of suitable datasets, we re-organize two existing datasets and make them tailored for composition-IL. Then, we propose a prompt-based Composition Incremental Learner (CompILer), to overcome the ambiguous composition boundary. Specifically, we exploit multi-pool prompt learning, and ensure the inter-pool prompt discrepancy and intra-pool prompt diversity. Besides, we devise object-injected state prompting which injects object prompts to guide the selection of state prompts. Furthermore, we fuse the selected prompts by a generalized-mean strategy, to eliminate irrelevant information learned in the prompts. Extensive experiments on two datasets exhibit state-of-the-art performance achieved by CompILer. Code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/Yanyi-Zhang/CompILer.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object can also require recognizing its state, such as its color or material. The paper argues that incremental learners focus too heavily on object categories and therefore struggle with combinations of states and objects. It introduces Compositional Incremental Learning and reorganizes two existing datasets to support studying this task.

The proposed learner, CompILer, uses several prompt pools and encourages both differences between pools and diversity within each pool. Object prompts guide the selection of state prompts, explicitly connecting the object being considered with its possible state description. The selected prompts are combined through a generalized-mean strategy intended to remove irrelevant learned information.

Experiments on the two adapted datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution includes both a task formulation for learning state-object combinations incrementally and a prompt-based method for handling their ambiguous boundaries. The findings support treating state recognition and object recognition as connected parts of incremental learning, with object information helping determine which state prompts are relevant.
summary.tldr: CompILer uses object-guided state prompts to learn combinations of objects and their states incrementally.

title: Not Just Object, But State: Compositional Incremental Learning without Forgetting

abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP have remarkably adapted to various downstream tasks. Nonetheless, their performance heavily depends on the specificity of the input text prompts, which requires skillful prompt template engineering. Instead, current approaches to prompt optimization learn the prompts through gradient descent, where the prompts are treated as adjustable parameters. However, these methods tend to lead to overfitting of the base classes seen during training and produce prompts that are no longer understandable by humans. This paper introduces a simple but interpretable prompt optimizer (IPO), that utilizes large language models (LLMs) to generate textual prompts dynamically. We introduce a Prompt Optimization Prompt that not only guides LLMs in creating effective prompts but also stores past prompts with their performance metrics, providing rich in-context information. Additionally, we incorporate a large multimodal model (LMM) to condition on visual content by generating image descriptions, which enhance the interaction between textual and visual modalities. This allows for the creation of dataset-specific prompts that improve generalization performance, while maintaining human comprehension. Extensive testing across 11 datasets reveals that IPO not only improves the accuracy of existing gradient-descent-based prompt learning methods but also considerably enhances the interpretability of the generated prompts. By leveraging the strengths of LLMs, our approach ensures that the prompts remain human-understandable, thereby facilitating better transparency and oversight for vision-language models.

Optimizing prompts as numerical parameters can produce unreadable results and overfit the classes used during training. IPO addresses this problem by using a language model to generate actual text prompts that people can inspect and understand.

Its central Prompt Optimization Prompt guides generation while retaining earlier candidate prompts and their performance measurements. That history supplies context for subsequent proposals. A large multimodal model also produces descriptions of image content, giving the optimization process visual information from which to develop prompts suited to a particular dataset.

Testing across 11 datasets reports improved accuracy over existing gradient-based prompt-learning methods alongside more interpretable prompts. The approach also aims to improve generalization by combining readable language, performance feedback, and descriptions of the visual data. Its practical significance is that prompt optimization produces an inspectable textual artifact, connecting the search for stronger predictions with human understanding of what the model is being asked.
summary.tldr: IPO uses language models, prompt-performance history, and image descriptions to optimize readable prompts for vision-language models.

title: IPO: Interpretable Prompt Optimization for Vision-Language Models

abstract: The task of layout-to-image generation involves synthesizing images based on the captions of objects and their spatial positions. Existing methods still struggle in complex layout generation, where common bad cases include object missing, inconsistent lighting, conflicting view angles, etc. To effectively address these issues, we propose a \textbf{Hi}erarchical \textbf{Co}ntrollable (HiCo) diffusion model for layout-to-image generation, featuring object seperable conditioning branch structure. Our key insight is to achieve spatial disentanglement through hierarchical modeling of layouts. We use a multi branch structure to represent hierarchy and aggregate them in fusion module. To evaluate the performance of multi-objective controllable layout generation in natural scenes, we introduce the HiCo-7K benchmark, derived from the GRIT-20M dataset and manually cleaned. https://github.com/360CVGroup/HiCo_T2I.

paragraphs: Layout-to-image generation creates an image from descriptions of objects and their intended spatial positions. Complex layouts remain difficult: objects may disappear, lighting may become inconsistent, and different parts of the scene may imply conflicting viewing angles. HiCo addresses this problem through a hierarchical design for conditioning a diffusion model.

The model uses separate conditioning branches for objects and a multi-branch structure to represent the layout hierarchy. A fusion module combines those branches. The central idea is to disentangle spatial information through hierarchical modeling, giving the architecture a way to represent separate layout components and then bring their information together during generation. This makes the organization of conditioning information a central part of the proposed solution.

The paper also introduces HiCo-7K, a benchmark for evaluating controllable generation involving multiple objectives in natural scenes. It is derived from GRIT-20M and manually cleaned. Together, the architecture and benchmark address how to represent complex layout instructions and how to evaluate the resulting generation task; the abstract does not state a numerical performance gain.
summary.tldr: HiCo organizes layout conditioning into hierarchical object branches and introduces HiCo-7K for evaluating complex controllable image generation.

title: HiCo: Hierarchical Controllable Diffusion Model for Layout-to-image Generation

abstract: We develop and analyze data subsampling techniques for Poisson regression, the standard model for count data $y\in\mathbb{N}$. In particular, we consider the Poisson generalized linear model with ID- and square root-link functions. We consider the method of \emph{coresets}, which are small weighted subsets that approximate the loss function of Poisson regression up to a factor of $1\pm\varepsilon$. We show $\Omega(n)$ lower bounds against coresets for Poisson regression that continue to hold against arbitrary data reduction techniques up to logarithmic factors. By introducing a novel complexity parameter and a domain shifting approach, we show that sublinear coresets with $1\pm\varepsilon$ approximation guarantee exist when the complexity parameter is small. In particular, the dependence on the number of input points can be reduced to polylogarithmic. We show that the dependence on other input parameters can also be bounded sublinearly, though not always logarithmically. In particular, we show that the square root-link admits an $O(\log(y_{\max}))$ dependence, where $y_{\max}$ denotes the largest count presented in the data, while the ID-link requires a $\Theta(\sqrt{y_{\max}/\log(y_{\max})})$ dependence. As an auxiliary result for proving the tightness of the bound with respect to $y_{\max}$ in the case of the ID-link, we show an improved bound on the principal branch of the Lambert $W_0$ function, which may be of independent interest. We further show the limitations of our analysis when $p$th degree root-link functions for $p\geq 3$ are considered, which indicate that other analytical or computational methods would be required if such a generalization is even possible.

paragraphs: Poisson regression models count data, but fitting it to a large dataset motivates finding a smaller substitute. This paper studies coresets: weighted subsets that approximate the original regression loss within a multiplicative factor of one plus or minus epsilon. It focuses on identity and square-root link functions.

The authors first establish limits on compression. In general, coresets may require size proportional to the number of data points, and related lower bounds extend to arbitrary data reduction up to logarithmic factors. They then introduce a complexity parameter and a domain-shifting approach. When that parameter is small, sublinear coresets become possible, with only polylogarithmic dependence on the number of observations.

The choice of link function also matters. Dependence on the largest observed count is logarithmic for the square-root link, whereas the identity link requires a larger dependence characterized by a tight bound. The analysis additionally improves a bound on the Lambert W function. For root links of degree three or higher, the authors identify limitations of their analysis, leaving any possible extension dependent on other methods.
summary.tldr: Poisson regression generally resists strong data compression, but small weighted subsets have approximation guarantees when a proposed complexity parameter is small.

title: Data subsampling for Poisson regression with pth-root-link

abstract: We introduce a novel score-based diffusion framework named Twigs that incorporates multiple co-evolving flows for enriching conditional generation tasks. Specifically, a central or trunk diffusion process is associated with a primary variable (e.g., graph structure), and additional offshoot or stem processes are dedicated to dependent variables (e.g., graph properties or labels). A new strategy, which we call loop guidance, effectively orchestrates the flow of information between the trunk and the stem processes during sampling. This approach allows us to uncover intricate interactions and dependencies, and unlock new generative capabilities. We provide extensive experiments to demonstrate strong performance gains of the proposed method over contemporary baselines in the context of conditional graph generation, underscoring the potential of Twigs in challenging generative tasks such as inverse molecular design and molecular optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/Diffusion_twigs.
