paragraphs: Inductive matrix completion seeks to recover a low-rank matrix using both observed information and known features supplied as prior information. The central question here is whether those features can reduce both the amount of data needed and the computational effort required for recovery. The paper studies a rank-r matrix with ambient dimension d and n supplied features.

The authors introduce and analyze a gradient-based nonconvex optimization algorithm. They establish linear convergence to the underlying matrix, meaning that recovery error decreases at a geometric rate in their analysis. Its sample complexity depends linearly on the number of features and logarithmically on the ambient dimension.

These two properties address a tradeoff in earlier work: according to the authors, previous algorithms had either quadratic feature dependence in sample complexity or sublinear computational convergence. The proposed method combines improved feature dependence with fast convergence. Experiments on synthetic and real data further demonstrate its effectiveness, complementing the theoretical analysis of data requirements and optimization speed.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex gradient method combines linear convergence for inductive matrix completion with sample complexity linear in the number of supplied features.

title: Fast and Sample Efficient Inductive Matrix Completion via Multi-Phase Procrustes Flow

abstract: Most model-free reinforcement learning methods leverage state representations (embeddings) for generalization, but either ignore structure in the space of actions or assume the structure is provided a priori. We show how a policy can be decomposed into a component that acts in a low-dimensional space of action representations and a component that transforms these representations into actual actions. These representations improve generalization over large, finite action sets by allowing the agent to infer the outcomes of actions similar to actions already taken. We provide an algorithm to both learn and use action representations and provide conditions for its convergence. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated on large-scale real-world problems.

These representations improve generalization over large, finite action sets by allowing the agent to infer the outcomes of actions similar to actions already taken. We provide an algorithm to both learn and use action representations and provide conditions for its convergence. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated on large-scale real-world problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often use state representations to generalize across situations, while treating available actions as unrelated choices or relying on a supplied action structure. This paper learns representations of actions themselves. The aim is to share information across a large finite action set, so experience with one action can help predict the effects of similar actions.

The policy is separated into two components. The first makes a choice in a low-dimensional space of action representations. The second translates that representation into an actual action. This decomposition gives the policy a compact space in which to reason, while preserving the connection to the concrete actions the environment accepts.

The authors provide an algorithm that both learns these representations and uses them for decision-making, along with conditions for convergence. They demonstrate its effectiveness on large-scale real-world problems. The central contribution is to make action similarity something an agent can learn and exploit, extending representation-based generalization beyond states to the choices available in each interaction.
summary.tldr: Learning a compact action representation lets reinforcement learning agents generalize across similar actions in large finite action sets.

title: Learning Action Representations for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Estimating and optimizing Mutual Information (MI) is core to many problems in machine learning, but bounding MI in high dimensions is challenging. To establish tractable and scalable objectives, recent work has turned to variational bounds parameterized by neural networks. However, the relationships and tradeoffs between these bounds remains unclear. In this work, we unify these recent developments in a single framework. We find that the existing variational lower bounds degrade when the MI is large, exhibiting either high bias or high variance. To address this problem, we introduce a continuum of lower bounds that encompasses previous bounds and flexibly trades off bias and variance. On high-dimensional, controlled problems, we empirically characterize the bias and variance of the bounds and their gradients and demonstrate the effectiveness of these new bounds for estimation and representation learning.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures how much information two quantities share. Estimating or optimizing it becomes difficult in high-dimensional settings, motivating tractable bounds represented by neural networks. This paper brings several such variational bounds into a common framework so that their relationships and statistical tradeoffs can be examined together.

The analysis finds that existing lower bounds deteriorate when mutual information is large. Some have high bias, producing systematically distorted estimates, while others have high variance, producing unstable estimates across samples. The authors introduce a continuous family of lower bounds that includes earlier bounds and allows the balance between these two problems to be adjusted.

Experiments on controlled high-dimensional problems characterize both the estimates and their gradients. Examining gradients matters because a bound may serve as a training objective as well as a numerical estimate of information. The authors demonstrate that the new bounds are effective for estimation and representation learning. The contribution provides a way to navigate bias and variance rather than claiming that a single bound removes both problems in every setting.
summary.tldr: A unified family of mutual-information lower bounds lets practitioners trade bias against variance, addressing weaknesses that become pronounced at high mutual information.

title: On Variational Bounds of Mutual Information

abstract: We investigate meta-learning procedures in the setting of stochastic linear bandits tasks. The goal is to select a learning algorithm which works well on average over a class of bandits tasks, that are sampled from a task-distribution. Inspired by recent work on learning-to-learn linear regression, we consider a class of bandit algorithms that implement a regularized version of the well-known OFUL algorithm, where the regularization is a square euclidean distance to a bias vector. We first study the benefit of the biased OFUL algorithm in terms of regret minimization. We then propose two strategies to estimate the bias within the learning-to-learn setting. We show both theoretically and experimentally, that when the number of tasks grows and the variance of the task-distribution is small, our strategies have a significant advantage over learning the tasks in isolation.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning across a collection of stochastic linear bandit tasks drawn from a task distribution. Its goal is to select a learning algorithm that performs well on average across those tasks. The central question is whether experience with earlier tasks can improve the exploration and learning required for another task from the same distribution.

The authors modify OFUL by adding regularization toward a bias vector, using squared Euclidean distance as the penalty. This vector provides a shared reference point for learning individual tasks. They first analyze how the biased algorithm affects regret, then propose two strategies for estimating the bias in a learning-to-learn setting. The shared information is therefore itself learned from the task collection.

Theory and experiments show a significant advantage over learning tasks independently when the number of tasks grows and the task distribution has low variance. These conditions matter: the stated benefit concerns collections with enough experience and relatively limited variation between tasks. The results support learning a common bias as a useful way to transfer information among related bandit problems.
summary.tldr: Learning a shared regularization bias improves stochastic linear bandit learning when many tasks come from a low-variance task distribution.

title: Meta-learning with Stochastic Linear Bandits

abstract: Autonomous agents that must exhibit flexible and broad capabilities will need to be equipped with large repertoires of skills. Defining each skill with a manually-designed reward function limits this repertoire and imposes a manual engineering burden. Self-supervised agents that set their own goals can automate this process, but designing appropriate goal setting objectives can be difficult, and often involves heuristic design decisions. In this paper, we propose a formal exploration objective for goal-reaching policies that maximizes state coverage. We show that this objective is equivalent to maximizing goal reaching performance together with the entropy of the goal distribution, where goals correspond to full state observations. To instantiate this principle, we present an algorithm called Skew-Fit for learning a maximum-entropy goal distributions. We prove that, under regularity conditions, Skew-Fit converges to a uniform distribution over the set of valid states, even when we do not know this set beforehand. Our experiments show that combining Skew-Fit for learning goal distributions with existing goal-reaching methods outperforms a variety of prior methods on open-sourced visual goal-reaching tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that Skew-Fit enables a real-world robot to learn to open a door, entirely from scratch, from pixels, and without any manually-designed reward function.

Setting its own goals offers an alternative, but the goal-selection rule still needs a principled objective. This paper proposes maximizing state coverage for policies trained to reach goals defined by full state observations.

The authors show that this objective is equivalent to combining goal-reaching performance with high entropy in the goal distribution. Skew-Fit implements the goal-distribution part of this principle. Under regularity conditions, it converges to a uniform distribution over valid states even when the set of valid states is initially unknown. The conditions are part of the convergence claim.

When paired with existing goal-reaching methods, Skew-Fit outperforms several prior approaches on the evaluated visual goal-reaching tasks. The paper also demonstrates a real robot learning to open a door from pixels, starting from scratch and without a manually designed reward. These results connect a formal coverage objective to practical self-supervised skill learning, with goal selection providing the mechanism for encouraging broader experience.
summary.tldr: Skew-Fit learns diverse self-generated goals, with conditional state-coverage guarantees and demonstrations of visual skill learning without manually designed rewards.

title: Skew-Fit: State-Covering Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Collaborative machine learning (ML) is an appealing paradigm to build high-quality ML models by training on the aggregated data from many parties. However, these parties are only willing to share their data when given enough incentives, such as a guaranteed fair reward based on their contributions. This motivates the need for measuring a party’s contribution and designing an incentive-aware reward scheme accordingly. This paper proposes to value a party’s reward based on Shapley value and information gain on model parameters given its data. Subsequently, we give each party a model as a reward. To formally incentivize the collaboration, we define some desirable properties (e.g., fairness and stability) which are inspired by cooperative game theory but adapted for our model reward that is uniquely freely replicable. Then, we propose a novel model reward scheme to satisfy fairness and trade off between the desirable properties via an adjustable parameter. The value of each party’s model reward determined by our scheme is attained by injecting Gaussian noise to the aggregated training data with an optimized noise variance. We empirically demonstrate interesting properties of our scheme and evaluate its performance using synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning can improve models by pooling data from several parties, but participation depends on whether contributors receive worthwhile rewards. This paper studies a scheme in which each party receives a model as its reward. It values contributions using Shapley value and the information that a party’s data provides about model parameters, connecting reward allocation to the usefulness of contributed data.

The authors define desirable properties, including fairness and stability, drawing on cooperative game theory. Those properties are adapted to an unusual feature of the reward: models can be copied freely. The proposed allocation scheme satisfies fairness and uses an adjustable parameter to trade off among the other desirable properties.

To realize the assigned reward values, the method injects Gaussian noise into the aggregated training data, optimizing the noise variance. This links the abstract allocation of value to the models actually delivered to participants. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets examine the scheme’s properties and performance, illustrating how contribution measurement and model construction can jointly support incentives for collaboration.
summary.tldr: A collaborative learning scheme rewards data contributors with models whose values reflect their contributions and adjustable fairness-related tradeoffs.

title: Collaborative Machine Learning with Incentive-Aware Model Rewards

abstract: We propose a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood of Gaussian process regression models that can be computed without matrix factorisation of the full kernel matrix. We show that approximate maximum likelihood learning of model parameters by maximising our lower bound retains many benefits of the sparse variational approach while reducing the bias introduced into hyperparameter learning. The basis of our bound is a more careful analysis of the log-determinant term appearing in the log marginal likelihood, as well as using the method of conjugate gradients to derive tight lower bounds on the term involving a quadratic form. Our approach is a step forward in unifying methods relying on lower bound maximisation (e.g. variational methods) and iterative approaches based on conjugate gradients for training Gaussian processes. In experiments, we show improved predictive performance with our model for a comparable amount of training time compared to other conjugate gradient based approaches.

paragraphs: Training Gaussian process regression models involves choosing parameters using the log marginal likelihood, whose computation depends on a kernel matrix. This paper proposes a lower bound that avoids factorizing the full matrix. Maximizing the bound provides an approximate maximum-likelihood route to learning the model's parameters.

The construction improves the treatment of two parts of the objective. It analyzes the log-determinant term more carefully and uses conjugate gradients to obtain tight lower bounds for a quadratic-form term. This brings iterative linear-algebra methods into an objective that can be optimized through lower-bound maximization.

The authors show that their approach retains many advantages of sparse variational training while reducing the bias introduced into hyperparameter learning. Experiments report better predictive performance than other conjugate-gradient approaches at comparable training time. The contribution therefore goes beyond replacing a matrix operation: it links the quality of the training bound to parameter selection and prediction, while moving toward a unified treatment of variational-style bounds and iterative Gaussian process training.
summary.tldr: A tighter Gaussian process likelihood bound combines improved analysis with conjugate gradients, reducing hyperparameter-learning bias and improving predictions in experiments.

title: Tighter Bounds on the Log Marginal Likelihood of Gaussian Process Regression Using Conjugate Gradients

abstract: The reliability of deep learning algorithms is fundamentally challenged by the existence of adversarial examples, which are incorrectly classified inputs that are extremely close to a correctly classified input. We explore the properties of adversarial examples for deep neural networks with random weights and biases, and prove that for any p$\geq$1, the \ell^p distance of any given input from the classification boundary scales as one over the square root of the dimension of the input times the \ell^p norm of the input. The results are based on the recently proved equivalence between Gaussian processes and deep neural networks in the limit of infinite width of the hidden layers, and are validated with experiments on both random deep neural networks and deep neural networks trained on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. The results constitute a fundamental advance in the theoretical understanding of adversarial examples, and open the way to a thorough theoretical characterization of the relation between network architecture and robustness to adversarial perturbations.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples expose a troubling property of classifiers: a small change to an input can move it across a decision boundary and produce an incorrect prediction. This paper studies that boundary geometry for deep neural networks whose weights and biases are random, seeking a mathematical account of how input dimension affects robustness.

The authors prove a scaling relationship for every p at least one. The distance from a given input to the classification boundary, measured with the corresponding norm, scales with the input’s norm divided by the square root of its dimension. Expressing distance relative to input magnitude makes the dimensional dependence explicit.

The analysis uses the connection between Gaussian processes and deep networks in the infinite-width limit. Experiments examine both random networks and networks trained on MNIST and CIFAR10, supporting the stated scaling results. The theoretical setting and empirical checks play different roles: together they advance understanding of adversarial proximity and motivate further analysis of how network architecture relates to robustness.
summary.tldr: For random deep networks, classification-boundary distance scales with input magnitude divided by the square root of input dimension.

title: Adversarial Robustness Guarantees for Random Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We tackle the online ranking problem of assigning $L$ items to $K$ positions on a web page in order to maximize the number of user clicks. We propose an original algorithm, easy to implement and with strong theoretical guarantees to tackle this problem in the Position-Based Model (PBM) setting, well suited for applications where items are displayed on a grid. Besides learning to rank, our algorithm, GRAB (for parametric Graph for unimodal RAnking Bandit), also learns the parameter of a compact graph over permutations of $K$ items among $L$. The logarithmic regret bound of this algorithm is a direct consequence of the unimodality property of the bandit setting with respect to the learned graph. Experiments against state-of-the-art learning algorithms which also tackle the PBM setting, show that our method is more efficient while giving regret performance on par with the best known algorithms on simulated and real life datasets.

paragraphs: Online ranking systems must place items where users are most likely to click while learning which items are attractive. This paper studies assigning items to page positions under the Position-Based Model, a setting suited to displays such as grids. The combinatorial number of possible rankings makes efficient exploration important.

The proposed algorithm, GRAB, learns both a ranking and the parameter of a compact graph over permutations of K items chosen from L candidates. The bandit problem is unimodal with respect to this learned graph, a property that supports its logarithmic regret guarantee. The graph supplies structure that the algorithm can exploit rather than treating every ranking independently.

On simulated and real-world datasets, GRAB is more efficient than compared methods while matching the regret performance of the strongest alternatives. The result combines implementation simplicity with theoretical control. Its guarantees and evaluation are tied to the Position-Based Model, whose assumptions determine how item attractiveness and display position relate to clicks.
summary.tldr: GRAB learns a compact graph over rankings to obtain efficient online ranking with logarithmic regret in the Position-Based Model.

title: Parametric Graph for Unimodal Ranking Bandit

abstract: We consider the construction of neural network architectures for data on simplicial complexes. In studying maps on the chain complex of a simplicial complex, we define three desirable properties of a simplicial neural network architecture: namely, permutation equivariance, orientation equivariance, and simplicial awareness. The first two properties respectively account for the fact that the node indexing and the simplex orientations in a simplicial complex are arbitrary. The last property encodes the desirable feature that the output of the neural network depends on the entire simplicial complex and not on a subset of its dimensions. Based on these properties, we propose a simple convolutional architecture, rooted in tools from algebraic topology, for the problem of trajectory prediction, and show that it obeys all three of these properties when an odd, nonlinear activation function is used. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of this architecture in extrapolating trajectories on synthetic and real datasets, with particular emphasis on the gains in generalizability to unseen trajectories.

paragraphs: This paper develops neural networks for data represented on simplicial complexes, with trajectory prediction as the application. It begins by specifying three properties an architecture should satisfy. These properties address arbitrary representation choices and ensure that the network uses the broader structure of the complex when producing its output.

Permutation equivariance accounts for arbitrary node indexing, while orientation equivariance accounts for arbitrary simplex orientations. Simplicial awareness requires the output to depend on the entire complex rather than only a subset of its dimensions. Together, the criteria distinguish meaningful structural information from choices made when encoding that structure for computation.

Using tools from algebraic topology, the authors propose a simple convolutional architecture and show that it satisfies all three properties when it uses an odd nonlinear activation function. Experiments demonstrate effective trajectory extrapolation on synthetic and real datasets, particularly improved generalization to unseen trajectories. The contribution links explicit architectural principles to a concrete model and supports their usefulness through the reported prediction results.
summary.tldr: A simplicial convolutional architecture satisfies three structural principles under an odd nonlinear activation and improves generalization to unseen trajectories.

title: Principled Simplicial Neural Networks for Trajectory Prediction

abstract: We introduce learning and planning algorithms for average-reward MDPs, including 1) the first general proven-convergent off-policy model-free control algorithm without reference states, 2) the first proven-convergent off-policy model-free prediction algorithm, and 3) the first off-policy learning algorithm that converges to the actual value function rather than to the value function plus an offset. All of our algorithms are based on using the temporal-difference error rather than the conventional error when updating the estimate of the average reward. Our proof techniques are a slight generalization of those by Abounadi, Bertsekas, and Borkar (2001). In experiments with an Access-Control Queuing Task, we show some of the difficulties that can arise when using methods that rely on reference states and argue that our new algorithms are significantly easier to use.

All of our algorithms are based on using the temporal-difference error rather than the conventional error when updating the estimate of the average reward. Our proof techniques are a slight generalization of those by Abounadi, Bertsekas, and Borkar (2001). In experiments with an Access-Control Queuing Task, we show some of the difficulties that can arise when using methods that rely on reference states and argue that our new algorithms are significantly easier to use.

paragraphs: Average-reward Markov decision processes focus on the reward achieved over ongoing interaction. This paper introduces learning and planning algorithms for that setting, including off-policy methods, which learn about a policy using experience that can come from another policy. A central aim is to provide convergence guarantees without awkward dependence on designated reference states.

The shared algorithmic change is to update the average-reward estimate using temporal-difference error instead of the conventional error. The authors establish a general convergent off-policy model-free control algorithm without reference states and a convergent off-policy model-free prediction algorithm. They also introduce an off-policy algorithm that reaches the actual value function rather than a version shifted by an offset.

These are presented as first results of their respective kinds. Experiments on an access-control queuing task illustrate difficulties that reference-state methods can encounter, and the authors argue that their alternatives are significantly easier to use. The paper thus connects a change in the reward-estimation update to both convergence results and a reduction in practical setup difficulties.
summary.tldr: Temporal-difference updates enable new proven-convergent off-policy algorithms for average-reward learning, including control without reference states.

title: Learning and Planning in Average-Reward Markov Decision Processes

abstract: While probabilistic circuits have been extensively explored for tabular data, less attention has been paid to time series. Here, the goal is to estimate joint densities among the entire time series and, in turn, determining, for instance, conditional independence relations between them. To this end, we propose the first probabilistic circuits (PCs) approach for modeling the joint distribution of multivariate time series, called Whittle sum-product networks (WSPNs). WSPNs leverage the Whittle approximation, casting the likelihood in the frequency domain, and place a complex-valued sum-product network, the most prominent PC, over the frequencies. The conditional independence relations among the time series can then be determined efficiently in the spectral domain. Moreover, WSPNs can naturally be placed into the deep neural learning stack for time series, resulting in Whittle Networks, opening the likelihood toolbox for training deep neural models and inspecting their behaviour. Our experiments show that Whittle Networks can indeed capture complex dependencies between time series and provide a useful measure of uncertainty for neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies joint probability models for multivariate time series, with the aim of capturing relationships among entire series. Such models can also support questions about conditional independence: whether relationships remain after accounting for other information. The authors bring probabilistic circuits, previously explored extensively for tabular data, into this time-series setting.

Experiments show that the resulting networks can capture complex dependencies between series and provide a useful uncertainty measure, supporting both probabilistic analysis and neural-network applications.
summary.tldr: Whittle Networks model time-series likelihoods in the frequency domain to capture dependencies and provide useful neural-network uncertainty estimates.

title: Whittle Networks: A Deep Likelihood Model for Time Series

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is a recent training method that relies on worst-case weight perturbations which significantly improves generalization in various settings. We argue that the existing justifications for the success of SAM which are based on a PAC-Bayes generalization bound and the idea of convergence to flat minima are incomplete. Moreover, there are no explanations for the success of using m-sharpness in SAM which has been shown as essential for generalization. To better understand this aspect of SAM, we theoretically analyze its implicit bias for diagonal linear networks. We prove that SAM always chooses a solution that enjoys better generalization properties than standard gradient descent for a certain class of problems, and this effect is amplified by using m-sharpness. We further study the properties of the implicit bias on non-linear networks empirically, where we show that fine-tuning a standard model with SAM can lead to significant generalization improvements. Finally, we provide convergence results of SAM for non-convex objectives when used with stochastic gradients. We illustrate these results empirically for deep networks and discuss their relation to the generalization behavior of SAM. The code of our experiments is available at https://github.com/tml-epfl/understanding-sam.

title: Towards Understanding Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: We design an algorithm for finding counterfactuals with strong theoretical guarantees on its performance. For any monotone model $f : X^d \to \{0,1\}$ and instance $x^\star$, our algorithm makes \[{S}(f)^{O(\Delta_f(x^\star))}\cdot \log d\]{queries} to $f$ and returns an {\sl optimal} counterfactual for $x^\star$: a nearest instance $x’$ to $x^\star$ for which $f(x’)\ne f(x^\star)$. Here $S(f)$ is the sensitivity of $f$, a discrete analogue of the Lipschitz constant, and $\Delta_f(x^\star)$ is the distance from $x^\star$ to its nearest counterfactuals. The previous best known query complexity was $d^{\,O(\Delta_f(x^\star))}$, achievable by brute-force local search. We further prove a lower bound of $S(f)^{\Omega(\Delta_f(x^\star))} + \Omega(\log d)$ on the query complexity of any algorithm, thereby showing that the guarantees of our algorithm are essentially optimal.

paragraphs: A counterfactual identifies a change to an input that would reverse a model’s decision. This paper studies how to find the nearest such input while making few queries to the model. Its guarantee applies to monotone models with binary outputs, and it returns an optimal counterfactual rather than merely a nearby example with a different prediction.

The key improvement changes how the number of queries depends on the problem. Previous brute-force local search required the input dimension raised to a power proportional to the distance to the nearest counterfactual. The new algorithm instead places model sensitivity inside that exponential dependence, with only a logarithmic factor in the dimension. Sensitivity measures how responsive the model is to discrete input changes.

The authors also prove a lower bound on the queries any algorithm can require. Together, the upper and lower bounds establish essentially optimal guarantees. The result makes sensitivity central to counterfactual search complexity, while retaining an exponential dependence on counterfactual distance.
summary.tldr: For monotone binary models, a counterfactual search algorithm achieves essentially optimal query guarantees governed by sensitivity and counterfactual distance.

title: A query-optimal algorithm for finding counterfactuals

abstract: Prompt-Tuning is a new paradigm for finetuning pre-trained language models in a parameter efficient way. Here, we explore the use of HyperNetworks to generate hyper-prompts: we propose HyperPrompt, a novel architecture for prompt-based task-conditioning of self-attention in Transformers. The hyper-prompts are end-to-end learnable via generation by a HyperNetwork. HyperPrompt allows the network to learn task-specific feature maps where the hyper-prompts serve as task global memories for the queries to attend to, at the same time enabling flexible information sharing among tasks. We show that HyperPrompt is competitive against strong multi-task learning baselines with as few as 0.14% of additional task-conditioning parameters, achieving great parameter and computational efficiency. Through extensive empirical experiments, we demonstrate that HyperPrompt can achieve superior performances over strong T5 multi-task learning baselines and parameter-efficient adapter variants including Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++ on Natural Language Understanding benchmarks of GLUE and SuperGLUE across many model sizes.

paragraphs: A Transformer serving several tasks needs a way to adapt its behavior to each task while sharing useful information across them. HyperPrompt addresses this through learned prompts that condition self-attention. A separate HyperNetwork generates these hyper-prompts, and the entire system learns them end to end rather than relying on manually written instructions.

The generated prompts act as task-level memories that attention queries can consult. This allows the model to learn task-specific feature maps while retaining flexible information sharing between tasks. The design therefore places task conditioning within the attention mechanism, with a small additional parameter budget devoted to expressing differences among tasks.

The authors report competitive results against strong multitask baselines with as little as 0.14% additional task-conditioning parameters. Across many model sizes on GLUE and SuperGLUE, experiments show that HyperPrompt can outperform T5 multitask baselines and parameter-efficient alternatives including Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++. These results support its combination of parameter efficiency, computational efficiency, and effective task adaptation in the evaluated language-understanding settings.
summary.tldr: HyperPrompt generates task-specific attention prompts with a HyperNetwork, enabling efficient multitask adaptation and strong language-understanding results.

title: HyperPrompt: Prompt-based Task-Conditioning of Transformers

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) undergoes complicated multiplicative noise for the mean-square loss. We use this property of SGD noise to derive a stochastic differential equation (SDE) with simpler additive noise by performing a random time change. Using this formalism, we show that the log loss barrier $\Delta\log L=\log[L(\theta^s)/L(\theta^*)]$ between a local minimum $\theta^*$ and a saddle $\theta^s$ determines the escape rate of SGD from the local minimum, contrary to the previous results borrowing from physics that the linear loss barrier $\Delta L=L(\theta^s)-L(\theta^*)$ decides the escape rate. Our escape-rate formula strongly depends on the typical magnitude $h^*$ and the number $n$ of the outlier eigenvalues of the Hessian. This result explains an empirical fact that SGD prefers flat minima with low effective dimensions, giving an insight into implicit biases of SGD.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent introduces noise through its updates, and that noise influences how training leaves local minima. For mean-square loss, the noise has a multiplicative structure that complicates analysis. This paper uses a random change of time to obtain a stochastic differential equation with a simpler additive-noise description.

Within that formalism, the escape rate depends on the logarithm of the ratio between the loss at a saddle and the loss at a local minimum. This differs from earlier physics-inspired results based on the difference between those two loss values. The distinction makes the relative height of the barrier central to the escape-rate formula.

The formula also depends strongly on the typical magnitude and number of outlying eigenvalues of the Hessian, which characterizes local curvature. The authors use this dependence to explain the empirical tendency of SGD to favor flat minima with low effective dimension. The result offers an account of SGD’s implicit preferences through its noise and local loss geometry in the analyzed mean-square-loss setting.
summary.tldr: An analysis of SGD noise links escape from minima to logarithmic loss barriers and curvature, explaining preferences for flat, low-dimensional minima.

title: Power-Law Escape Rate of SGD

abstract: The ability to separate signal from noise, and reason with clean abstractions, is critical to intelligence. With this ability, humans can efficiently perform real world tasks without considering all possible nuisance factors. How can artificial agents do the same? What kind of information can agents safely discard as noises? In this work, we categorize information out in the wild into four types based on controllability and relation with reward, and formulate useful information as that which is both controllable and reward-relevant. This framework clarifies the kinds information removed by various prior work on representation learning in reinforcement learning (RL), and leads to our proposed approach of learning a Denoised MDP that explicitly factors out certain noise distractors. Extensive experiments on variants of DeepMind Control Suite and RoboDesk demonstrate superior performance of our denoised world model over using raw observations alone, and over prior works, across policy optimization control tasks as well as the non-control task of joint position regression. Project Page: https://ssnl.github.io/denoised_mdp/ Code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/denoised_mdp/

paragraphs: An agent observing an environment encounters information that matters for its task alongside distracting variation. This paper asks which information a learned world model should retain. It organizes environmental information along two dimensions: whether the agent can control it and whether it relates to reward, producing four categories.

Within this framework, useful information is defined as both controllable and relevant to reward. The authors use this distinction to clarify what different earlier representation-learning approaches remove. They then introduce Denoised MDPs, a way to learn world models that explicitly separate out certain distracting components, giving the agent a cleaner representation for reasoning and learning.

Experiments use variants of DeepMind Control Suite and RoboDesk. The denoised model performs better than raw observations and the compared prior approaches on policy optimization tasks and on joint position regression, which is not a control task. These results suggest that deliberately filtering observations can produce representations useful beyond the immediate task of choosing actions.
summary.tldr: Denoised MDPs learn world models that separate controllable, reward-relevant information from distractions, improving performance on the evaluated control and regression tasks.

title: Denoised MDPs: Learning World Models Better Than the World Itself

abstract: Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), which combines Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum, would be the most popular stochastic optimizer for accelerating the training of deep neural networks. However, it is empirically known that Adam often generalizes worse than Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). The purpose of this paper is to unveil the mystery of this behavior in the diffusion theoretical framework. Specifically, we disentangle the effects of Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum of the Adam dynamics on saddle-point escaping and flat minima selection. We prove that Adaptive Learning Rate can escape saddle points efficiently, but cannot select flat minima as SGD does. In contrast, Momentum provides a drift effect to help the training process pass through saddle points, and almost does not affect flat minima selection. This partly explains why SGD (with Momentum) generalizes better, while Adam generalizes worse but converges faster. Furthermore, motivated by the analysis, we design a novel adaptive optimization framework named Adaptive Inertia, which uses parameter-wise adaptive inertia to accelerate the training and provably favors flat minima as well as SGD. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed adaptive inertia method can generalize significantly better than SGD and conventional adaptive gradient methods.

paragraphs: Adam combines adaptive learning rates with momentum, but the two ingredients may influence training differently. This paper separates their effects within a diffusion-based theoretical framework. It focuses on escaping saddle points, where optimization can stall, and selecting flat minima, regions where nearby parameter changes have relatively little effect on the training objective.

The analysis shows that adaptive learning rates can escape saddle points efficiently but do not select flat minima in the way SGD does. Momentum instead supplies a drift that helps training pass through saddle points while having almost no effect on flat-minimum selection. The authors present this as a partial explanation for the observed contrast between Adam’s faster convergence and SGD’s often better generalization.

Motivated by this distinction, the paper proposes Adaptive Inertia, which adapts inertia separately for individual parameters. The framework accelerates training while provably favoring flat minima as SGD does. Extensive experiments report significantly better generalization than SGD and conventional adaptive gradient methods. These experimental findings complement the theoretical account of how different optimizer components affect training.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Inertia separates adaptation from learning-rate scaling to accelerate training while preserving SGD-like preference for flat minima.

title: Adaptive Inertia: Disentangling the Effects of Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum

abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian inference framework for distributed differentially private linear regression. We consider a distributed setting where multiple parties hold parts of the data and share certain summary statistics of their portions in privacy-preserving noise. We develop a novel generative statistical model for privately shared statistics, which exploits a useful distributional relation between the summary statistics of linear regression. We propose Bayesian estimation of the regression coefficients, mainly using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, while we also provide a fast version that performs approximate Bayesian estimation in one iteration. The proposed methods have computational advantages over their competitors. We provide numerical results on both real and simulated data, which demonstrate that the proposed algorithms provide well-rounded estimation and prediction.

We develop a novel generative statistical model for privately shared statistics, which exploits a useful distributional relation between the summary statistics of linear regression. We propose Bayesian estimation of the regression coefficients, mainly using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, while we also provide a fast version that performs approximate Bayesian estimation in one iteration. The proposed methods have computational advantages over their competitors. paragraphs: In distributed linear regression, different parties hold different portions of the data. This paper considers a privacy-preserving arrangement in which those parties share selected summary statistics after adding noise. The inference problem is therefore to estimate regression coefficients from privately released summaries, accounting for the statistical structure of what has been shared.

The authors build a generative statistical model for these noisy statistics. It uses a distributional relationship between the summary quantities involved in linear regression, allowing the estimation procedure to exploit their connections. They then develop Bayesian inference for the regression coefficients, primarily through Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. This makes the model for the shared statistics an explicit part of the inference framework.

The paper also offers a faster alternative that produces an approximate Bayesian estimate in one iteration. The proposed methods have computational advantages over competing approaches, and numerical evaluations on real and simulated data show well-rounded estimation and prediction. The contribution combines a model of privacy-preserving summaries with both sampling-based and fast approximate inference, addressing computation alongside the quality of regression results.
summary.tldr: A statistical model of privately shared summaries enables distributed Bayesian linear regression with MCMC and a fast approximate alternative.

title: Differentially Private Distributed Bayesian Linear Regression with MCMC

abstract: The reward hypothesis posits that, "all of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (reward)." We aim to fully settle this hypothesis. This will not conclude with a simple affirmation or refutation, but rather specify completely the implicit requirements on goals and purposes under which the hypothesis holds.
originalAbstract: The reward hypothesis posits that, "all of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (reward)." paragraphs: The reward hypothesis proposes that goals and purposes can be understood through maximising the expected cumulative value of a scalar reward signal. This formulation expresses an objective using a single numerical signal accumulated over time, with expectation accounting for the resulting cumulative value. The paper addresses the scope of this proposal.

The authors frame their intended resolution in terms of conditions on goals and purposes. Their aim is to specify completely the implicit requirements under which the reward hypothesis holds. The question therefore concerns which requirements make the reward-based description appropriate, rather than seeking an unconditional acceptance or rejection of the hypothesis.

This framing matters because a claim about all goals depends on what is admitted as a goal and what representing it through expected cumulative reward requires. Identifying those requirements would clarify the reach of the hypothesis and the commitments involved in adopting it. The abstract presents this conditional characterisation as the paper's objective, without stating the individual requirements. Its central message is that settling the hypothesis means making its conditions explicit.
summary.tldr: The paper aims to settle the reward hypothesis by specifying the requirements under which goals can be represented as expected cumulative reward maximisation.

title: Settling the Reward Hypothesis

abstract: When applying differential privacy to sensitive data, we can often improve performance using external information such as other sensitive data, public data, or human priors. We propose to use the learning-augmented algorithms (or algorithms with predictions) framework—previously applied largely to improve time complexity or competitive ratios—as a powerful way of designing and analyzing privacy-preserving methods that can take advantage of such external information to improve utility. This idea is instantiated on the important task of multiple quantile release, for which we derive error guarantees that scale with a natural measure of prediction quality while (almost) recovering state-of-the-art prediction-independent guarantees. Our analysis enjoys several advantages, including minimal assumptions about the data, a natural way of adding robustness, and the provision of useful surrogate losses for two novel ”meta” algorithms that learn predictions from other (potentially sensitive) data. We conclude with experiments on challenging tasks demonstrating that learning predictions across one or more instances can lead to large error reductions while preserving privacy.

paragraphs: Differentially private analysis can benefit from outside information, including public data, other sensitive datasets, or human expectations. This paper uses the learning-augmented algorithms framework to incorporate that information into private computation. It focuses on releasing multiple quantiles, which describe positions within a data distribution while preserving privacy.

The algorithms use predictions, and their error guarantees depend on a measure of prediction quality. This makes the potential benefit of useful outside information explicit in the analysis. At the same time, the guarantees almost recover leading bounds that do not depend on predictions, providing protection against relying entirely on accurate external guidance.

The analysis makes minimal assumptions about the data, offers a way to introduce robustness, and supplies surrogate losses for two methods that learn predictions from other potentially sensitive data. Experiments show that learning across one or more instances can substantially reduce error while preserving privacy. The contribution combines prediction-sensitive improvements with nearly retained prediction-independent guarantees in a concrete private estimation task.
summary.tldr: Prediction-guided private quantile algorithms improve accuracy with useful external information while nearly retaining prediction-independent error guarantees.

title: Learning-augmented private algorithms for multiple quantile release

abstract: Learning shared structures across changing environments enables an agent to efficiently retain obtained knowledge and transfer it between environments. A skill is a promising concept to represent shared structures. Several recent works proposed unsupervised skill discovery algorithms that can discover useful skills without a reward function. However, they focused on discovering skills in stationary environments or assumed that a skill being trained is fixed within an episode, which is insufficient to learn and represent shared structures. In this paper, we introduce a new unsupervised skill discovery algorithm that discovers a set of skills that can represent shared structures across changing environments. Our algorithm trains incremental skills and encourages a new skill to expand state coverage obtained with compositions of previously learned skills. We also introduce a skill evaluation process to prevent our skills from containing redundant skills, a common issue in previous work. Our experimental results show that our algorithm acquires skills that represent shared structures across changing maze navigation and locomotion environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our skills are more useful than baselines on downstream tasks.

paragraphs: An agent operating across changing environments benefits from behaviors that preserve useful shared structure. Unsupervised skill discovery seeks such behaviors without a reward function, but earlier approaches often focused on stationary environments or kept the trained skill fixed within each episode. This paper develops a method intended to represent structure shared across environmental changes.

The algorithm learns skills incrementally. Each new skill is encouraged to extend the states reachable through compositions of skills already learned. This gives skill discovery a cumulative objective: new behavior should expand what the existing collection can accomplish. A separate evaluation process aims to prevent redundant skills from accumulating in that collection.

Experiments in changing maze-navigation and locomotion environments show that the resulting skills represent shared structure. The authors also demonstrate greater usefulness than baseline skills on downstream tasks. The contribution is a way to build and assess reusable behavior over time, with state-coverage expansion and redundancy control providing complementary guidance for what should be added.
summary.tldr: The method incrementally discovers reusable skills by expanding the coverage of existing skill compositions and screening for redundancy.

title: Unsupervised Skill Discovery for Learning Shared Structures across Changing Environments

abstract: Retrosynthetic planning aims to devise a complete multi-step synthetic route from starting materials to a target molecule. Current strategies use a decoupled approach of single-step retrosynthesis models and search algorithms, taking only the product as the input to predict the reactants for each planning step and ignoring valuable context information along the synthetic route. In this work, we propose a novel framework that utilizes context information for improved retrosynthetic planning. We view synthetic routes as reaction graphs and propose to incorporate context through three principled steps: encode molecules into embeddings, aggregate information over routes, and readout to predict reactants. Our approach is the first attempt to utilize in-context learning for retrosynthesis prediction in retrosynthetic planning. The entire framework can be efficiently optimized in an end-to-end fashion and produce more practical and accurate predictions. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that by fusing in the context information over routes, our model significantly improves the performance of retrosynthetic planning over baselines that are not context-aware, especially for long synthetic routes. Code is available at https://github.com/SongtaoLiu0823/FusionRetro.

paragraphs: Retrosynthetic planning seeks a complete sequence of reactions connecting starting materials to a desired molecule. Existing approaches commonly combine a single-step reactant predictor with a separate search algorithm. When each prediction uses only the current product, it leaves out information available elsewhere along the developing synthetic route.

FusionRetro represents routes as reaction graphs so that this broader context can inform reactant predictions. Its pipeline encodes molecules as embeddings, aggregates information across routes, and uses the resulting representations to predict reactants. The framework can be optimized end to end, connecting molecule representation learning directly to the context-aware prediction task.

The authors describe this as an initial use of in-context learning for retrosynthesis prediction within planning. Experiments show significant planning improvements over baselines that do not use route context, particularly for long synthetic routes. The stated findings suggest that considering how reactions fit into a larger route can produce more practical and accurate predictions than evaluating each product in isolation.
summary.tldr: FusionRetro improves retrosynthetic planning by combining molecular representations with context from the surrounding reaction route.

title: FusionRetro: Molecule Representation Fusion via In-Context Learning for Retrosynthetic Planning

abstract: We introduce the framework of performative reinforcement learning where the policy chosen by the learner affects the underlying reward and transition dynamics of the environment. Following the recent literature on performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020), we introduce the concept of performatively stable policy. We then consider a regularized version of the reinforcement learning problem and show that repeatedly optimizing this objective converges to a performatively stable policy under reasonable assumptions on the transition dynamics. Our proof utilizes the dual perspective of the reinforcement learning problem and may be of independent interest in analyzing the convergence of other algorithms with decision-dependent environments. We then extend our results for the setting where the learner just performs gradient ascent steps instead of fully optimizing the objective, and for the setting where the learner has access to a finite number of trajectories from the changed environment. For both the settings, we leverage the dual formulation of performative reinforcement learning, and establish convergence to a stable solution. Finally, through extensive experiments on a grid-world environment, we demonstrate the dependence of convergence on various parameters e.g. regularization, smoothness, and the number of samples.

Following the recent literature on performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020), we introduce the concept of performatively stable policy. We then consider a regularized version of the reinforcement learning problem and show that repeatedly optimizing this objective converges to a performatively stable policy under reasonable assumptions on the transition dynamics. Our proof utilizes the dual perspective of the reinforcement learning problem and may be of independent interest in analyzing the convergence of other algorithms with decision-dependent environments. We then extend our results for the setting where the learner just performs gradient ascent steps instead of fully optimizing the objective, and for the setting where the learner has access to a finite number of trajectories from the changed environment. For both the settings, we leverage the dual formulation of performative reinforcement learning, and establish convergence to a stable solution. Finally, through extensive experiments on a grid-world environment, we demonstrate the dependence of convergence on various parameters e.g. regularization, smoothness, and the number of samples.

paragraphs: In many reinforcement learning formulations, the environment is treated as fixed while the learner improves its policy. This paper studies a different situation: the deployed policy changes the environment’s rewards and transition dynamics. The resulting feedback between decisions and the world is formalized as performative reinforcement learning.

The authors introduce a notion of a performatively stable policy and analyze repeated optimization of a regularized objective. Under assumptions on the transition dynamics, this process converges to a stable policy. The proof uses a dual formulation of reinforcement learning, providing a way to reason about optimization when the environment itself depends on the learner’s decisions.

The analysis also covers taking gradient-ascent steps instead of fully optimizing each objective, and learning from a finite number of trajectories collected in the changed environment. Convergence results are established for both extensions. Grid-world experiments examine how regularization, smoothness, and sample count affect convergence. The contribution gives conditional stability guarantees for this feedback-driven setting, including versions closer to incremental, data-limited learning.
summary.tldr: Performative reinforcement learning models policy-induced environmental change and establishes conditional convergence to stable policies.

title: Performative Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Data used for analytics and machine learning often take the form of tables with categorical entries. We introduce a family of lossless compression algorithms for such data that proceed in four steps: (i) Estimate latent variables associated to rows and columns; (ii) Partition the table in blocks according to the row/column latents; (iii) Apply a sequential (e.g. Lempel-Ziv) coder to each of the blocks; (iv) Append a compressed encoding of the latents. We evaluate this approach on several benchmark datasets, and study optimal compression in a probabilistic model for tabular data, whereby latent values are independent and table entries are conditionally independent given the latent values. We prove that the model has a well defined entropy rate and satisfies an asymptotic equipartition property. We also prove that classical compression schemes such as Lempel-Ziv and finite-state encoders do not achieve this rate. On the other hand, the latent estimation strategy outlined above achieves the optimal rate.

paragraphs: Categorical tables contain structure across both rows and columns, and that structure can help compress them without losing information. The proposed algorithms first estimate hidden variables associated with rows and columns. They use those estimates to divide the table into blocks, then apply a sequential compressor, such as Lempel-Ziv, separately to each block.

The compressed output also includes an encoding of the estimated hidden variables. This makes their storage part of the overall compression scheme rather than treating the learned organization as free information. The authors evaluate the approach on benchmark datasets and analyze a probabilistic model in which the latent values are independent and entries become independent once those values are given.

For that model, they establish a well-defined entropy rate and an asymptotic equipartition property, providing a theoretical basis for optimal compression. They show that classical Lempel-Ziv and finite-state schemes do not reach the rate, while the latent-estimation strategy does. The optimality claim belongs to this model and shows why reorganizing a table can unlock compressible structure that a conventional sequential encoding misses.
summary.tldr: Estimating hidden row and column structure enables lossless table compression that reaches the optimal rate under the paper’s probabilistic model.

title: Compressing Tabular Data via Latent Variable Estimation

abstract: We propose a delay-agnostic asynchronous coordinate update algorithm (DEGAS) for computing operator fixed points, with applications to asynchronous optimization. DEGAS includes novel asynchronous variants of ADMM and block-coordinate descent as special cases. We prove that DEGAS converges with both bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions. We also validate by theory and experiments that DEGAS adapts well to the actual delays. The effectiveness of DEGAS is demonstrated by numerical experiments on classification problems.

DEGAS includes novel asynchronous variants of ADMM and block-coordinate descent as special cases. We prove that DEGAS converges with both bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions. We also validate by theory and experiments that DEGAS adapts well to the actual delays. The effectiveness of DEGAS is demonstrated by numerical experiments on classification problems.

paragraphs: Asynchronous coordinate updates allow different parts of a computation to advance without all updates occurring together. Delays are therefore part of the problem the algorithm must handle. This paper introduces DEGAS, a delay-agnostic method for computing operator fixed points: solutions that remain unchanged when the relevant operator is applied.

The fixed-point formulation provides a common framework for asynchronous optimization. In particular, the proposed method includes new asynchronous versions of ADMM and block-coordinate descent as special cases. This matters because the contribution extends beyond a single optimization procedure, connecting several update schemes through the same algorithmic construction.

The authors prove convergence for both bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions. They also provide theoretical and experimental evidence that DEGAS adapts to the delays actually encountered. Numerical classification experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The central result is therefore a combination of convergence guarantees that do not require delay-dependent parameter conditions and evidence that the algorithm responds well to actual asynchronous execution.
summary.tldr: DEGAS provides asynchronous fixed-point updates with convergence guarantees for bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions.

title: Delay-agnostic Asynchronous Coordinate Update Algorithm

abstract: Heterogeneous graphs are ubiquitous to model complex data. There are urgent needs on powerful heterogeneous graph neural networks to effectively support important applications. We identify a potential semantic mixing issue in existing message passing processes, where the representations of the neighbors of a node v are forced to be transformed to the feature space of v for aggregation, though the neighbors are in different types. That is, the semantics in different node types are entangled together into node v’s representation. To address the issue, we propose SlotGAT with separate message passing processes in slots, one for each node type, to maintain the representations in their own node-type feature spaces. Moreover, in a slot-based message passing layer, we design an attention mechanism for effective slot-wise message aggregation. Further, we develop a slot attention technique after the last layer of SlotGAT, to learn the importance of different slots in downstream tasks. Our analysis indicates that the slots in SlotGAT can preserve different semantics in various feature spaces. The superiority of SlotGAT is evaluated against 13 baselines on 6 datasets for node classification and link prediction. Our code is at https://github.com/scottjiao/SlotGAT_ICML23/.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous graphs contain different kinds of nodes, whose features can carry different meanings. This paper identifies a potential problem in ordinary message aggregation: transforming every neighbor into the receiving node’s feature space can entangle those meanings. SlotGAT addresses this issue by maintaining separate slots associated with different node types.

Messages pass through these slots so that representations remain in their own type-specific feature spaces. Within each message-passing layer, an attention mechanism aggregates information slot by slot. After the final layer, another attention mechanism learns how important the different slots are for the downstream task. This separates preserving distinct representations from deciding how much each should contribute.

The authors’ analysis indicates that the slots can preserve different semantics across feature spaces. They evaluate SlotGAT against 13 baselines on six datasets for node classification and link prediction, reporting superior performance. The findings support a design in which information from multiple node types remains distinguishable during propagation and is weighted according to the prediction task.
summary.tldr: SlotGAT preserves node-type semantics in separate message-passing slots and learns how to combine them for graph prediction tasks.

title: SlotGAT: Slot-based Message Passing for Heterogeneous Graphs

abstract: We study deep neural networks for the multi-label classification (MLab) task through the lens of neural collapse (NC). Previous works have been restricted to the multi-class classification setting and discovered a prevalent NC phenomenon comprising of the following properties for the last-layer features: (i) the variability of features within every class collapses to zero, (ii) the set of feature means form an equi-angular tight frame (ETF), and (iii) the last layer classifiers collapse to the feature mean upon some scaling. We generalize the study to multi-label learning, and prove for the first time that a generalized NC phenomenon holds with the "pick-all-label” formulation, which we term as MLab NC. While the ETF geometry remains consistent for features with a single label, multi-label scenarios introduce a unique combinatorial aspect we term the "tag-wise average" property, where the means of features with multiple labels are the scaled averages of means for single-label instances. Theoretically, under proper assumptions on the features, we establish that the only global optimizer of the pick-all-label cross-entropy loss satisfy the multi-label NC. In practice, we demonstrate that our findings can lead to better test performance with more efficient training techniques for MLab learning.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a geometric pattern in a network's final features and classifiers. Earlier studies focused on classification where each example has one label: within-class features converge together, class means adopt a regular arrangement, and classifier directions align with those means. This paper asks how that picture extends when examples can have multiple labels.

For the pick-all-label formulation, the authors establish a generalized pattern called multi-label neural collapse. Single-label feature means retain the equi-angular tight-frame geometry. Multi-label feature means follow an additional tag-wise average property: they are scaled averages of the means associated with their individual labels. This gives label combinations a structured relationship to the single-label representations.

The theoretical result depends on appropriate assumptions about the features and characterizes the global optimizer of the pick-all-label cross-entropy loss. It should therefore be read within that setting. In practice, the authors show that these findings can guide more efficient training techniques with better test performance, connecting the geometric analysis to improvements in multi-label learning.
summary.tldr: Under stated feature assumptions, pick-all-label learning exhibits a neural-collapse geometry in which multi-label means are scaled averages of single-label means.

title: Neural Collapse in Multi-label Learning with Pick-all-label Loss

abstract: To mitigate the computational complexity in the self-attention mechanism on long sequences, linear attention utilizes computation tricks to achieve linear complexity, while state space models (SSMs) popularize a favourable practice of using non-data-dependent memory pattern, i.e., emphasize the near and neglect the distant, to processing sequences. Recent studies have shown the priorities by combining them as one. However, the efficiency of linear attention remains only at the theoretical level in a causal setting, and SSMs require various designed constraints to operate effectively on specific data. Therefore, in order to unveil the true power of the hybrid design, the following two issues need to be addressed: (1) hardware-efficient implementation for linear attention and (2) stabilization of SSMs. To achieve this, we leverage the thought of tiling and hierarchy to propose CHELA (short-long Convolutions with Hardware-Efficient Linear Attention), which replaces SSMs with short-long convolutions and implements linear attention in a divide-and-conquer manner. This approach enjoys global abstraction and data-dependent selection from stable SSM and linear attention while maintaining real linear complexity. Our comprehensive experiments on the Long Range Arena benchmark and language modeling tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Long-sequence models need to manage both information flow and computational cost. Linear attention offers linear theoretical complexity, while state space models provide memory patterns that favor nearby information. Combining them is promising, but the paper identifies two obstacles: realizing linear attention's efficiency on hardware in causal settings and stabilizing state space components.

CHELA addresses these obstacles through short-long convolutions and a divide-and-conquer implementation of linear attention. The convolutions replace the state space component, while tiling and hierarchy organize the attention computation. This connects the model's architectural design with the way its operations are actually executed, making implementation efficiency part of the method.

The resulting combination aims to retain global abstraction and data-dependent selection while maintaining real linear complexity. Short-long convolutions supply the structured sequence-processing component, and linear attention contributes selection based on the data. Experiments on the Long Range Arena benchmark and language-modeling tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a hybrid sequence architecture whose claimed efficiency extends beyond a theoretical operation count to its hardware-oriented implementation.
summary.tldr: CHELA combines short-long convolutions with hardware-oriented linear attention for efficient long-sequence processing.

title: Short-Long Convolutions Help Hardware-Efficient Linear Attention to Focus on Long Sequences

abstract: Second-order Recurrent Neural Networks (2RNNs) extend RNNs by leveraging second-order interactions for sequence modelling. These models are provably more expressive than their first-order counterparts and have connections to well-studied models from formal language theory. However, their large parameter tensor makes computations intractable. To circumvent this issue, one approach known as MIRNN consists in limiting the type of interactions used by the model. Another is to leverage tensor decomposition to diminish the parameter count. In this work, we study the model resulting from parameterizing 2RNNs using the CP decomposition, which we call CPRNN. Intuitively, the rank of the decomposition should reduce expressivity. We analyze how rank and hidden size affect model capacity and show the relationships between RNNs, 2RNNs, MIRNNs, and CPRNNs based on these parameters. We support these results empirically with experiments on the Penn Treebank dataset which demonstrate that, with a fixed parameter budget, CPRNNs outperforms RNNs, 2RNNs, and MIRNNs with the right choice of rank and hidden size.

paragraphs: Second-order recurrent neural networks model sequences using richer interactions than ordinary recurrent networks. These interactions give them greater expressive power, but their parameters form a large tensor that makes computation difficult. The paper studies whether a compact tensor representation can retain useful modeling capacity while making better use of a limited parameter budget.

The resulting model, CPRNN, represents this tensor through CP decomposition. Two design choices become central: the decomposition rank and the size of the hidden state. The authors analyze how these choices affect capacity and establish relationships among ordinary RNNs, second-order RNNs, interaction-restricted MIRNNs, and CPRNNs. This connects compression choices to what the models can represent.

Experiments on Penn Treebank support the analysis: with a fixed parameter budget and an appropriate combination of rank and hidden size, CPRNNs outperform the other three model families. The qualification matters because compression alone is not the reported explanation for success. The contribution is a theoretical and empirical account of how to allocate parameters within a richer recurrent architecture.
summary.tldr: CPRNN uses tensor decomposition to make second-order recurrent networks compact, with strong results when rank and hidden size are chosen appropriately.

title: A Tensor Decomposition Perspective on Second-order RNNs

abstract: In this paper, we present two key theorems that should have significant implications for machine learning practitioners working with binary classification models. The first theorem provides a formula to calculate the maximum and minimum Precision-Recall AUC ($AUC_{PR}$) for a fixed Receiver Operating Characteristic AUC ($AUC_{ROC}$), demonstrating the variability of $AUC_{PR}$ even with a high $AUC_{ROC}$. This is particularly relevant for imbalanced datasets, where a good $AUC_{ROC}$ does not necessarily imply a high $AUC_{PR}$. The second theorem inversely establishes the bounds of $AUC_{ROC}$ given a fixed $AUC_{PR}$. Our findings highlight that in certain situations, especially for imbalanced datasets, it is more informative to prioritize $AUC_{PR}$ over $AUC_{ROC}$. Additionally, we introduce a method to determine when a higher $AUC_{ROC}$ in one model implies a higher $AUC_{PR}$ in another and vice versa, streamlining the model evaluation process.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often assessed using the areas under ROC and precision-recall curves. These summaries capture different aspects of performance, so a strong value for one does not automatically establish a strong value for the other. This paper gives theoretical bounds that make the relationship between the two measures explicit.

The first theorem determines the largest and smallest precision-recall AUC compatible with a fixed ROC AUC. It shows how much precision-recall performance can vary even when ROC performance looks good, a concern especially relevant to imbalanced datasets. The second theorem works in the opposite direction, bounding ROC AUC when precision-recall AUC is fixed.

The authors also introduce a method for determining when an ordering of models under one measure implies an ordering under the other. This can clarify when comparing both metrics adds information and when a relationship can already be established. Their conclusions support prioritizing precision-recall AUC in certain settings, particularly some imbalanced problems, rather than treating either metric as universally preferable.
summary.tldr: The paper derives bounds connecting ROC and precision-recall AUC, explaining when strong performance or model rankings under one metric transfer to the other.

title: Interplay of ROC and Precision-Recall AUCs: Theoretical Limits and Practical Implications in Binary Classification

abstract: This paper explores challenges in training Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), emphasizing the role of the loss landscape in the training process. We examine difficulties in minimizing the PINN loss function, particularly due to ill-conditioning caused by differential operators in the residual term. We compare gradient-based optimizers Adam, L-BFGS, and their combination Adam+L-BFGS, showing the superiority of Adam+L-BFGS, and introduce a novel second-order optimizer, NysNewton-CG (NNCG), which significantly improves PINN performance. Theoretically, our work elucidates the connection between ill-conditioned differential operators and ill-conditioning in the PINN loss and shows the benefits of combining first- and second-order optimization methods. Our work presents valuable insights and more powerful optimization strategies for training PINNs, which could improve the utility of PINNs for solving difficult partial differential equations.
