The authors report an effective balance between global task adaptation and generalization across these conditions. The framework matters because it tackles two distinct sources of difficulty together: disagreement among clients and excessive adaptation within each client.
summary.tldr: FedDTL combines separated encoder training with supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning to balance federated task adaptation and generalization.

title: Decoupled Training with Local Reinforcement Fine-Tuning in Federated Learning

abstract: Training-data attribution for vision generative models aims to identify which training data influenced a given output. While most methods score individual examples, practitioners often need group-level answers (e.g., artistic styles or object classes). Group-wise attribution is counterfactual: how would a model’s behavior on a generated sample change if a group were absent from training? A natural realization of this counterfactual is Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) retraining, which retrains the model with each group removed; however, it becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of groups grows. We propose GUDA (Group Unlearning-based Data Attribution) for diffusion models, which approximates each counterfactual model by applying machine unlearning to a shared full-data model instead of training from scratch. GUDA quantifies group influence using differences in a likelihood-based scoring rule (ELBO) between the full model and each unlearned counterfactual. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and artistic style attribution with Stable Diffusion show that GUDA identifies primary contributing groups more reliably than semantic similarity, gradient-based attribution, and instance-level unlearning approaches, while achieving $\sim$100$\times$ speedup on CIFAR-10 over LOGO retraining. The code is available at https://github.com/sony/guda.

paragraphs: GUDA asks which groups of training examples influenced a diffusion model's generated image. Groups might represent artistic styles or object classes. The question is counterfactual: how would the model's behavior on that image change if a particular group had been absent from training? Answering it directly by repeated retraining becomes expensive as group counts grow.

The method starts from one model trained on all the data and applies machine unlearning separately for each group. These unlearned models approximate the models that would result from leaving groups out. GUDA measures influence through changes in an ELBO-based likelihood score between the full model and each approximate counterfactual.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and artistic-style attribution with Stable Diffusion find more reliable identification of primary contributing groups than semantic similarity, gradient-based attribution, and instance-level unlearning. On CIFAR-10, it achieves roughly a hundredfold speedup over leave-one-group-out retraining. The contribution is a practical approximation to group-removal attribution that directly examines model behavior under unlearning.
summary.tldr: GUDA uses group unlearning to approximate counterfactual training-data attribution for diffusion models much faster than repeated retraining.

title: GUDA: Counterfactual Group-wise Training Data Attribution for Diffusion Models via Unlearning

abstract: Credit assignment is a core challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), especially in large-scale systems with structured, local interactions. Graph-based Markov decision processes (GMDPs) capture such settings via an influence graph, but standard critics are poorly aligned with this structure: global value functions provide weak per-agent learning signals, while existing local constructions can be difficult to estimate and ill-behaved in infinite-horizon settings. We introduce the Diffusion Value Function (DVF), a factored value function for GMDPs that assigns to each agent a value component by diffusing rewards over the influence graph with temporal discounting and spatial attenuation. We show that DVF is well-defined, admits a Bellman fixed point, and decomposes the global discounted value via an averaging property. DVF can be used as a drop-in critic in standard RL algorithms and estimated scalably with graph neural networks. Building on DVF, we propose Diffusion A2C (DA2C) and a sparse message-passing actor, Learned DropEdge GNN (LD-GNN), for learning decentralised algorithms under communication costs. Across the firefighting benchmark and three distributed computation tasks (vector graph colouring and two transmit power optimisation problems), DA2C consistently outperforms local and global critic baselines, improving average reward by up to 11%.

Existing local value estimates can also be difficult to compute or behave poorly over an infinite time horizon. This paper addresses that credit-assignment problem in systems whose interactions are represented by an influence graph.

Its Diffusion Value Function assigns each agent a value component by spreading rewards through the graph. Temporal discounting reduces the weight of later rewards, while spatial attenuation reduces influence across the graph. The authors show that these components are well-defined, satisfy a Bellman fixed-point relationship, and recover the global discounted value through averaging.

summary.tldr: Diffusing rewards across an interaction graph provides mathematically grounded per-agent value estimates and improves learning in the evaluated multi-agent tasks.

title: Factored Value Functions for Graph-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Foundation models are increasingly central to high-stakes AI systems, and governance frameworks now depend on evaluations to assess their risks and capabilities. Although general capability evaluations are widespread, social impact assessments covering bias, fairness, privacy, environmental costs, and labor remain uneven. To characterize this landscape, we conduct the first comprehensive analysis of social impact evaluation reporting, examining 186 first-party release reports and 248 third-party evaluation sources, supplemented by developer interviews. We find a stark division of labor: first-party reporting is sparse, often superficial, and declining in areas like environmental impact and bias, while third-party evaluators provide broader, more rigorous coverage of bias, harmful content, and performance disparities. However, only developers can authoritatively report on data provenance, content moderation labor, costs, and infrastructure, yet interviews reveal these disclosures are deprioritized unless tied to product adoption or compliance. Current practices leave major gaps in assessing societal impacts, underscoring the need for policies that mandate developer transparency, strengthen independent evaluation ecosystems, and create shared infrastructure for aggregating third-party evaluations.
originalAbstract: Foundation models are increasingly central to high-stakes AI systems, and governance frameworks now depend on evaluations to assess their risks and capabilities. Although general capability evaluations are widespread, social impact assessments covering bias, fairness, privacy, environmental costs, and labor remain uneven. To characterize this landscape, we conduct the first comprehensive analysis of social impact evaluation reporting, examining 186 first-party release reports and 248 third-party evaluation sources, supplemented by developer interviews. We find a stark division of labor: first-party reporting is sparse, often superficial, and declining in areas like environmental impact and bias, while third-party evaluators provide broader, more rigorous coverage of bias, harmful content, and performance disparities. However, only developers can authoritatively report on data provenance, content moderation labor, costs, and infrastructure, yet interviews reveal these disclosures are deprioritized unless tied to product adoption or compliance. Current practices leave major gaps in assessing societal impacts, underscoring the need for policies that mandate developer transparency, strengthen independent evaluation ecosystems, and create shared infrastructure for aggregating third-party evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper examines who reports on the social effects of foundation models and which issues receive attention. The authors analyze 186 developer release reports and 248 third-party evaluation sources, supplemented by developer interviews. Their scope includes bias, fairness, privacy, environmental costs, and labor, extending beyond general capability testing.

The analysis finds an uneven division of work. Developer reporting is often sparse or superficial, with declining attention to areas such as environmental impact and bias. Independent evaluators provide broader and more rigorous coverage of bias, harmful content, and performance disparities. However, developers alone can authoritatively disclose important details about data provenance, moderation labor, costs, and infrastructure.

Interviews suggest that these disclosures receive lower priority unless connected to product adoption or compliance. Independent testing therefore leaves gaps where the necessary information remains with developers. The authors argue for mandatory developer transparency, stronger independent evaluation ecosystems, and shared infrastructure for collecting external assessments. Their findings connect gaps in evaluation coverage to differences in access and reporting incentives.
summary.tldr: Independent evaluators cover many AI social impacts more thoroughly, but major gaps persist in information only developers can disclose.

title: Who Evaluates AI’s Social Impacts? Mapping Coverage and Gaps in First and Third Party Evaluations

abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation, yet their reliance on Transformer backbones limits inference efficiency due to quadratic attention or KV-cache overhead. We introduce DiffuMamba, a masked diffusion language model built on a bidirectional Mamba backbone that combines the diffusion objective with linear-time sequence modeling, and DiffuMamba-H, a hybrid variant with interleaved attention. Across scales up to 1.3B parameters, our models match Transformer-based diffusion in downstream performance while achieving up to 8.2$\times$ and 4.3$\times$ higher inference throughput, respectively, on long sequences. We further present a systematic analysis of inference efficiency across modern DLM variants, combining asymptotic complexity with empirical measurements. Notably, cache-efficient block diffusion with Mamba mixers emerges as the only strategy that scales linearly with sequence length and achieves the strongest performance across all baselines, suggesting a promising direction for future diffusion-based generation systems.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models offer an alternative to autoregressive text generation, but their backbone can make inference expensive. The paper identifies quadratic attention costs and key-value cache overhead as obstacles in Transformer-based designs. DiffuMamba addresses this by combining a masked diffusion objective with a bidirectional Mamba backbone that models sequences in linear time.

The authors also introduce DiffuMamba-H, which interleaves attention with the Mamba components. Across model sizes up to 1.3 billion parameters, both variants match the downstream performance of Transformer-based diffusion models. On long sequences, the reported peak inference-throughput improvements are 8.2 times for DiffuMamba and 4.3 times for the hybrid variant.

Beyond these models, the paper compares modern diffusion language-model strategies using both complexity analysis and measured efficiency. Within that comparison, cache-efficient block diffusion using Mamba mixers is the only strategy that scales linearly with sequence length and delivers the strongest performance across the baselines. This points to the combination of backbone and generation strategy as an important direction for efficient diffusion-based text generation.
summary.tldr: DiffuMamba replaces Transformer-heavy diffusion backbones with Mamba to increase long-sequence throughput while matching reported downstream performance.

title: DiffuMamba: High-Throughput Diffusion LMs with Mamba Backbone

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) create new opportunities for automating optimization modeling, but they also make post-training more delicate. In this task, strong performance often requires the model to formulate the problem, write solver code, run it, inspect the output, and revise when needed. We show that directly fine-tuning LRMs on already written-out Operations Research (OR) solutions can improve easier cases while hurting harder ones, suggesting that this training signal can interfere with the model’s own way of solving the task. We therefore propose CALM (Corrective Adaptation with Lightweight Modification), which lets the base LRM attempt the problem first, then inserts a short hint at the first detected mistake and lets the model continue from there. These hints modify fewer than 2.6% of generated tokens. The corrected solutions are used for supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning, producing STORM, a 4B optimization-modeling specialist that reaches 68.9% macro-average accuracy across five benchmarks and matches 671B DeepSeek-R1-0528. Under a matched hard-benchmark control, CALM also yields stronger final RL performance than direct distillation baselines that train on complete teacher-generated solutions from much stronger models. Overall, for this task, local repair of the base model’s own solution is more effective than full teacher-solution replacement. Code and models are available at https://github.com/tangzhy/STORM.

paragraphs: Optimization modeling requires a model to turn a problem into a mathematical formulation, write and run solver code, inspect the result, and revise its solution. The authors find that training reasoning models on complete, prewritten solutions can help easier problems while damaging performance on harder ones. They suggest this supervision can interfere with the model’s existing problem-solving process.

CALM instead lets the base model begin its own solution. At the first detected error, it adds a brief corrective hint and allows generation to continue. These interventions change fewer than 2.6% of generated tokens. The repaired solutions then support supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.

The resulting 4B model, STORM, achieves 68.9% macro-average accuracy across five benchmarks, matching 671B DeepSeek-R1-0528. A matched control on hard benchmarks also favors CALM over learning from complete solutions supplied by stronger teachers. For this task, the results support local correction as a more effective training signal than replacing the model’s entire solution.
summary.tldr: CALM trains optimization models by briefly correcting their own solutions, producing a 4B specialist that matches a much larger model on five benchmarks.

title: CALM Before the STORM: Unlocking Native Reasoning for Optimization Modeling

abstract: Benchmarks play a central role in reinforcement learning (RL) research, yet their computational constraints often shape what is studied. Despite the motivation of lifelong learning, most continual RL papers consider only 3–10 sequential tasks, as CPU-bound environments make longer sequences impractical. Meanwhile, continual learning in cooperative multi-agent settings remains largely unexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce MEAL (Multi-agent Environments for Adaptive Learning), the first benchmark for continual multi-agent RL. By leveraging JAX and GPU acceleration, MEAL enables training on sequences of 100 tasks on a single GPU in a few hours. We find that long task sequences reveal failure modes that do not appear at smaller scales.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning studies agents that keep learning as tasks change, but the length of benchmark sequences limits what researchers can observe. The paper notes that most studies use only three to ten sequential tasks because CPU-bound environments make longer runs impractical. Learning continually in cooperative multi-agent settings has also received relatively little attention.

MEAL provides a benchmark for this combination of ongoing adaptation and cooperation among agents. Its implementation uses JAX and GPU acceleration to make much longer task sequences practical. The authors report that training across 100 tasks can run on a single GPU in a few hours, substantially expanding the sequence lengths available for evaluation.

The study finds that long sequences expose failure modes that do not appear at smaller scales. That result makes benchmark efficiency scientifically consequential: changing the feasible duration of an experiment changes which weaknesses can be detected. MEAL supplies infrastructure for examining cooperative continual learning over longer sequences and testing whether apparent success persists as task changes accumulate.
summary.tldr: MEAL makes 100-task continual multi-agent reinforcement-learning evaluations practical and reveals failures hidden by shorter task sequences.

title: MEAL: A Benchmark for Continual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) imposes fundamental trade-offs between privacy and statistical fidelity in synthetic data generation. While access to public data has been shown to improve these trade-offs empirically, existing approaches use public data only indirectly, through pre-processing (e.g., using pre-trained generative models) or post-processing steps (e.g., matching target statistics estimated from public datasets), while relying on domain-agnostic DP mechanisms. In this work, we lay the theoretical framework to study the principled incorporation of public data into DP mechanisms themselves. We consider normalized histograms as distribution estimators and characterize the asymptotically optimal domain-aware privacy mechanism within a specific class of DP mechanisms. We introduce PubMix, a public-data-aware DP mechanism that can be used in histogram-based data synthesis pipelines. Our experiments demonstrate that PubMix significantly improves synthetic data generation quality compared to domain-agnostic privacy mechanisms.

paragraphs: Differentially private synthetic data generation must balance privacy with fidelity to the original distribution. Public data can help, but existing approaches typically use it around the privacy mechanism, such as through a pre-trained generator or subsequent statistical matching. This paper studies how public information can instead enter the privacy mechanism itself.

The theoretical framework uses normalized histograms to estimate distributions. Within a specified class of differentially private mechanisms, the authors characterize the asymptotically optimal mechanism that accounts for the data domain. This is a scoped optimality result: it concerns that mechanism class and asymptotic setting, rather than every possible approach to private synthetic data.

The authors introduce PubMix, a mechanism that incorporates public data and can be used in histogram-based synthesis pipelines. Experiments show significant improvements in synthetic-data quality compared with domain-agnostic privacy mechanisms. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: public information becomes part of the design of the privacy-preserving operation, providing a principled route to better statistical fidelity under privacy constraints.
summary.tldr: PubMix incorporates public information directly into a differential privacy mechanism, improving histogram-based synthetic-data quality within a theoretically studied framework.

title: Optimal Domain-Aware Privacy Mechanisms for Synthetic Data Generation

abstract: Neural simulators promise efficient surrogates for physics simulation, but scaling them is bottlenecked by the prohibitive cost of generating high-fidelity training data. Pre-training on abundant off-the-shelf geometries offers a natural alternative, yet faces a fundamental gap: supervision on static geometry alone ignores dynamics and can lead to negative transfer on physics tasks. We present GeoPT, a unified pre-trained model for general physics simulation based on lifted geometric pre-training. The core idea is to augment geometry with synthetic dynamics, enabling dynamics-aware self-supervision without physics labels. Pre-trained on over one million samples, GeoPT consistently improves industrial-fidelity benchmarks spanning fluid mechanics for cars, aircraft, and ships, and solid mechanics in crash simulation, reducing labeled data requirements by 20-60% and accelerating convergence by 2$\times$. These results show that lifting with synthetic dynamics bridges the geometry-physics gap, unlocking a scalable path for neural simulation and potentially beyond. Code is available at https://github.com/Physics-Scaling/GeoPT.

paragraphs: Neural physics simulators need expensive, high-fidelity training examples, which makes scaling them difficult. Readily available geometric shapes offer a cheaper source of pretraining data, but static shape information does not describe how physical systems evolve. The paper identifies this mismatch as a source of possible negative transfer to simulation tasks.

GeoPT augments geometry with synthetic dynamics before pretraining. This creates self-supervised learning signals that include change and motion without requiring physics labels. The aim is to make pretraining relevant to later simulation, rather than asking a model trained only on static geometry to bridge that gap during supervised adaptation.

Pretrained on more than one million samples, GeoPT consistently improves the reported industrial-fidelity benchmarks. These cover fluid mechanics for cars, aircraft, and ships, as well as solid mechanics in crash simulation. The authors report 20–60% lower labeled-data requirements and twice-as-fast convergence. These findings support synthetic dynamics as a useful bridge between abundant geometric data and costly physics supervision across the tested applications.
summary.tldr: GeoPT adds synthetic dynamics to geometric pretraining data, reducing physics-label requirements and accelerating convergence on simulation benchmarks.

title: GeoPT: Scaling Physics Simulation via Lifted Geometric Pre-Training

abstract: Modern decision-making increasingly relies on contextual features (covariates) to improve optimization under uncertainty. In practice, however, such covariates are often only partially observed due to, e.g., data source heterogeneity or costly data collection. Nonetheless, most existing methods assume fully observed historical data and can become unreliable when this assumption is violated. We address this gap by proposing a distributionally robust optimization approach that exploits incomplete covariates to produce robust decisions without imputing a complete dataset. Our method builds ambiguity sets from the observed partial data and incorporates the general structure of the missingness mechanism, ensuring candidate distributions remain consistent with what is observed. Across settings with discrete or continuous covariates and outcomes, we derive tractable reformulations and establish finite-sample out-of-sample performance guarantees. Empirical results across a range of contextual decision-making tasks demonstrate that the proposed integrated approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including various impute-then-optimize pipelines, in both out-of-sample performance and reliability.

paragraphs: Contextual optimization uses features about a situation to choose actions under uncertainty. In practice, historical features may be incomplete because data sources differ or collection is costly. This paper develops a decision-making method that works directly with those partial observations instead of first filling in a complete dataset.

The approach builds ambiguity sets: collections of candidate distributions compatible with the available evidence. It incorporates the general structure of how values become missing, keeping candidate distributions consistent with what was observed. Decisions are then chosen through distributionally robust optimization, so uncertainty from incomplete information enters the decision problem itself.

For settings with discrete or continuous features and outcomes, the authors derive tractable reformulations and finite-sample guarantees for performance on new data. Experiments report better out-of-sample performance and reliability than leading baselines, including impute-then-optimize approaches. The findings support integrating missing-data uncertainty into optimization rather than resolving it entirely in a separate preprocessing step before making decisions.
summary.tldr: The method makes robust contextual decisions directly from incomplete features by optimizing over distributions consistent with observed data and missingness structure.

title: Robust Contextual Optimization with Missing Covariates

abstract: World models enable learning policies via latent imagination, offering benefits such as history compression and sample efficiency. The primary challenge in applying world models to multi-agent tasks is that modeling multi-agent dynamics in latent space requires integrating information from different agents, often creating spurious correlations between their latent states. Existing methods either reconstruct the observation for each agent or employ communication to maintain correlation during execution, failing to learn disentangled latent states that are crucial for effective decentralized control. To address this, we present the Disentangled Multi-Agent World Model (DMAWM). It facilitates learning decentralized policies in the latent space through a novel architecture comprising independent agent modules and a shared environment module. During real-environment execution, agent modules independently process local information to form a factorized latent representation. The environment module is then trained to mirror the factorized structure generated by the agent modules, effectively disentangling individual latent states from the interaction dynamics. Consequently, imaginary rollouts generated by the environment module more faithfully simulate decentralized execution dynamics, facilitating the transfer of policies from imagination to decentralized execution. Empirically, DMAWM outperforms existing model-based and model-free approaches in convergence speed and final performance, with additional visualization demonstrating its efficacy in capturing agent interactions.

paragraphs: World models let agents learn from imagined trajectories, but multi-agent imagination must represent interactions without creating misleading dependencies between agents' internal states. This is particularly important for decentralized execution, where each agent acts using local information. The paper argues that existing approaches do not adequately separate individual latent states from interaction dynamics.

DMAWM divides the model into independent agent modules and a shared environment module. During real execution, each agent module forms its own latent representation from local information. The environment module is trained to reproduce this factorized structure while modeling interactions. As a result, imagined trajectories more closely reflect how information is actually available to the agents during decentralized operation.

This alignment is intended to make policies learned through imagination transfer more effectively to real-environment execution. Empirically, DMAWM achieves faster convergence and better final performance than the evaluated model-based and model-free methods. Visualizations also support its ability to capture agent interactions. The contribution connects representation structure directly to the information constraints of decentralized control.
summary.tldr: DMAWM separates individual agent representations from shared interaction dynamics to improve learning and transfer for decentralized control.

title: Learning Disentangled Multi-Agent World Model for Decentralized Control

abstract: Existing methods for expressive music performance rendering rely on supervised learning over small labeled datasets, which limits scaling of both data volume and model size, despite the availability of vast unlabeled music, as in vision and language. To address this gap, we introduce Pianist Transformer, with three key contributions: 1) introducing large-scale self-supervised learning into expressive piano performance rendering through a unified Musical Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI) representation, enabling pre-training on 10B tokens of unlabeled MIDI data; 2) an efficient asymmetric Transformer with note-level compression, substantially improving training efficiency, memory usage, and inference speed for long-context music modeling; 3) a state-of-the-art rendering model with an editable workflow, achieving strong objective and subjective results and enabling integration into real-world music production workflows. Overall, Pianist Transformer outlines a scalable path toward human-like performance synthesis in the music domain. Code, audio samples, and model checkpoints are available on our project page: https://yhj137.github.io/pianist-transformer-demo/.

paragraphs: Expressive piano rendering has largely depended on supervised learning from small labeled datasets. That limits how much training data and model capacity existing approaches can use, despite the availability of substantial unlabeled music. Pianist Transformer introduces large-scale self-supervised pretraining to expand the data available for learning expressive performance.

A unified MIDI representation enables pretraining on 10 billion tokens of unlabeled MIDI data. The architecture uses an asymmetric transformer with compression at the note level to make long-context music modeling more efficient. The authors report substantial improvements in training efficiency, memory usage, and inference speed, addressing the computational demands that accompany larger-scale learning.

The resulting rendering model achieves state-of-the-art performance with strong objective and subjective evaluation results. It also provides an editable workflow intended for integration into practical music production. These contributions connect scalable learning with both computational efficiency and user control. The paper presents this combination as a path toward more human-like synthesized performances, supported by the reported rendering results.
summary.tldr: Pianist Transformer uses large-scale self-supervised MIDI pretraining and note-level compression to improve expressive piano rendering with an editable workflow.

title: Pianist Transformer: Towards Expressive Piano Performance Rendering via Scalable Self-Supervised Pre-Training

abstract: Building scalable and reusable multi-agent decision policies from offline datasets remains a challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), as existing methods often rely on fixed observation formats and action spaces that limit generalization. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer a flexible modeling interface that can naturally accommodate heterogeneous observations and actions. Motivated by this, we propose the Decision Language Model (DLM), which formulates multi-agent decision making as a dialogue-style sequence prediction problem under the centralized training with decentralized execution paradigm. DLM is trained in two stages: a supervised fine-tuning phase, which leverages dialogue-style datasets for centralized training with inter-agent context and generates executable actions from offline trajectories, followed by a group relative policy optimization phase to enhance robustness to out-of-distribution actions through lightweight reward functions. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that a unified DLM outperforms strong offline MARL baselines and LLM-based conversational decision-making methods, while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to unseen scenarios across tasks.

paragraphs: Learning reusable multi-agent policies from recorded trajectories is difficult when methods expect fixed observation formats and action spaces. The Decision Language Model uses a language-model interface to accommodate heterogeneous observations and actions. It represents sequential decisions as dialogue-style sequence prediction, making one model applicable across different multi-agent decision settings.

Training follows a centralized-training, decentralized-execution setup. First, supervised fine-tuning uses dialogue-style datasets that include context from multiple agents and teaches the model to produce executable actions from offline trajectories. A second stage applies group relative policy optimization with lightweight reward functions to improve robustness to actions outside the training distribution.

Across multiple benchmarks, a unified DLM outperforms strong offline multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines and conversational decision methods built around language models. It also demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to unseen scenarios across tasks. These findings support the use of a shared language-based decision interface, together with staged training, as a way to build policies that transfer beyond a single fixed observation and action format.
summary.tldr: DLM learns multi-agent decisions as dialogue-style prediction, enabling a unified policy to handle varied observations, actions, and unseen scenarios.

title: DLM: Unified Decision Language Model for Offline Multi-Agent Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Existing human attention (saliency) modeling methods persist as highly fragmented across modalities, scenes, and task formulations. Consequently, even with increasing model capacity and data scale, current models predominantly remain scene-dependent and task-specific, failing to practically generalize in real-world applications. To address the fundamental limitations, we present the Attend to Anything Model (AAM), a multi-modal foundation model that unifies attention modeling across various image, video, and audio-visual tasks and scenes. AAM reformulates attention as a cognitive entailment relationship organized in a general-to-specific hierarchy, implemented through language prompts with hierarchical embeddings in hyperbolic space. Furthermore, to unify static image and dynamic video attention, we adopt a fluid-dynamics perspective, formulating video-frame attention as a diffusive temporal evolution governed by the Fokker–Planck equation. Extensive experiments on 16 benchmarks demonstrate that AAM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6% across various scenarios, while achieving approximately a 4$\times$ speedup in video inference. Overall, these results demonstrate that AAM provides a principled foundation for future research on attention and saliency-related tasks. The dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/wz-zhao/Attend-to-Anything.

paragraphs: Human attention modeling predicts which parts of sensory content attract attention. Existing approaches are often specialized for particular scenes, modalities, or task definitions, making broader application difficult. The Attend to Anything Model, or AAM, brings image, video, and audiovisual attention tasks into a shared multimodal framework.

AAM organizes attention through a hierarchy from general concepts to specific ones. Language prompts express these relationships, and hierarchical embeddings in hyperbolic space represent their structure. To connect still images with changing video, the model also treats attention across frames as a process that evolves over time. This evolution is formulated using the Fokker–Planck equation from a fluid-dynamics perspective.

These choices address both differences between attention tasks and the temporal behavior of attention in video. Across 16 benchmarks, the paper reports an average improvement of 6% over state-of-the-art methods and approximately fourfold faster video inference. The results support a shared modeling approach across the evaluated scenarios, combining a common representation of attention with an explicit account of how it changes over time.
summary.tldr: AAM unifies image, video, and audiovisual attention modeling through hierarchical language representations and temporal diffusion.

title: Attend to Anything: Foundation Model for Unified Human Attention Modeling

abstract: The scaling of large language models (LLMs) is currently bottlenecked by the rigidity of distributed programming. While high-performance libraries like CuBLAS and NCCL provide optimized primitives, they lack the flexibility required for rapidly evolving model architectures. Conversely, existing tensor compilers fail to address the complex memory hierarchy of distributed clusters effectively. To bridge this gap, we propose DITRON, a scalable tile-level compiler that democratizes high-performance distributed kernel development. DITRON introduces a novel hierarchical programming abstraction spanning Core, Device, and Task levels to map tensor programs efficiently onto heterogeneous distributed hardware. This abstraction allows DITRON to support diverse parallelism strategies while abstracting away the complexity of inter-node and intra-node communication. Evaluated across large-scale clusters, DITRON achieves performance parity with or exceeding expert-tuned CUDA libraries, delivering speedups of 6%–30% on isolated kernels and 5%–30% on end-to-end inference in vLLM. Furthermore, DITRON demonstrates strong portability, achieving significant speedups on both NVIDIA and AMD platforms.

paragraphs: Distributed language-model computation needs both fast operations and flexibility as model architectures change. title: DITRON: Distributed Multi-level Tiling Compiler for Parallel Tensor Programs

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have catalyzed vibe coding, where users leverage LLMs to generate and iteratively refine code through natural language interactions until it passes their vibe check. Vibe check reflects human preference and goes beyond functionality: the solution should feel right, read cleanly, preserve intent, and remain correct. However, current code evaluation remains anchored to pass@k and captures only functional correctness, overlooking non-functional instructions that users routinely apply. In this paper, we hypothesize that instruction following is the missing piece underlying vibe check besides functional correctness. To quantify models’ code instruction-following capabilities with measurable signals, we present VeriCode, a taxonomy of 30 verifiable code instructions together with deterministic verifiers. We use the taxonomy to augment established evaluation suites, resulting in SWE-IF, a testbed to assess both instruction following and functional correctness. Evaluating 31 LLMs, we show that even the strongest models struggle to comply with multiple instructions and exhibit functional regression. Most importantly, a composite score of functional correctness and instruction following correlates best with human preference, with instruction following emerging as the primary differentiator among LLMs. Our code, data, and taxonomy are available at https://github.com/maszhongming/SWE-IF.

paragraphs: Code can pass functional tests while failing to satisfy what a user requested about how the solution should be written. This paper hypothesizes that instruction following helps explain human preferences beyond correctness alone. It investigates that idea by making non-functional code instructions measurable rather than relying only on whether generated programs work.

The researchers introduce VeriCode, a taxonomy of 30 verifiable code instructions paired with deterministic checkers. They use it to augment established evaluation suites, creating SWE-IF. The resulting testbed assesses functional correctness and instruction compliance together, making it possible to examine whether satisfying additional requests comes at the expense of working code.

The findings support broader code evaluation that measures both what the program does and how faithfully it follows the user's requirements.
summary.tldr: SWE-IF evaluates code instruction following alongside correctness, producing a combined measure that better correlates with human preference.

title: SWE-IF: Aligning Code Evaluation with Human Preference

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a de facto paradigm for building LLM-based agents that act, interact, and reason over extended task horizons. However, in active reasoning where agents must elicit new observations through interaction with the environment to solve the task, we find that outcome-based RL can induce a systematic failure mode which we call information self-locking (SeL): agents fail both to elicit informative feedback and to internalize obtained evidence. To understand the issue, we trace agentic behaviors into two coupled capabilities: Action Selection (AS), which determines observation streams, and Belief Tracking (BT), which updates the agent’s internal task understanding. Theoretical and empirical analyses reveal a bidirectional bottleneck that leads to SeL: weak BT obscures the credit of informative actions, while weak AS deprives BT of useful evidence. This coupling weakens the learning signal for both capabilities and leads to SeL. To mitigate this issue, we propose AREW, a simple yet effective Advantage Reweighting method that uses easy-to-obtain directional critiques to reallocate credit within trajectories. Extensive experiments across 9 agentic tasks of varying complexity show that AREW significantly mitigates SeL, yielding up to 60-point gains in final performance. Code is available at https://github.com/unimpor/T3.

paragraphs: Agents solving interactive tasks must both seek useful observations and incorporate what they learn. This paper identifies a failure mode in outcome-based reinforcement learning called information self-locking. An agent can become poor at gathering informative feedback and poor at using evidence it already receives, leaving both abilities difficult to improve.

The analysis separates action selection, which determines the observations available, from belief tracking, which updates the agent’s understanding. The two capabilities create a bidirectional bottleneck: weak belief tracking hides the value of informative actions, while weak action selection withholds useful evidence from belief tracking. Theoretical and empirical analyses connect this coupling to weakened learning signals.

The proposed Advantage Reweighting method, AREW, uses readily obtainable directional critiques to redistribute credit within trajectories. This changes how learning rewards are attributed across the interaction, aiming to weaken the bottleneck between gathering and using information. Across nine agentic tasks of varying complexity, the paper reports substantial mitigation of self-locking and gains of up to 60 points in final performance.
summary.tldr: AREW reassigns credit within agent trajectories to mitigate a feedback loop between weak information gathering and weak belief updating.

abstract: Supervised clustering is the problem of training a clustering algorithm to produce desirable clusterings: given sets of items and complete clusterings over these sets, we learn how to cluster future sets of items. Example applications include noun-phrase coreference clustering, and clustering news articles by whether they refer to the same topic. In this paper we present an SVM algorithm that trains a clustering algorithm by adapting the item-pair similarity measure. The algorithm may optimize a variety of different clustering functions to a variety of clustering performance measures. We empirically evaluate the algorithm for noun-phrase and news article clustering.

paragraphs: The paper studies supervised clustering: learning how to group future sets of items from examples of complete clusterings. The training information describes how entire sets should be partitioned. Applications include grouping noun phrases that refer to the same entity and grouping news articles that concern the same topic.

The proposed support-vector-machine algorithm trains a clustering procedure by adapting its measure of similarity between pairs of items. This makes the pairwise similarity a learned component of the overall grouping process. The approach can optimize a variety of clustering functions against a variety of clustering performance measures, allowing training to reflect different definitions of a desirable clustering.

The authors evaluate the algorithm empirically on noun-phrase clustering and news-article clustering. These applications connect the training formulation to two stated uses of supervised grouping. The central contribution is a way to learn the similarity measure from complete clustering examples while accommodating different clustering procedures and evaluation objectives within the proposed SVM-based approach.
summary.tldr: An SVM learns pairwise similarity from example clusterings to train clustering algorithms for future item sets.

title: Supervised clustering with support vector machines

abstract: This paper describes the use of machine learning to improve the performance of natural language question answering systems. We present a model for improving story comprehension through inductive generalization and reinforcement learning, based on classified examples. In the process, the model selects the most relevant and useful pieces of lexical information to be used by the inference procedure. We compare our approach to three prior non-learning systems, and evaluate the conditions under which learning is effective. We demonstrate that a learning-based approach can improve upon “matching and extraction”only techniques.

We compare our approach to three prior non-learning systems, and evaluate the conditions under which learning is effective. We demonstrate that a learning-based approach can improve upon “matching and extraction”only techniques.

paragraphs: Answering questions about a story can involve deciding which pieces of language knowledge are useful for drawing an answer. This paper presents a learning model intended to improve that process. It combines inductive generalization and reinforcement learning, using classified examples to support better story comprehension in a natural-language question-answering system.

The model selects relevant lexical information for use by an inference procedure. This makes the choice of information part of what the system learns. The approach therefore links learning to the reasoning process: improvements can come from identifying which available pieces of lexical knowledge are most useful for answering the question.

The authors compare their approach with three earlier systems that do not learn and examine the conditions under which learning helps. They demonstrate that a learning-based approach can outperform techniques limited to matching and extraction. The significance is evidence that learned information selection and inference can improve question answering, with effectiveness examined as dependent on conditions rather than assumed universally.
summary.tldr: A story question-answering model learns which lexical information to use for inference and can improve on matching-and-extraction techniques.

title: Learning strategies for story comprehension: a reinforcement learning approach

abstract: Comparative evaluation of Machine Learning (ML) systems used for Information Extraction (IE) has suffered from various inconsistencies in experimental procedures. This paper reports on the results of the Pascal Challenge on Evaluating Machine Learning for Information Extraction, which provides a standardised corpus, set of tasks, and evaluation methodology. The challenge is described and the systems submitted by the ten participants are briefly introduced and their performance is analysed.
originalAbstract: Comparative evaluation of Machine Learning (ML) systems used for Information Extraction (IE) has suffered from various inconsistencies in experimental procedures. This paper reports on the results of the Pascal Challenge on Evaluating Machine Learning for Information Extraction, which provides a standardised corpus, set of tasks, and evaluation methodology. The challenge is described and the systems submitted by the ten participants are briefly introduced and their performance is analysed.

paragraphs: Comparing information extraction systems becomes difficult when their experimental procedures differ. A reported performance difference can be hard to interpret if systems were evaluated on different material or under different rules. This paper addresses that evaluation problem through a report on the Pascal Challenge for machine learning in information extraction.

The challenge supplies a standardized corpus, a common set of tasks, and a shared evaluation methodology. These three pieces establish what the systems process, what they are asked to do, and how their outputs are assessed. Bringing them together provides a consistent setting for examining the submitted systems.

The paper describes the challenge, briefly introduces submissions from ten participants, and analyzes their performance. Its contribution is therefore an organized comparative evaluation rather than a new extraction algorithm. The resulting comparisons are grounded in shared experimental conditions, directly addressing the inconsistencies identified by the authors and providing a basis for understanding the participating systems' results within the challenge.
summary.tldr: The Pascal Challenge standardizes data, tasks, and evaluation to compare ten machine-learning systems for information extraction.

title: Evaluating machine learning for information extraction

abstract: We present an intuitive scheme for lossy color-image compression: Use the color information from a few representative pixels to learn a model which predicts color on the rest of the pixels. Now, storing the representative pixels and the image in grayscale suffice to recover the original image. A similar scheme is also applicable for compressing videos, where a single model can be used to predict color on many consecutive frames, leading to better compression. Existing algorithms for colorization – the process of adding color to a grayscale image or video sequence – are tedious, and require intensive human-intervention. We bypass these limitations by using a graph-based inductive semi-supervised learning module for colorization, and a simple active learning strategy to choose the representative pixels. Experiments on a wide variety of images and video sequences demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper treats color prediction as a tool for lossy compression. It learns a model from the colors of a few representative pixels and uses that model to predict colors elsewhere. The stored representation contains the grayscale image and the representative pixels, supplying the information used to reconstruct a color version of the image.

The colorization component uses graph-based inductive semi-supervised learning. A simple active learning strategy chooses the representative pixels that provide color information. These components address the intensive human involvement required by existing colorization approaches, making the selection of color examples and the prediction of remaining colors part of the proposed compression scheme.

For video, a single model can predict color across many consecutive frames, leading to better compression through reuse of that model. Experiments on a wide variety of images and video sequences demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. Because the scheme is explicitly lossy, reconstruction means recovering a predicted color image or video rather than guaranteeing an exact copy of every original color value.
summary.tldr: The method compresses images and videos by storing grayscale content and selected pixel colors, then learning to reconstruct the remaining colors.

title: Learning to compress images and videos

abstract: Abstraction of complex, longer motor tasks into simpler elemental movements enables humans and animals to exhibit motor skills which have not yet been matched by robots. Humans intuitively decompose complex motions into smaller, simpler segments. For example when describing simple movements like drawing a triangle with a pen, we can easily name the basic steps of this movement. Surprisingly, such abstractions have rarely been used in artificial motor skill learning algorithms. These algorithms typically choose a new action (such as a torque or a force) at a very fast time-scale. As a result, both policy and temporal credit assignment problem become unnecessarily complex - often beyond the reach of current machine learning methods. We introduce a new framework for temporal abstractions in reinforcement learning (RL), i.e. RL with motion templates. We present a new algorithm for this framework which can learn high-quality policies by making only few abstract decisions.

paragraphs: Complex movements can often be described as sequences of simpler movements. Drawing a triangle, for example, has recognizable component steps. This paper uses that observation to motivate temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning for motor skills: a learner can make decisions about motion templates that represent more extended pieces of behavior.

The authors argue that selecting forces or torques at a very fast timescale makes learning unnecessarily difficult. It complicates both the policy and temporal credit assignment, the problem of determining which earlier decisions contributed to an outcome. Organizing behavior around simpler motion templates changes the scale at which those decisions are made.

The paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework built around these templates and presents an algorithm that can learn high-quality policies using only a few abstract decisions. The stated benefit is a reduction in decision complexity through meaningful movement units. This connects the decomposition of a long motor task with a learning procedure that sequences its simpler components.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning framework sequences motion templates to learn high-quality motor policies with few abstract decisions.

title: Learning complex motions by sequencing simpler motion templates

abstract: We propose a general and efficient algorithm for learning low-rank matrices. The proposed algorithm converges super-linearly and can keep the matrix to be learned in a compact factorized representation without the need of specifying the rank beforehand. Moreover, we show that the framework can be easily generalized to the problem of learning multiple matrices and general spectral regularization. Empirically we show that we can recover a 10,000x10,000 matrix from 1.2 million observations in about 5 minutes. Furthermore, we show that in a brain-computer interface problem, the proposed method can speed-up the optimization by two orders of magnitude against the conventional projected gradient method and produces more reliable solutions.

This paper introduces an augmented Lagrangian algorithm that retains such a compact representation during learning. It does so without requiring the matrix rank to be specified beforehand, combining a flexible representation with an efficient optimization procedure.

The authors report superlinear convergence, describing how rapidly the algorithm approaches its solution. They also show that the framework extends to learning several matrices and to general spectral regularization, which controls properties associated with a matrix's spectrum. The contribution therefore includes both a particular solver and a framework that accommodates related matrix-learning objectives.

The empirical examples make the computational claims concrete. The method recovers a 10,000-by-10,000 matrix from 1.2 million observations in about five minutes. In a brain-computer interface problem, it accelerates optimization by two orders of magnitude relative to conventional projected gradient and produces more reliable solutions. These are reported outcomes for the studied problems, illustrating the practical value of combining compact storage with fast optimization.
summary.tldr: A fast low-rank matrix-learning algorithm maintains compact factors without a preset rank and shows substantial computational gains.

title: A Fast Augmented Lagrangian Algorithm for Learning Low-Rank Matrices

abstract: We study an interesting and challenging problem, online streaming feature selection, in which the size of the feature set is unknown, and not all features are available for learning while leaving the number of observations constant. In this problem, the candidate features arrive one at a time, and the learner's task is to select a �best so far� set of features from streaming features. Standard feature selection methods cannot perform well in this scenario. Thus, we present a novel framework based on feature relevance. Under this framework, a promising alternative method, Online Streaming Feature Selection (OSFS), is presented to online select strongly relevant and non-redundant features. In addition to OSFS, a faster Fast-OSFS algorithm is proposed to further improve the selection efficiency. Experimental results show that our algorithms achieve more compactness and better accuracy than existing streaming feature selection algorithms on various datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learning setting in which the observations stay fixed while new candidate features arrive one at a time. The final number of features is unknown, and the learner cannot access all of them at the start. Its task is to maintain the best feature set found so far as the stream develops.

The authors introduce a framework based on feature relevance and an algorithm called Online Streaming Feature Selection, or OSFS. It selects strongly relevant features while avoiding redundancy, addressing both whether a feature is useful and whether its information is already represented. A second algorithm, Fast-OSFS, is designed to improve selection efficiency further.

Experiments across various datasets show that the proposed algorithms produce more compact feature sets and better accuracy than existing streaming feature-selection algorithms. The combination matters because a smaller set alone would not establish that the selection preserved useful predictive information. The work directly addresses the practical consequences of receiving features progressively rather than assuming a complete feature space is available before learning begins.
summary.tldr: OSFS and Fast-OSFS select relevant, nonredundant features as features arrive, with improved compactness and accuracy in experiments.

title: Online Streaming Feature Selection

abstract: Numerous applications in statistics, signal processing, and machine learning regularize using Total Variation (TV) penalties. We study anisotropic (l1-based) TV and also a related l2-norm variant. We consider for both variants associated (1D) proximity operators, which lead to challenging optimization problems. We solve these problems by developing Newton-type methods that outperform the state-of-the-art algorithms. More importantly, our 1D-TV algorithms serve as building blocks for solving the harder task of computing 2- (and higher)-dimensional TV proximity. We illustrate the computational benefits of our methods by applying them to several applications: (i) image denoising; (ii) image deconvolution (by plugging in our TV solvers into publicly available software); and (iii) four variants of fused-lasso. The results show large speedups--and to support our claims, we provide software accompanying this paper.

paragraphs: Total variation penalties appear in statistics, signal processing, and machine learning, making their computational cost relevant to many applications. This paper studies anisotropic total variation based on the l1 norm and a related l2-norm variant. For both, it focuses on the optimization problems defining their one-dimensional proximity operators.

The authors develop Newton-type methods for these problems and report that they outperform state-of-the-art algorithms. The one-dimensional solvers also serve as building blocks for computing total variation proximity in two and higher dimensions. This connection matters because improvements to a basic optimization component can support the more difficult multidimensional computation.

The paper demonstrates computational benefits in image denoising, image deconvolution, and four fused-lasso variants. For deconvolution, the authors integrate their solvers into publicly available software, showing how the component fits into an existing application. The reported results show large speedups, and accompanying software supports those claims. The contribution centers on faster optimization routines and their use across several total-variation applications.
summary.tldr: Newton-type total-variation solvers accelerate one-dimensional proximity computations and support faster multidimensional applications.

title: Fast Newton-type Methods for Total Variation Regularization

abstract: This paper re-visits the spectral method for learning latent variable models defined in terms of observable operators. We give a new perspective on the method, showing that operators can be recovered by minimizing a loss defined on a finite subspace of the domain. A non-convex optimization similar to the spectral method is derived. We also propose a regularized convex relaxation of this optimization. We show that in practice the availabilty of a continuous regularization parameter (in contrast with the discrete number of states in the original method) allows a better trade-off between accuracy and model complexity. We also prove that in general, a randomized strategy for choosing the local loss will succeed with high probability. Its central finding is that these operators can be recovered by minimizing a loss defined on a finite subspace of the domain. This gives spectral learning an optimization interpretation and makes the choice of a local loss part of the learning procedure.

From this perspective, the authors derive a non-convex optimization resembling the spectral method and propose a regularized convex relaxation. The relaxation introduces a continuous regularization parameter. This supplies a smoother way to adjust model complexity than choosing the discrete number of states used by the original method, creating another means of balancing fit and complexity.

In practice, the continuous control is shown to yield a better accuracy–complexity trade-off. The paper also proves that a randomized strategy for choosing the local loss succeeds with high probability in general. Together, these results connect an alternative formulation of spectral learning with both a practical model-selection advantage and a probabilistic guarantee for constructing the local objective.
summary.tldr: An optimization view of spectral learning yields a regularized convex alternative with finer control over model complexity.
